It runs along the covered level above the step, racked in salvaged trays and repurposed containers, with the commonly used items at hand height and everything else somewhere that requires a ladder and an explanation. Customers are served from it directly, usually while being told more than they asked about what the part is for. Neighbours come for a single fastener and are not charged for it. Running out of a common fastener here is treated as a family failure rather than a supply problem.

Test Wall.description: A braced wall panel used to load-test joins, seals and structural assemblies before they go into somebody's home. It stands at the Stack's base where the process is visible from the lane, fitted with load frames and a gauge that is checked against a second gauge because Hana does not trust a single reading. It is scarred, patched and honest, carrying the record of every assembly that failed on it. Customers are invited to watch, and children from the lane gather whenever something is being taken to destruction. Hana will fail her own work on it in front of a paying customer rather than ship a join she does not trust.

Shared Family Rooms.description: The Pelorr family's living space through the Stack, including the upper residential portion the household simply calls upstairs. Rooms are fitted out between the working levels rather than set apart from them, personalised with paint, fabric and salvaged furniture, and every one of them has material stored in it that is supposedly about to be used. Meals, arguments and the children's homework happen among stacked material. Neighbours' children are as likely to be in here as their own, since the Rows share childcare across whoever is home. Living inside the business means a customer's emergency and a family evening occupy the same floor.

Rooftop Material Rack.description: A roof rack of plate, beam stock and salvaged structural material, weighted down against the wind and slowly deteriorating in the sun. It is the highest thing on the Stack apart from the collectors, lashed and braced and re-lashed after every bad stretch of weather, with the good material buried under the material nobody wants and a tarp over the part that must not get wet. It represents most of the family's working capital, held as stock because stock is more reliable than supply. Sorting it is a job that gets started and abandoned repeatedly. Neighbours borrow from it and return less than they took, which is an ongoing and affectionate grievance.

Collapsed Prototype Corner.description: The corner where Velan's failed structural prototype came down and was never fully cleared, now half storage and half monument. Twisted frame members lie where they fell, with crates and offcuts stacked into the gaps around them, and the whole thing has weathered to the same colour as the ground so that newcomers walk past it without registering what it is. He explains what went wrong to anyone who asks and to several people who do not, using the actual pieces and improving the account considerably over the years. Apprentices from across the district get walked through it as a lesson. Hana has stopped suggesting they remove it.

Frontier Care House.name: Frontier Care House
Frontier Care House.basicInfo: The Frontier Care House is Dustfall's medical and civilian support location, set apart from the bars and the repair district. It is a low building of cargo modules and old stone with reinforced glass along one side, sealed harder than anything else in the settlement because dust and clinical work do not mix, and lit evenly by good lamps rather than by the hard daylight outside. It handles treatment, recovery, trauma care and refugee assistance with no major-house institution behind it, surviving because people keep bringing supplies, labour and patients. The equipment is advanced and maintained by people who have no manufacturer to call, so what runs short is stock and consumables rather than capability. Ordinary work fills most days: a child's fever, a crushed hand out of a salvage yard, a pregnancy followed through, an elderly resident whose systems failed and who came in cold. Emergency work prioritises stabilisation, care follows clinical need rather than standing or payment, and nothing anyone did before they walked in changes what happens next. It is practical, compassionate, exhausted and under-supplied.
Frontier Care House.hiddenInfo: The current supply failure has forced rationing, which means the staff are making explicit decisions about limited medicine in front of the people affected. Eyla Marris works here quietly despite living inside the Black Pennant's compound, and Maela Drin covers what the Last Line Company can spare; neither arrangement is formal and both would collapse under scrutiny. Patients arrive who are being pursued, and staff regularly identify restraint damage on people who have not said where they came from. Emergency work prioritises stabilisation; onward referral follows clinical need and patient choice where feasible, with receiving capacity and safe transport confirmed, and no automatic Vexorath referral or transfer of patient control to a House follows from needing advanced care. The house's hardest recurring conflict is between gang loyalty and patient protection, since treating someone does not oblige the staff to surrender them and refusing to surrender them has consequences the building cannot absorb. Medical supply theft here is among the few acts that reliably ends a person's welcome in Dustfall.

Main Treatment Room.description: The central clinical space: adjustable supports, maintained monitoring equipment and clean storage, all of it visibly repaired and visibly cared for. Surfaces are sealed, the floor is washable, the air handling runs constantly and the whole room is kept to a standard the rest of the settlement could not manage. Stabilisation happens here regardless of who the patient is or who is asking about them, and a person who carried someone in does not thereby speak for them. Volunteers are put to work at the edges, fetching, holding, keeping a frightened family informed. The lighting is the best in the building, which is itself a statement of priorities.

Modification Injury Bench.description: A specialised bench for injuries caused by equipment modification, unsafe prototypes and the Refit Row interpretation of safety standards. It stands apart from the main room, fitted with extraction, restraint-free supports and tooling for getting damaged equipment off a person before anything else can be done. Halvora Orvantis is called in for the dangerous ones, since removing a failed modification is as much a technical problem as a clinical one. The bench sees burns, embedded fragments, crush injuries and the results of a dampener letting go. Advanced biology does not remove pain, contamination risk or the consequences of a bad weld against skin.

Recovery Cots.description: A row of cots behind partitions where patients stay through the days after treatment, watched by whoever is on shift. The partitions are fabric on salvaged frames, the cots themselves are good, the bedding is clean, and families bring in food, objects and noise that nobody has the heart to prohibit. Somebody is usually reading aloud. Recovery here is ordinary and slow: people sit up, complain about the food, argue about when they can leave and are told they cannot, and a neighbour drops in because the walk is short. Children are kept where a parent can be with them. The cots are the reason the house counts as care rather than first aid, and they are the first thing occupied during any emergency.

Quiet Consultation Room.description: A screened room for conversations about prognosis, choice and what the house cannot do. It holds chairs rather than a treatment surface, a water jug, good sealing against the noise of the rest of the building, and a door that shuts. Patients decide who else hears, and are asked rather than assumed at. Onward referral is discussed here according to clinical need and the patient's own choice where feasible, with receiving capacity and safe transport confirmed before anything is promised. A transport sponsor does not become a patient's spokesperson here, a rule stated plainly to people who assume otherwise and repeated to those who argue.

Medical Supply Locker.description: The secured store of medicine, sterile stock and consumables, currently rationed and counted daily. It is a plated room with a good lock and climate control that is maintained ahead of almost everything else in the building, shelved and labelled, with the counts kept where the staff can all see them. Stock arrives from Grit and Supply, from what crews bring in and from what other households can spare, which means the shelves are deep in one thing and empty of another. Withdrawals are logged by name. During shortage the locker is where the house's ethics stop being abstract and become a list of who gets what this week.

Refugee Intake Corner.description: A corner near the ground entrance where people arriving from Quilrath are assessed, given water and asked only what treatment requires. There are benches, a screen that can be drawn across, shade from the entrance glare and space for someone to sit down with a child still in their arms. Names and contacts come later, if at all, and no outside classification changes the order of care. Staff do not ask where a person came from, and the ones who volunteer it are listened to without being written down. Restraint injuries, untreated infection and exhaustion are the three findings the staff expect before they see the patient.

Prosthetic Repair Table.description: A bench for fitting, adjusting and repairing prosthetics and mobility equipment, with tooling borrowed permanently from Refit Row. It has a good working height, a power feed, a rack of components sorted by compatibility and a chair positioned so the user can see what is being done. Work is done with the user present and consulted, and an adjustment is tested by walking or flying it rather than by measuring it. Children come in for refitting as they grow, which is the most routine and least remarked work the table does. A comfortable fit matters more here than an elegant one, and the staff will argue the point with any technician who disagrees.

Emergency Flight Landing Pad.description: A marked pad at the building's edge for urgent arrivals carried in by flight, with clear ground approach for anyone who cannot fly. The surface is plated and swept, the markings repainted often, and the route from the pad into the treatment room is kept clear of everything including furniture people keep putting there. Brask Hollan brings in the heavy transfers. Arrivals come in carried, supported or under their own power at a stagger, and volunteers meet them at the edge rather than at the door. The pad is lit continuously, which in a settlement this short of power is a deliberate and expensive choice.

Volunteer Treatment Station.description: A station where trained volunteers handle minor wounds, dressings and follow-up so the clinical staff can work. It is a counter and two working positions near the entrance, stocked with the ordinary consumables, with a board of instructions that assumes nothing and is followed exactly. Training happens on the job and continuously, taught by whoever is competent and has ten minutes. The people working it are a cook, a hauler, a shopkeeper, somebody's grandmother, and they are trusted with exactly as much as they have been shown. The volunteer roster is the clearest available list of who in Dustfall will show up for other people without being paid.

The North Routehead.name: The North Routehead
The North Routehead.basicInfo:
The North Routehead is where Dustfall ends and the corridor begins: escort assembly, cargo inspection, route warnings and the last water station before the frontier. It is open ground of hard pale surface and sparse tropical-desert scrub at the settlement's northern edge, built up from salvaged plating, old stone footings and cargo modules, with shade frames doing what they can against the daylight and beacons and work lamps taking over after it. Transport contracts are signed here, bounty crews camp here and the Bent Halo's landing shelf is built beneath it. No authority runs the ground: inspections are operators protecting themselves, warnings are posted by whoever received them, and a warrant issued elsewhere is not automatically recognised. Ordinary traffic fills most of the day, with households booking transport, crews loading household freight and somebody's relatives waiting for an arrival that is late. Beyond this point the route is shared encounter space that neither Dravon nor Ignivex effectively controls and no patrol schedule can be relied on, so departures are prepared thoroughly and farewells are said properly. It is busy, suspicious, mobile and exposed, and it is the final permanent Dustfall location before the corridor.

Work on offer here: Corridor — The Manifest That Lies (ask Saevik Ruun); Corridor — Around the Eastern Mountains (ask Neyra Vey).
The North Routehead.hiddenInfo: This is the final permanent Dustfall location; beyond it the route is shared encounter space that neither Dravon nor Ignivex effectively controls, and no patrol schedule can be relied on. The Claimants camp here with outside warrants and keep raising the question of which authorities Dustfall should recognise — Ravik Rusk currently holds one that Sennra Sol has refused, and a client the Last Line Company walked away from has hired his crew. Miren Tal may be selling route records to Dravon intermediaries, which would explain how an organised interception knew the Corsair shipment's timing. The Crooked Landing beneath the routehead moves refugees, medicine and restricted cargo behind false manifests; damage to it would stop Bent Halo extraction entirely and force Dustfall to decide whether scarce legitimate gate components should repair an illegal smuggling site. Serik Varn runs the most dependable transport out of Cold Wake Transit and is widely believed to have murdered several former partners, at least one to the town's quiet benefit. Passengers have disappeared from otherwise perfect runs.

Route Marker Post.description: The last maintained marker before the corridor, carrying distance notations that stopped being accurate long ago and warnings that have not. It is a welded post of mismatched plate standing where the hard ground gives way to scrub, its upper section repainted by whoever last cared and its lower section left alone on purpose. Crews touch it on the way out, a habit nobody admits is superstition. Departing groups gather at it for the last few minutes, which is where families say goodbye, where a parent gives the same instruction for the fourth time and where somebody always remembers one more thing that should have been loaded. Names are scratched into the base, some of them by people who did not come back.

Escort Assembly Yard.description: An open staging yard where crews, carriers, passengers and escorts form up before departure. It is hard standing with sling frames, shade sheets and a scatter of crates used as furniture, noisy with loading and with the arguments loading produces. Loads are divided by cargo type, terrain, current warnings and passenger needs, and the division is negotiated between operators rather than assigned by anyone. Passengers with children, medical cases and fragile stock all change the plan, and saying so late changes it worse. Escorts are hired and refused in the open. The yard is at its most honest in the last ten minutes before a departure, when everyone finally says what they are actually carrying.

Cargo Inspection Ramp.description: A ramp where loads are checked for weight, balance, seal integrity and whatever the carrier insists on verifying personally. It is a plated incline with a weighing plate set into it, good lighting overhead and a rail along one side to lean loads against. There is no authority conducting inspections, only operators protecting themselves, and the standard varies with who is carrying and how much they trust the shipper. A carrier who signs for a load takes responsibility for what is in it, which is why the checks get thorough and personal. Disagreements about a load's declared contents are settled here or the load does not go.

Hidden Compartment Bench.description: A working bench where concealed spaces are built, checked and defeated, depending on who is paying. It sits under a shade frame in full view of the yard, equipped with cutting, joining and scanning tools, with example panels bolted to the end as demonstration pieces. Crews use it to hide cargo and to find what a previous owner hid, and the same technician will do either job on consecutive mornings. What is concealed ranges from restricted goods to a household's savings to a person who cannot be seen crossing the route. It is entirely open, which visitors find more unsettling than if it were not.

Patrol Notice Board.description: Posted sightings of patrols, skirmishes and hostile movement along the shared route, each entry attributed and dated relative to receipt. It is a glazed panel in a braced housing, angled out of the glare, with a stylus on a cord and space beneath for the entries nobody wants to erase yet. Competing claims affect the route without producing control of it, and ongoing skirmishes prevent regular patrol, so what gets posted is intermittent and often contradictory by nature. Crews read it against what they already know rather than taking it as fact. An old sighting presented as current is the fastest way to lose standing here. The board is contradicted by itself roughly once a week.

Dust Condition Scanner.description: A mounted atmospheric scanner reporting visibility, particulate load and the conditions that decide whether a crew flies, drives or waits. It stands on a braced mast at the yard's edge with its display set at reading height and a shade hood over it, powered off a line somebody maintains without being asked or paid. It is one of the few pieces of equipment here that nobody has tried to modify, which several people mention with more feeling than the subject seems to warrant. Crews check it as the last act before committing to a departure, and a bad reading empties the yard into the shade for an afternoon of waiting and complaint. Its readings are trusted, which in Dustfall is remarkable.

Last Water Station.description: The final potable supply point before the corridor: tanks, a dispensing rack and a hard rule about filling before departure. The tanks are braced and shaded, the rack is plated and repaired, and the treatment gear behind it is maintained by whoever has the competence that week rather than by any operator. Water here comes from local treatment, recycling and purchased delivery like everything else in the settlement, and the station's reliability is a cost and maintenance question rather than a technical one. Arrivals coming the other way reach it exhausted. Nobody is charged for a first container, and that custom has survived every shortage Dustfall has had.

Abandoned Dravon Sign.description: A Dravon route sign left standing at the edge of the yard, its authority markings intact and meaningless. It is a heavy panel on a post, scoured and faded but perfectly legible, and the mark on it proves nothing about who put it there or when, since infrastructure along this route has been reused and re-marked by everyone who ever passed through. Crews use it as a landmark and as a joke, and new arrivals are directed by it before they understand why people smile when they say the name. Somebody has added annotations down one side in paint that has lasted better than the original. Nobody has removed it, which is either indifference or a point being made, depending on who is asked.

Cold Wake Transit.description: Serik Varn's ground transport garage with his plain room above it, running Dustfall's most dependable cargo and passenger service. The garage is a deep plated bay with vehicles maintained to a standard visible from the lane, a parts wall, and a waiting bench by the door with a posted list of what runs and when. Vehicles arrive when promised, prices stay stable and he has never abandoned a paying passenger. Households book him for the things flight cannot carry: furniture, an injured relative, a family moving. He never threatens anyone; he simply remembers who needs transport and who no longer does.

The Crooked Landing.description: The Bent Halo's landing shelf built beneath the routehead, shielded from casual aerial observation by old structural plating. It is a wide cut of hard ground roofed by salvaged plate and the routehead's own footings, lit by work lamps that never reach the edges, with the air cooler down here and the noise from the yard above arriving flat and distorted. Saevik Ruun's crew moves refugees, medicine, restricted cargo and people who cannot use official gates. The shielding is real but bounded and everybody working here knows it; the Landing survives on approach discipline rather than on invisibility. The humanitarian work and the criminal contracts run out of the same dock.

Bent Dock.description: The shelf's main dock, angled under the plating so that nothing on it is visible from above. The surface is plated and kept clear, the approach marked with low lights that can be killed from the dock itself, and the crew's craft sit nose-out because leaving quickly matters more than parking neatly. Craft come in low and fast, and the approach is the crew's principal skill, taught to new members over many attempts in daylight before anyone tries it otherwise. The dock is busiest in the hours either side of a run, when loading, arguing and last-minute reweighing all happen at once. Neyra Vey will explain the landing line to anyone, then compete with them about it.

False Manifest Desk.description: A desk of document work where cargo acquires a plausible history and passengers acquire a plausible reason. It is a well-lit working position with current equipment, reference material and sample documents pinned up as patterns, set where the dock can be watched while the work is done. The forgeries are technically excellent and legally worthless outside the corridor, which is understood and priced accordingly. A passenger is walked through their own cover story until they can hold it, which is the part that actually matters. Brannoc Kest treats a badly built manifest as a personal insult to the crew.

Cargo Sling Bay.description: A bay of slings, nets and lifting frames for moving loads between craft and ground carriers without a crane. The frames are welded salvage anchored into the rock, the slings are inspected before each run by somebody who has watched one fail, and the floor is marked out for where loads may and may not be set down. Everything is rated well below its marking and used well above it, which is a running argument between the crew and anyone who has to sign for the load afterwards. Medicine, structural stock, personal belongings and things nobody names all cross the same bay under the same hands. The bay is where a load's real weight finally becomes undeniable.

Refugee Bench.description: A shielded bench where people waiting for extraction sit out the hours before a run. It is a long welded bench against the rock under a panel that keeps the light and the noise off, with water, a container of preserved food and space for people to lie down if the wait runs long. Water, shade and no questions. Children sleep through most of it; adults do not. The crew is straight about timings and straight about the risk, and a run can be called off in front of the people it was for. The crew's humanitarian record is real and does not mean the person on the next seat is who they said they were at the desk.

Hidden Fuel Cell Rack.description: A concealed rack of exchangeable fuel cells and charge modules, the crew's most valuable and most stealable asset. It is set back into the rock behind a panel that reads as structure, racked and secured, with the charge state of each unit logged where two people can check it against each other. Stock is rotated constantly so that a single loss is survivable, and cells are drawn and returned by a procedure that gets followed even when everyone is in a hurry, because the one time it was not is still brought up. Nothing here is improvised equipment; it is ordinary current hardware that is simply hard to replace. Saevik buys the legitimate ones openly across a counter at Grit and Supply.

Route Map Wall.description: A wall of route overlays, marked hazards and annotated approaches built up over years of runs. Sheets and panels are layered over one another with the superseded material left visible underneath, marked in several hands and several colours, lit by a lamp on a swinging arm that somebody is always repositioning. It is not a master map of the corridor and does not unmask any cell or safe house, and the crew is deliberate about keeping it that way. Crews argue in front of it before every run, and the argument is the point: ground changes, cover moves and last month's good line is this month's exposure. What it does show is which ground has killed people, and when.

Ysara's Observation Slot.description: Ysara Sorn's narrow observation position looking out along the northern approach, fitted with optics and very little comfort. It is a cut through the plating barely wide enough to work in, with a ledge, a mount for the optics, a water container and a seat that nobody has ever improved and she has never asked anyone to. The daylight along the approach is flat and glaring, and the broken ground out there gives up detail slowly, which is why she is good at this and most people are not. She passes selected warnings to the Unbroken Accord and selects them herself. What she chooses not to pass on is her own business and occasionally somebody else's disaster.

Concealed Departure Cut.description: A shielded cut through the rock and plating by which craft and people leave without crossing the open shelf. It runs as a narrow channel with the plating overhead broken into a pattern that confuses an overhead view, its turns marked by paint visible only from inside and its floor kept swept so that nothing catches a foot in the dark. It is the crew's answer to aerial observation and the reason the Landing still functions. Nothing about it is guaranteed: cover shelters danger as readily as travellers and confers no invisibility, which the crew states plainly to passengers rather than letting them assume otherwise. Using it requires a crew member; the route is not obvious even when described.

Emergency Drop Tunnel.description: A last-resort tunnel dropping away from the shelf toward broken ground, kept clear and rehearsed. It is a plated shaft with hand lines and footholds, its entrance unobstructed by standing order, and its condition checked on a schedule that holds even when everything else on the shelf slips. It is meant for people, not cargo, and the crew is explicit about that priority, to passengers and to clients who would very much prefer otherwise. Waiting families are shown it and walked through it before a run, children included, and the walkthrough is done calmly enough that it reassures rather than frightens. Its existence is one of the few reasons refugees trust a smuggling operation with their families.

Claim Camp.description: The Claimants' transient bounty camp near the routehead: shelters, gear, a warrant board and a ready-launch pad. It is laid out on open ground with everything packable, nothing built into the surface and the shelters oriented against the prevailing wind rather than toward the settlement. They bring outside warrants, money, intelligence and a persistent argument about which authorities Dustfall should recognise. Locals walk through it freely, which the crew tolerates because being watched is cheaper than being resented, and children from the settlement come to look at the equipment until somebody sends them away. The camp is temporary by design and has been here longer than temporary implies.

Warrant Board.description: A display of active warrants, claim values and disputed identities, most of them backed by Dravon-aligned authority that Dustfall does not accept. It is a mounted panel under a shade hood at the camp's outer edge, deliberately readable from the public side, with entries added and struck through by hand. A warrant is not proof of guilt here and refugee status is not proof of innocence, so the board persuades nobody and informs everybody. Locals read it to find out who is being hunted, and occasionally to find out that somebody they know is on it. The board is the crew's advertising and the settlement's standing provocation.

Capture Gear Rack.description: Racked restraints, nets, suppressors and non-lethal equipment maintained to a professional standard. The rack is a portable frame with everything in labelled positions, cleaned and checked after every use, and the maintenance is done in the open where anyone can see how good the equipment is. The crew's stated preference is to take people intact, which is both a professional argument and a commercial one since a damaged claim pays less. Residents look at the restraints and think about what restraint damage looks like on a patient. Which of that preference is ethics and which is pricing depends on the warrant and on who is asking.

Ravik's Negotiation Awning.description: Ravik Rusk's shaded table for negotiating surrenders, settlements and the occasional withdrawal of a claim. It is a stretched awning over a folding table and seating, set at the edge of the camp so that anyone coming to talk does not have to walk through the gear to do it, with water on the table as a matter of course. He prefers a bought outcome to a violent one and says so, at length, to people who came expecting something else. Settlements are made in credits, in information or in an agreement about where somebody goes instead. He is also testing how far Dustfall will actually go to defend its refusal of Dravon warrants.

Cyrra's Tracking Station.description: Cyrra Hale's station of sensor gear, sighting logs and route correlation, where a person's movements are reconstructed from fragments. It is a covered working position with screens shaded against the daylight, portable equipment set up properly rather than quickly, and her own annotations layered over everything the crew's records contain. She is genuinely good at it, and marks what she is uncertain about instead of rounding it into a conclusion, which has cost the crew at least one claim and probably saved somebody the wrong arrest. Route records, water station stops and a load's declared weight all feed the same picture. The station's outputs are only as honest as the records feeding them, which is a problem she has raised internally.

Dask's Restraint Bay.description: Dask Ren's bay for securing and transporting claimed people, fitted for safe restraint rather than comfort. It is a plated module with fixed points, padding where padding prevents injury, a water supply and lighting that stays on, cleaned and inspected between uses whether or not anyone will check. He checks fittings personally and objects loudly to damage, to his own crew as readily as to anyone else, on the grounds that a person delivered hurt is a job done badly. Claimed people are spoken to plainly about what is happening and when, and are not left uninformed for hours. What happens to a claim after it leaves the bay is not something he asks about.

Miren's Record Module.description: Miren Tal's identity and records module, holding files that do not always agree with Ovar Kethrin's missing-person lists or with Nyra Sorel's account of herself. It is a sealed unit with its own power and its own lock, worked from a seat inside it rather than in the open, and the discrepancies between sources are flagged rather than resolved. He sorts and cross-references constantly, which is what makes the crew's work possible and what makes it dangerous to the people in the files. He may also be selling route records to Dravon intermediaries, which would explain more than one recent interception.

Prisoner Bench.description: A secured bench where claimed people wait, visible from the camp and therefore visible to Dustfall. It stands under a shade panel with water within reach and fixed points along its length, positioned so that nobody sitting on it is hidden from the settlement side and nobody guarding it can pretend not to be seen. The visibility is deliberate on both sides: the crew wants it known that people on the bench are intact, and the settlement wants it known that it is looking. Residents walk past deliberately and slowly, and some of them stop. More than one claim has been abandoned because the wrong local walked past and recognised a face.

Ready-Launch Pad.description: A cleared pad kept permanently available for immediate departure, since the crew's business depends on leaving before a dispute becomes a confrontation. It is swept ground marked out in paint, positioned on the outward side of the camp with nothing parked across the approach, and the rule about keeping it clear is the one camp rule nobody breaks or argues about. Craft sit fuelled and loaded, with personal gear stowed rather than spread out, and the departure check is run daily whether or not anything is planned. Locals notice that the craft never face the settlement. The pad's readiness is the clearest sign that the Claimants do not consider themselves welcome here.

Sleeping Pods.description: Compact sealed sleeping pods for a crew that expects to move at short notice, stacked against the camp's windward side. Each is a hard shell with its own seal and air handling, dust-tight, quiet and exactly large enough, and the whole stack can be broken down and loaded in a single movement of the camp. They are efficient, cramped and entirely impersonal. Nothing is stored outside them and nothing is left out overnight, so the camp looks the same at the end of a month as it did at the start, which is the opposite of every other dwelling in Dustfall. Nobody in the Claimants has put anything on a wall, which locals have noticed and drawn conclusions from.

The Grand Waypoint.name: The Grand Waypoint
The Grand Waypoint.basicInfo:
The flagship Corsair logistics centre and the place where Nexara's economy is physically transacted. It stands on the First Terrace within walking distance of Routefall Market, a high-roofed hall of controlled chaos where cargo arrives from the Barge Quays below and the Skyhook Docks above while travellers come down from the Gate Hub. Route-boards stack three galleries high above a trade floor that never empties, and smart-cable transfer runs loads out toward the terraces overhead. It is polished where the public sees it and worn where the work happens, and public argument here is normal. The building opens with the barge tide and does not stop: route clerks, brokers, permit officers, courier dispatchers and contract callers working through the day in river-slate blue and rope-tan under warm lantern amber, with the bright standardised colour-codes of route and cargo marking every counter lane. Fliers and pedestrians both enter at floor level, and nobody is turned away for wanting to look. Corsair runs the floor, the Helvyra Gate Compact governs gate-bound freight, House Varriko holds a standing desk inside it and Contair collaborates on the underlying system infrastructure. Everything passes through and nothing settles, which is the city's own theme stated in a single room.

Work on offer here: Helvyra — A Run on the Skyhooks; Helvyra — Three Signed Records (ask Dren Varriko); Trade — A Consignment for the Ashglass Canopies (ask Raxen Caelrix).
The Grand Waypoint.hiddenInfo: Theft from a Waypoint is the one crime Helvyra is merciless about, and everyone in the building knows it, which is exactly why the Lost Cargo Desk's ledger of unclaimed and near-claimed consignments is read so carefully by anyone chasing a pattern. House Varriko holds a standing desk inside Corsair's own floor by agreement, and the Ledger Court Annex is currently settling more on-site cargo disputes than usual because forged Common Scale certification has begun surfacing in ordinary goods and the claims cannot wait for the ferry. Contair collaborates on the underlying system infrastructure, which gives its people reasons to be in rooms Corsair would otherwise control. Courier Dispatch is the Caelrix firm's working base and the fastest way to move something across the city without it appearing on a manifest anyone reads. Xyren Corsair is applied public pressure here rather than obeyed, and the Signmaker's Wall keeps the record of it. Yalven manufacturing orders, Veltrax escort contracts and the Dustfall supply chain all route through these counters, so a single delayed shipment can reach four houses before the day ends.

Central Trade Floor.description: The open heart of the building, floored in scuffed pale composite and ringed by counter rows. Brokers, factors and route clerks work standing, closing deals in the middle of other people's arguments. The Smokeless custom holds here: a shouted dispute is a recognised channel, not a disturbance, and almost nobody looks up. The roof is high enough to swallow several hundred transactions at once, and the smart-cable runs beneath it keep a load moving overhead for as long as the doors are open. Barge crews come in still wet from the quays and stand beside house factors in clean coats. The composite is worn into pale tracks between the busiest counters, a map of the building's real traffic that no display shows.

Route Board Gallery.description: Three stacked galleries of public route-boards refreshing faster than anyone can read them: departures, prices, delays, contract calls. Runners work the upper rails where the refresh lands first and shout the changes down. The clatter of updating displays is the sound Helvyrans mean when they say the city is awake. The galleries ring the trade floor, so from below the boards read as a wall of moving colour-code and resolve into detail only for someone willing to climb. The dawn refresh draws the day's largest crowd to the rails, and brokers who cannot get a place up there pay someone who can. Handrails are polished bare along the stretches with the best sightlines, and arguments about what a board said a moment ago are unwinnable, because the boards keep no visible history.

Shipment Counters.description: Long worn counters where cargo is booked, weighed, sealed and released, each lane marked in the standardised route colour-codes. Clerks argue grades with warehouse keepers whose frontages have already logged the contents and disagree with the manifest. A queue here moves faster than it looks, because nobody is browsing. The counters run in a long rank beneath the galleries, each with its own scale bench, seal station and reader gear. Common Scale grading decides what a load is called and therefore what it costs to move, so the grade is what people argue about hardest. Sealed consignments go straight out to the cable runs; contested ones go to a holding bay and start collecting a record. The counter tops are dented where crate corners have been set down by people in a hurry.

Courier Dispatch.description: The fast end of the building: job boards, sealed pouches, and fliers taking off from an open frontage rather than walking out of a door. The Caelrix firm works out of this room. Dispatch clerks match a parcel to a courier by temperament as much as by route, and they remember exactly who came back late. The room is loud in short bursts and idle between them, with the frontage open to the terrace air and a rail where couriers check harness and load frame before stepping off. The boards carry the small urgent work the bulk systems will not touch: a signature, a sealed instruction, a sample that has to arrive today rather than correctly. Pouch storage sits behind the counter under the dispatcher's eye, and nothing leaves it without a name against it.

Permit Offices.description: Narrow offices behind the trade floor handling route access, gate-bound freight paperwork and Compact compliance. Slow, exact work in a building that does nothing else slowly. Applicants wait on a bench polished by decades of impatience while an officer reads a manifest line by line and asks the one awkward question. The corridor is quieter than the floor by a single wall's thickness, lit low and warm, with the route colour-codes reduced to small filed tabs rather than shouted signage. Officers work from precedent and decline to be hurried by the size of the house asking, and a refusal arrives in the same tone as an approval. Failed applications come back with the failing line marked, which most applicants take as a courtesy and a few take as an insult.

Lost Cargo Desk.description: A single counter with a wall of tagged crates behind it, holding everything that arrived without an owner or left without arriving. The clerk keeps a ledger of claims, near-claims and consignments nobody has ever come for. It is the quietest desk in the Waypoint and the first one an investigator walks to. The crates are shelved by the day they were tagged rather than by route, so the wall reads as an accumulation rather than a system, and the oldest tags have faded out of their colour-codes toward rope-tan. A claim requires a description before the crate is shown, which stops the obvious kind of theft and catches nothing cleverer. The desk is watched far more closely than its quiet suggests.

Ledger Court Annex.description: House Varriko's satellite desk inside Corsair's own building, granted by standing agreement: pale stone, no shouting, a sealed record system that does not care whose floor it stands on. It settles on-site cargo disputes that cannot wait for the ferry, while full proceedings escalate across the river to the Ledger Hall. The room is deliberately unlike everything around it, quiet enough that the trade floor's roar arrives as weather rather than noise, with plain tables and a clerk whose first move is to pull up the record rather than take a side. What the Annex may decide is bounded and publicly known, and a matter that exceeds it is written up and sent across the water, which makes the crossing part of the argument's cost.

Signmaker’s Wall.description: The frontage where the Xyren signs go up, a public wall of commissioned mockery the city treats with complete ceremonial seriousness. Retired boards are archived rather than binned. Visitors laugh at the joke; locals inspect the craftsmanship, because a badly made sign is the real insult and everyone knows who made it. The wall faces the trade floor and catches the light spilling from the galleries, which the makers account for in their materials: weathered copper, lantern-amber grounds, and cargo colour-codes borrowed off the crates and turned to other purposes. Signday's unveiling stops the floor for exactly as long as it takes, and between unveilings the wall serves as the building's meeting point, being the one landmark inside that needs no directions.

Private Contract Rooms.description: Screened rooms off the trade floor for deals that cannot be shouted: house factors, escort terms, restricted commissions. Acoustic damping, and a door that logs who entered without recording what was said. Booking one is public information, which is why some negotiations deliberately happen at an open counter instead. The rooms are small, identical and plainly finished, with a table, a display wall for terms, and nothing to indicate whose building they sit in. The damping is thorough enough that stepping inside feels like the building has been switched off, which unsettles people accustomed to working in noise. Bookings are timed and the next party waits in sight of the last, so who followed whom is public information too.

Routefall Market.name: Routefall Market
Routefall Market.basicInfo: The great open market where the routes fall into the city, a broad First Terrace of stall rows under tensioned canopies with food halls along the inner edge. Everything that arrives and is not bound onward is sold here, which makes the market the city's overflow valve as much as its shopfront: produce comes in from the Hauler Yards on the landward approach, river goods come up from the Barge Quays, and whatever the Grand Waypoint does not send onward is on a pitch by mid-morning. Contract callers work raised stones so their voices carry, and route-boards stand at every junction. Loud, crowded and colour-coded, it is where a stranger becomes a Helvyran. Colour is the market's working language, cargo markings and route flashes and certification marks in the bright standardised codes, read at a glance against canopy shade and pale composite underfoot. Nobody owns the ground. Stall assignment and vendor peace are the market moderator's work, Common Scale certification governs goods and Open Circle marks govern charms. Sharing a table with strangers is normal, the Smokeless custom makes a public argument a recognised dispute channel rather than a disturbance, and the noise climbs to its peak by mid-morning and does not really stop until the pitches come down.
Routefall Market.hiddenInfo: Bareth Kollo assigns every pitch on this terrace and knows every face on it, which is how he noticed that someone is paying rent on stalls that are never worked. The empty frames sit in good positions and nobody has claimed the goodwill, so the money is buying presence rather than trade. At the same time forged Common Scale seals have started appearing on premium goods moving through the Certified Goods Aisle, and the aisle's whole value is that its marks cannot be wrong, so a single confirmed forgery would push every affected claim across the river to the Ledger District. Open Circle students work the Charm Piecework Edge for fees, and some of that work is being done without certification for reasons the students think are good. The Smokeless custom means a public argument here is a recognised dispute channel rather than a disturbance, so a great deal gets said in the open that would never be written down, and the market moderator hears most of it first.

Stall Rows.description: Rank after rank of stalls under tensioned canopies, each pitch marked with its route flash and cargo code so a buyer can read an origin at twenty paces. Produce off the hauler trains sits beside river goods still cold from the quays. Pitches turn over fast, and an empty frame by mid-morning is worth noticing. The canopies are strung high enough for a flier to set down in the cross-aisles and low enough to keep the terrace in shade, so the light under them stays warm and even and the colour-codes stay legible all day. A stallholder holds a pitch by working it, and an assembled frame with nobody behind it draws the moderator's attention before it draws a buyer's.

Food Halls.description: The inner edge of the market, where dock kitchens and concession counters serve fast, hot, portable food to people between shifts. Shared tables are the default and strangers sit down without asking permission. Steam, route-board glow, and a permanent low roar of six conversations happening across one bench. The cooking is proudly mongrel: river fish and route-cargo produce arriving from opposite directions and meeting in the same bowl, served in whatever form can be carried back to a shift. Counters run continuously rather than by meal, because the city's hours are set by the barge tide and the skyhooks. A bench at the busy hour holds barge crew, clerks, a house factor and somebody's children in one unbroken line.

The Calling Stones.description: Raised stones where contract callers stand to be heard, announcing open work aloud, taking terms shouted back, and striking agreements in front of witnesses who count as witnesses. The stone is worn to a shine at standing height. A caller who loses their voice loses their week, so most of them ration it carefully. The stones stand clear of the canopy line so a voice carries down the aisles instead of into fabric, and callers work a loose rotation nobody has written down and everybody observes. Work called here runs from a day's quay labour to a season's route contract, and terms are stated in full, because contract literacy is taught early enough that the crowd follows the fine print in real time and says so.

Certified Goods Aisle.description: One aisle where every item carries a Common Scale grading or an Open Circle charm mark, and stallholders pay for the right to stand in it. Buyers come for preservation seals, ward-marked crates and anything where being wrong is expensive. The seals are being checked rather more often than they used to be. The aisle is narrower than the open rows and better lit, with the marks displayed at eye height rather than tucked under a lid, because the whole value of the pitch is that the mark can be read before the price is discussed. A stallholder found carrying an unmarked item loses the pitch rather than the sale, and the pitch is the expensive part.

Charm Piecework Edge.description: The market's outer fringe, where Open Circle students take paid commissions: route-charms, preservation seals and small ward-marks written on the spot. Most Helvyrans cannot cast and do not want to; they want to know the fee is fair. The work is done in the open, which is part of the certification culture. Benches and folding tables sit where the canopies end, inscription tools laid out in view and the finished work handed over while the client watches. The clientele is ordinary: a barge family renewing a hull seal, a stallholder wanting a crate marked before a cable run, a courier after a route-charm that will survive the upper terrace.

Morvane Apothecary Stall.description: The Morvane family's trading front, stocked with river-trade botanicals that arrive by barge and do not keep long. Sorted trays labelled in the family's own shorthand, and a bench where a keeper will explain what something is for before selling it. The Bankside Care Hall dispensary buys from this stall. Stock turns on the river's schedule rather than the market's, so regulars ask what came up this week rather than asking for a thing by name, and the trays that need preservation seals carry them visibly dated. The explaining is not salesmanship: the keeper will talk a buyer out of a purchase, and does it often enough that the stall's reputation rests on the refusals as much as the sales.

Moderator's Post.description: Bareth Kollo's working station: a raised desk with the stall map, the pitch ledger and a clear sightline down the main aisle. Vendor peace, pitch assignment and the first hearing of any dispute all happen here. He knows every face on the First Terrace, which some traders find less comfortable than others do. The post is a raised frame rather than an office, open on every side, because a moderator who cannot be approached is no use and one who cannot see the aisle is worse. Disputes arrive loudly under the Smokeless custom and are heard in the open, usually by making both parties say the whole thing again in front of whoever is standing there.

The Waiting Cup.description: A cafe concession under the food hall canopy with a borrowed view of the route-boards, warm counter lighting and a low acoustic screen against the noise. A fast-order counter, a collection ledge, short-stay tables and a quieter shared bench. The servers can tell who is waiting for a departure and who is waiting for a person. The screen does not silence the market so much as move it a step away, which is the whole product: somewhere to sit inside the noise rather than outside it. Regulars take the ledge over the tables because the ledge faces the boards. Somebody is always here at the wrong hour with nothing to do, and the staff do not move them on.

Three Seats More.description: A restaurant concession where the host asks how many are actually eating before moving tables, because shared dining is normal here but a smaller table can be requested without anyone performing sociability. Mixed-route bowls and filled Terva pockets come off a visible finishing station, with the kitchen audible and unshouted. Tables are light enough to be recombined mid-service, so the room's shape changes several times an evening around whoever has arrived together. The finishing station faces the room, which is the concession's answer to the market's certification habit applied to food. Service draws people who have finished a negotiation rather than people between shifts.

Cold Pour District.name: Cold Pour District
Cold Pour District.basicInfo: The entertainment bank: brew cellars cut back into the riverbank, cool year-round and warm-lit in lantern amber, with pour halls at street level and music rooms deeper in. It takes over after dark, when the skyhooks finally stop. Canon is explicit that this is where deals become friendships, which makes it business by other means. It is a walk from the First Terrace and from Riverrow, and travellers come down to it from the Gate Hub, so the district mixes crews off shift, brokers finishing what the Waypoint started, and people who arrived in the city that afternoon. The cellars stay cool through the year, which is the whole reason the trade settled in them, and the deeper the room the quieter it gets and the more of the work the lantern amber does. Cellar-masters and hall keepers run their own doors and no single authority runs any of it. The Bank Wardens work drunk retrieval along the water here nightly, which is a listed duty and an entirely unglamorous one. Sharing a table with strangers is normal, and since the cellars are where deals become friendships, a great deal of the city's actual business is settled in rooms that keep no record at all of having hosted it.
Cold Pour District.hiddenInfo: Essim Corle holds a Quilrath vintage in the Long Pour's cellar that nobody will admit importing, and the Dravon Disconnection is absolute: there is no legitimate route by which it could be here. It is the thread-end of a smuggling line, and Essim is a keeper of everyone's secrets precisely because he does not pull threads. Xyren Corsair is canon-attached to this district, which means the head of House Corsair is regularly in the one part of the city where conversations are not recorded. The Back Tables are discreet rather than invisible, and sitting at them is itself a statement, so the shrewdest business is done at an ordinary table in a loud hall where nobody can hear anything but the person opposite. Travelling musicians take the Music Rooms a night at a time and hear a great deal they were not meant to. The Bank Wardens work drunk retrieval on the Riverbank Steps nightly, which means the wardens have a standing, entirely legitimate reason to be here after dark.

Long Pour.description: The oldest cellar in the district and entirely aware of it: a main pour counter, conversational tables, a small listening corner, and a cellar viewing threshold that stays under staff control. Essim Corle keeps the room, the tradition and most of the city's secrets. One selection down there has no plausible import route. The room is low and warm, floored in worn stone, lit amber and arranged so the counter, the tables and the listening corner can all see one another. It is busy from early evening and does not empty so much as thin out. Essim is behind the counter most nights and remembers what a person drank the last time.

Cellar Row.description: The run of brew cellars cut back into the bank, each with its own door, its own keeper and its own regulars. Cool air spills out at street level even in high summer. Choosing a cellar in Helvyra says as much about a person as choosing a trade does, and switching between them gets noticed. The row runs along the bank with doors at street level and the cellars stepping back into the stone behind them, each a different depth, temperature and volume of noise, lantern amber spilling out of every doorway after dark. Keepers stand at their own doors early on, and a first-time visitor is usually walked to a suitable one by whoever they asked.

Pour Halls.description: Street-level halls, bigger and louder than the cellars, taking the crowd that comes down off shift once the skyhooks stop. Shared tables, fast service, and the Kessar-based drinks the district is known for. This is where the night starts, before it moves deeper into the bank and gets quieter. The halls are broad and high-ceilinged and lit brighter than the cellars, with long shared tables, standing room at the counters and doors open to the street for the air. They fill fast and stay loud for hours. Crews come in still in working gear, and a stranger is sat down at an occupied table without any discussion about it.

Music Rooms.description: Rooms further back where the acoustics work and the audience actually listens, booked evening by evening rather than held by any permanent band. Travelling musicians take a night and move on. A player who works the district regularly learns which tables to watch and which to forget having seen. The rooms sit deep in the bank where the stone does the acoustic work, small and warm and close-seated, lit low, with a raised corner rather than a stage. Talking through a set is badly received. An audience here listens with the attention the city otherwise gives a grading, which is why players cross a continent for the room.

Back Tables.description: Quiet tables set apart for business that would be conspicuous at a Waypoint counter, screened and unrecorded and understood by everyone to be discreet rather than invisible. Staff serve and leave. Sitting here is a statement in itself, which is why the shrewdest conversations happen at an ordinary table instead. They sit at the edges of the rooms rather than in a separate space, screened by stone and angle and the noise of everything else, with the lamps kept low. Everyone in the district can see who is sitting at them, which is the exact limit of their discretion and the reason experienced people use them for a second conversation.

Riverbank Steps.description: Steps down to the water outside the cellar doors, where people sit out between rounds and travellers get their first unhurried look at the night river. Bank Wardens work this stretch nightly, mostly retrieving people who overestimated their flying. It is the district's least private and most honest space. The steps go down in broad courses from the cellar doors to the water, lit by what spills out of the doorways and by the city on the far side, and cold enough at night to sober somebody usefully. People sit out on them in ones and twos and in whole crews, and the wardens get talked to far more freely here than anywhere in daylight.

Merchant Row.name: Merchant Row
Merchant Row.basicInfo: The residential face of Helvyra's commerce culture, a mid-level district of handsome stepped terraces where trade families live above their business relationships, mixed with the city's guest houses. Entry halls carry route-boards because visitors check departures before breakfast. Comfortable without being grand: this is prosperity, not aristocracy. It is a walk from the First Terrace, so a guest can be at the Waypoint or the market before the boards have finished their first refresh of the day. The terraces are pale composite and rope-tan with private frontages and doors opening onto the street, stepped so that every house has its own approach and its own view down the slope. Guests are in constant rotation, factors and buyers and house representatives not important enough for the Estate, and business is conducted at dinner as often as at a counter. There is no single authority here: private households and guest-house keepers run their own affairs and the district's discipline is entirely reputational. Corsair guest overflow lands here when the Estate is full, which regularly puts house representatives in the same breakfast room as the people they are negotiating against. The social bridge between the working city and the high terrace runs through these streets, and everyone living on them knows it.
Merchant Row.hiddenInfo: Guest-house keepers know their regulars' schedules better than the regulars do, and one current guest's movements do not match the manifest they arrived on. The district's whole economy runs on hospitality as an instrument: the Dinner Tables produce agreements with no minutes and no seals, held together by the expectation that they will hold, which makes a withdrawn invitation a genuine commercial weapon. The Caelrix Courier Office is here because clients stay next door, and private commissions taken at this office would be conspicuous if booked through the Waypoint's dispatch room, so the sensitive work goes through the Row. Corsair guest overflow lands here when the Estate is full, which regularly puts house representatives in the same breakfast room as the people they are negotiating against. A trade family in trouble is visible here long before it is legally visible: frontages stop having guests waiting outside them, and the street reads that immediately.

Guest House Row.description: A stepped street of guest houses catering to factors, buyers and house representatives not important enough for the Estate. Entry halls carry live route-boards and breakfast is served around departure times. Keepers know their regulars' schedules better than the regulars do, and notice when one stops matching. The houses are close-built and well kept, each with a lit frontage, a keeper's desk inside the door and a hall arranged so arrivals and departures do not collide. Breakfast runs early and long, and a guest can sit down opposite a stranger and be doing business by the time the plates are cleared, which is why the tables are shared.

Trade Family Terraces.description: Private frontages in pale composite and rope-tan, generations of the same families living above their business relationships. Doors open onto the street rather than onto courtyards, which is the district's entire social theory. A family's standing can be read from how often its frontage has guests waiting outside it. The frontages step along the slope, plain-faced, with lamps kept lit at the door and route-boards visible through the hall windows. Households are large and mixed, several generations and the business under one roof. Nothing is ostentatious, and the money shows only in maintenance, which is why a frontage that stops being repaired is read at once.

The Dinner Tables.description: The district's real institution: informal negotiation over dinner, in private dining rooms and at family tables where a deal is reached before the plates are cleared. No minutes, no seals, and an expectation that what was agreed will hold. Hospitality here is a currency, and it can be spent against someone. Physically it is a scatter of private dining rooms in the guest houses and family tables in the terraces, lit warm and unhurried and arranged so that six people can hear each other without anyone raising a voice. The food is good and deliberately not impressive. An invitation carries an obligation, and a withdrawn one carries a message.

Caelrix Courier Office.description: The Caelrix firm's premises, sited here because couriers live where routes meet and clients stay in the houses next door. A dispatch board, sealed-pouch storage, and a flight frontage for departures. Private commissions are taken here that would be conspicuous if booked at the Waypoint's dispatch room. The office is a working frontage with a counter, storage behind a grille and an open flight ledge above the street, and couriers come and go at all hours without disturbing the district, which is part of why it is tolerated in it. Clients walk over from the houses next door rather than crossing the city to do business.

Row Landing Steps.description: Broad steps and a small landing apron where fliers set down and walk the last stretch, because arriving at a frontage directly is considered rude. Luggage handlers wait at the bottom. It is the district's front door and the place where a visitor's standing is first and most informally assessed. The steps are broad pale composite with a rail and lamps at the turns, kept clean because they are the first thing anybody sees. The handlers know most of the regulars by sight. Walking up is the polite form even for people who could fly to the door, and declining to walk is noticed. The apron at the top is small enough that two parties arriving at once have to acknowledge each other, which the district considers a feature.

Veltrax Redcourt District.name: Veltrax Redcourt District
Veltrax Redcourt District.basicInfo:
House Veltrax's martial district on the west bank, angular and red-toned and forward-driving, with training lanes built long and direct and courtyards built to encourage public challenge. Challenges are taken in the open and escort contracts are negotiated on the premises. It is loud by design, and it wants an audience. It stands near but deliberately not directly beside Rux's school across the water, reached by ferry and by bridge, and the crossing itself is socially loaded in both directions. Nothing here is curved or decorative: red-toned stone, hard floors, straight lanes, and galleries built so that work can be watched from above. It is not lawless. The district is formal, proud and competitive, with procedure around every challenge and a written record of every result posted where clients can read it. Days run to aggressive open training, challenges answered in front of whoever is standing there, and escort contracts drafted and priced on the premises. House Veltrax operates all of it. Contracts tie back through the Grand Waypoint across the river, and injuries beyond what the district treats itself go up to Bankside Care Hall, where they are logged beside the other school's.

Work on offer here: Helvyra — The Escort Proof (ask Sava Veltrax).
Veltrax Redcourt District.hiddenInfo: Daxor Veltrax is working a forensic question that pairs exactly with Meya Orlin's unexplained injury pattern across the river, and the raw material is sitting in this district's own Recovery Room log. Neither bank has formally compared notes, because doing so would mean admitting the wounds did not come from either school. The House Veltrax Office is drafting escort commissions, and at least one of them is a provocation wearing a contract's clothes: the client wants a route walked, visibly, past people who will read it correctly. Contracts here tie back through the Grand Waypoint, so a Veltrax escalation becomes a Corsair scheduling problem within a day. The Pressure Hall is where students are trained to fail and keep going, and it is also where a proportion of them privately decide they want out of the house entirely, which is a harder thing to do in a district built to be watched. Arvessa, Kaelen, Mireth and Sava all hold positions that a defection would embarrass.

Veltrax Redcourt.description: The district's namesake court, red-toned stone stepped down to a hard floor and built so a crowd can see everything from every side. It is the address that gives the whole quarter its reputation. Empty it looks theatrical; full it is simply the most direct place in Helvyra to establish who is better. The stone is worked in flat planes and hard angles, and the floor takes a beating and shows it. The court is lit for visibility rather than atmosphere, and sound comes back off the steps, so a bout sounds larger from the seats than it does from the floor. Nothing in it is comfortable, which is part of the argument the district makes about itself.

Public Challenge Floor.description: An open floor where challenges are issued and answered in front of whoever happens to be standing there. Terms are stated aloud and refusals are permitted, and remembered. Veltrax argues that daylight keeps the practice honest; the argument from across the river is that daylight is what makes people accept. It is open on the district side, so a challenge issued here is heard by whoever is passing as well as by whoever came deliberately. Terms are recorded by a house clerk before anything begins and both parties are made to restate them. The floor is plain, hard, and marked only at its boundary.

Red Practice Lanes.description: Long straight lanes for drilling advance and pressure, marked in house red, with nothing curved or decorative anywhere in them. Students run the lanes until the movement is automatic. The sound of a full session carries across the water, which is not an accident of the acoustics. The lanes run the length of the training house in parallel, lit from above and floored to take repeated impact, with the house red laid into the marking rather than painted over it. Instructors call the rhythm and nobody counts aloud. Students finish a session soaked and say so loudly, which is also part of the training.

Instructor Gallery.description: A raised gallery from which instructors watch the lanes and the court together, calling corrections down without stopping the work. Assignments and gradings are decided here in full view of the students being graded. Standing in the gallery is itself a rank, and everyone below knows exactly who is standing. The gallery runs along one side at height, railed and open, with a bench, a record station and a clear line down every lane at once. Instructors stay up there for entire sessions and come down rarely. A correction called from the rail is heard by the whole floor, which is the method rather than an accident.

Student Sparring Yard.description: An enclosed yard where students spar outside formal challenge: rougher, less watched, and more honest about what a student cannot yet do. Kit is scuffed, tempers are shorter, and instructors intervene later than they would in the lanes. Most of the district's real friendships begin in this yard. The yard is walled on three sides, open to the sky and floored in hardstanding repaired more often than resurfaced. Gear is borrowed, mismatched and mended. Bouts start without ceremony, stop when somebody says so, and are refought immediately, and the noise is nothing like the court's. Instructors watch from the wall and let a bad habit run one exchange longer than they ever would out in the lanes.

Blade Maintenance Room.description: Benches, edge gear and modification stands where blades are kept to standard, much of the equipment ordered from the Yalven Forgeworks up the bank. A weapon is inspected and logged before any formal challenge. Gear that fails inspection is pulled, and whose it was becomes a small public fact within the hour. It is a working shop rather than a display room, with benches down both walls, test frames and racked stock waiting for adjustment. Work the district cannot do goes up the bank and comes back with its adjustment record attached. The inspection log by the door is the most consulted document in the quarter.

House Veltrax Office.description: The house's business room, where escort contracts are drafted, clients received and rates argued down. The contract file is the district's real spine and ties through to the Grand Waypoint across the river. Some commissions are escort work; some are escort work in the way a provocation is a scheduling matter. The office is formal and red-toned and built to receive clients rather than students, with a table for terms, a wall of completed contracts and nothing on display that is not a result. Rates are argued down and then written up exactly, and a client who reaches this room has been assessed by three people on the way in.

Recovery Room.description: A treatment room for what the lanes and the court produce, staffed to handle everything short of what needs Bankside. Ice, binding, and a physician's standing argument with the instructors about training volume. The injuries logged here are the raw material for a forensic question nobody has answered yet. The room is small, clean and well equipped for its purpose, with treatment benches, a cold store and bindings restocked daily because they are used daily. Students arrive on their own feet or are walked in, and the physician will send one across the water without discussion when the log says so.

Trophy Wall.description: A wall of results: challenge outcomes, gradings and completed contracts, displayed with the frankness of a business advertising its record. Losses are posted too, which the district treats as proof the wins are real. Students check their own line on it considerably more often than any of them will admit. It is a long wall of posted results in the district's own plain lettering, updated after every challenge and every completed contract, set where clients walk past it rather than where students do. Old entries are never removed. Prospective clients read it as a price list and students read it as a ranking.

The Pressure Hall.description: A closed hall for the school's hardest work, where students are trained under sustained assault to fail and keep going. Deliberately unpleasant, and deliberately not public. Coming out of it is when a Redcourt student stops being a beginner, and it is also when a few of them decide they want out. The hall is low and lit hard, with no gallery, no seating and no way for anyone outside to see in. Sessions run until the instructors stop them. Nothing about the room is comfortable or meant to be, and students coming out are met at the door and walked either to the recovery room or back to the yard.

Yalven Forgeworks.name: Yalven Forgeworks
Yalven Forgeworks.basicInfo: House Yalven's production compound inside the west bank's Forge Rows, handling manufacturing, crafting, armour fitting, weapon modification and support-model production. The public side is polished because Helvyran businesses know presentation sells; the deeper production floors are louder, hotter and more honest. An apprenticeship here outranks a classroom. Materials arrive from the Barge Quays and finished orders route out through the Grand Waypoint, so the compound sits inside the freight system rather than beside it, and a delay on the river reaches these floors within a day. The front is mod counters and fitting floors under clean even light; behind them parts lifts run between the fitting levels and the production lines below, and the noise changes completely at the counter wall. Customers come for fittings, adjustments and courier gear, couriers come to collect, apprentices come for the placement, and contract clients go through to the restricted floor. Common Scale certification applies to graded output and is checked again before anything leaves. Both sword schools are supplied from here, which the bay crews find funnier than either school does.
Yalven Forgeworks.hiddenInfo: The Quality Review Office is pulling material traces on a run of charm-bearing components, convinced the Circle Isle charm failures are a Yalven materials fault. Canon is explicit that Yalven is wrong, which makes the investigation a slow expensive way of arriving at the wrong bank of the river while the actual cause goes unexamined and the house's reputation erodes. The Restricted Contract Floor is sealed, staffed by people who do not rotate out, and stands out precisely because the rest of the compound is so open: at least one commission running through it has a purpose the fitters on the public side would refuse. Gear from these floors equips both sword schools, the courier trade and half the dock crews on the river, so a fault that survives Quality Review reaches the people least able to survive it failing. Apprenticeship placement here carries more prestige than any classroom, and the politics of who gets placed are fought out in the Worker Commons rather than anywhere official.

Public Mod Counter.description: The polished front room: sample gear on stands, a live order board, and fitters who talk a customer through options without condescending. Most of Helvyra's working population has stood at this counter at some point. Behind the counter wall the noise changes completely, which customers can hear and are not shown. The room is deliberately calm, floored in pale composite and lit evenly, with the samples set at handling height rather than behind glass. Fitters work standing and will spend as long as a customer needs on an order worth very little, and a job that cannot be done by the date asked for is refused here rather than taken and delivered late.

Armor Fitting Floor.description: Scanning frames, adjustment rigs and racked shells at every stage of fitting, for dock crews, escorts and sword students alike. A fitting takes as long as it takes and the fitters refuse to be hurried. Graded output carries a Common Scale mark, checked once more before it leaves the floor. The floor is open, bright and busier than it looks, with the frames along one wall and the rigs down the middle and a fitter's whole attention on one person at a time. Dock crews arrive in working gear straight off a shift and are deliberately fitted in it. The racks at the back hold shells tagged and dated, and nothing on them is collected early.

Weapon Adjustment Bays.description: Enclosed bays for balance, edge and modification work, with test frames and a logged record of every change made to every weapon. Both sword schools send work here, which the bay crews find considerably funnier than either school does. A weapon leaves with its adjustment record attached to it. The bays are enclosed for noise rather than for secrecy, each with its own test frame, measurement gear and bench, and the work in them is exact and unhurried. Crews here talk about balance the way riggers talk about wind, and a customer who cannot describe the problem is handed the weapon and asked to show them.

Courier Gear Workshop.description: Light, fast and flight-rated: harness, sealed pouches, load frames and the wearable interfaces couriers effectively live in. The Caelrix firm is a standing customer. Failures here are lethal rather than merely expensive, so the workshop tests harder than the mod counter and says a great deal less about it. It is a small, clean, brightly lit room full of harness on stands, where every fitting is made against the body that will wear it and testing is done on a rig and repeated until it is boring. Couriers wear this gear for whole working lives, so the workshop knows its regulars by build and by route and asks after both.

Parts Lift Atrium.description: A tall central atrium with parts lifts running between the fitting floors and the production lines below, the compound's circulatory system in full view. Everything crosses here, so everyone crosses here. It is the one place in the Forgeworks where public-side and deep-floor staff routinely meet by accident. The atrium runs the full height of the compound, railed at every level, with the lifts open enough that a load can be watched the whole way. The sound of the production floors comes up it, and the smell of hot metal comes up with the sound, so the front of the building always knows what the back is doing.

Worker Commons.description: The floor workers' room: benches, food, gear lockers and a permanent argument about apprenticeship placements. Prestige here is earned on the production floor and discussed nowhere official. Apprentices learn quickly whose opinion actually moves a placement and whose merely sounds as though it might.
