The room is warm, worn and comprehensively lived in, with long benches, a food counter, lockers and gear drying wherever it can be hung. Shift changes fill it twice a day and empty it in minutes. Placement arguments run for weeks in full hearing of the apprentices being argued about, which the floor considers fair rather than cruel.

Quality Review Office.description: Where output is tested, graded and signed, and where a batch gets held. Records, retained samples and the material-trace files. Somebody in this office has been pulling traces on a recent run of charm-bearing components, convinced the fault lies in the materials rather than anywhere further downstream. It is a plain office with sample storage, test benches and a wall of retained batches kept long past the point anyone expects to need them. Work stops when a review says so and the house backs the office over the schedule every time. The trace files are the most expensive documents in the compound.

Restricted Contract Floor.description: A sealed production floor for commissions that are not discussed on the public side, accessed on name and record only. Staff assigned to it do not rotate out casually. The compound's culture is otherwise open, which makes the mere existence of this floor the loudest thing anyone can say about Yalven. The entrance is a plain controlled door off an otherwise ordinary corridor, with a name check, a record and nothing to look at, and what comes off the floor leaves by its own route. The staff eat in the Worker Commons like everyone else and answer questions with a shrug the compound has learned to read.

The Support Model Line.description: The production line for Yalven's support models, running in long precise cycles with minimal human presence and an attending crew who read it the way sailors read weather. Output is graded and route-coded before it reaches the lift. Watching the line run is the closest the Forgeworks comes to public spectacle. The line runs the length of the deep floor behind safety marking, warm and bright and almost unattended, with the crew walking it rather than working it. Apprentices are brought down to watch a full cycle early, on the theory that nobody who has seen it run will afterwards guess at a tolerance.

Corsair Estate.name: Corsair Estate
Corsair Estate.basicInfo:
House Corsair's family compound on the high west terrace, looking down over the whole interchange the family made. It is a compound rather than a single mansion: a main house, a row of guest houses, gardens, and a private landing terrace for family flight. Residence, leadership seat, and the family's private face. It stands above the Ledger District and the Forgeworks, reached by the terrace routes up from the working quarters or directly by air, and it is not a fortress and has never needed to be. The buildings are pale composite and weathered copper, comfortable rather than grand, arranged for a family that works and receives in the same rooms. Days run to family life, house business, guests, branch-family visits and the constant low pressure of leading a city by being difficult to replace rather than by title: there is no throne here, no council of lords and no civic crown, and the estate's authority rests entirely on everyone else needing the routes to keep working. The family, branch families, invited guests, staff and house security move through it continuously. From the outer walls the whole interchange is visible at once, quays and terraces and skyhooks, which is the reason the compound stands where it does.

Work on offer here: House Corsair — Three Branches, One Answer (ask Xyren Corsair).
Corsair Estate.hiddenInfo: Xyren leads House Corsair by being difficult to replace rather than by title, carrying Commerce he never trained for on top of Magic Branch responsibilities he did, and the Legacy Chamber kept for his father Torvex is the unresolved centre of that. What becomes of the room is an inheritance question the family has not been willing to open. Branch tension runs through the guest houses: which branches are thin, which are stationed elsewhere, and who has not been invited back. Maelrix is based at the Open Circle and Seryn crosses to the Redcourt, so the Estate's own members are embedded in the two institutions most likely to embarrass it. The Family Vault holds the Corsair end of agreements whose other ends sit in the Varriko bond vaults down the bank, which matters a great deal while a forged bond is circulating. The Security Wing logs everything that enters a compound that is deliberately not a fortress, and the Private Landing Terrace records who arrived without walking up past the working quarters.

Main Corsair House.description: The family's principal residence, a long building of pale composite and weathered copper, more comfortable than grand, with route-boards in the entrance hall because even here people check departures. Family meals happen at one table. Staff move through it constantly and are treated as part of the household rather than around it. The building runs long rather than tall, with wide doors, worn floors and rooms that open into one another, and it is warm in the way a house is warm when somebody is always in it. Guests are received in the rooms the family actually uses, and nothing is displayed for effect except the maps.

Xyren’s Office.description: The head of house's working room, holding both branches at once: magic references along one wall, route and cargo ledgers along the other, neither shelf tidy. Xyren works here late by preference. The newest sign from the Waypoint wall usually ends up leaning in a corner, unremarked and never thrown away. The room is smaller than its occupant's position suggests, lit by a working lamp long after the rest of the house is dark, and it opens onto a corridor rather than onto anything ceremonial. Anyone with something genuinely urgent is let in, which is why the door stands propped rather than shut.

Family Council Room.description: Where house decisions are argued out among the branches, around a table old enough to have heard the same arguments before. Magic, Commerce and Swordsmanship sit at it as equals in theory. In practice whoever can show that the route works wins, which is how Corsair has always settled things. It is a plain room with one long table, seating on every side and a display wall at the end for the only kind of argument that ever settles anything. Sessions run long and are not recorded. The household can tell how a meeting went by how quickly people leave the room afterwards. Branch representatives travel in for a full session, and the guest houses fill the night before one whether or not anybody has said what it is about.

Old Route-Map Gallery.description: A long gallery of historical route maps, from hand-drawn early charts to current live displays, tracing how the family made itself indispensable. Guests are walked through it deliberately and slowly. Several maps show routes that no longer exist, and one shows a Quilrath link that nobody stops to discuss. The gallery is lit low and hung along both walls, the earliest charts under glass and the live displays running at the far end. Guests are walked from oldest to newest, and the walk is the argument. It is the only part of the estate that makes a claim out loud, and it makes it entirely in routes.

Legacy Chamber for Xyren’s father.description: A quiet room kept for Torvex Corsair, who died in the Second Dravon Conflict: his effects, his ledgers, and the branch responsibilities that fell to a son already carrying another. Nobody in the family uses it casually. What eventually happens to this room is an inheritance question the house has not resolved. The room is kept as it was, plainly furnished and clean, ledgers shelved in his order rather than anyone else's and the shutters opened during the day. Nothing has been catalogued or removed. Members of the family go in alone and do not mention afterwards that they have. Staff clean it on the same round as the rest of the house, which is the only routine the room has.

Family Vault.description: Secured storage for house instruments, seals, contracts, and the objects a family keeps for what they mean rather than what they are worth. Access is limited and recorded. The vault holds the Corsair end of agreements whose other ends sit in the Varriko bond vaults down the bank, which is not currently comfortable. It is a controlled room rather than a spectacle, set behind the security wing, held at steady conditions and opened by arrangement. What is inside is indexed and mostly unremarkable to look at, and the record of an opening is kept whether or not anything was actually moved. Access is by arrangement rather than on request, and an arrangement made at short notice is itself a thing the household remembers.

Estate Gardens.description: Terraced planting along the compound's river side, maintained but not manicured, with benches placed for the view down over the working quarters. Business gets done walking here that would be impossible sitting down. From the outer wall the whole interchange, quays and terraces and skyhooks, reads as one machine. The planting steps down in rope-tan stone beds, kept alive rather than shaped, with gravel paths and benches at the turns, warm in the afternoon and windy at the wall. The household treats a long circuit of the gardens as a sign that something is being decided. Guests are walked out here when a conversation needs to happen without a table in the middle of it.

Corsair Estate Guest Row.description: A row of separate guest houses for visitors the Estate hosts directly, each with its own entrance and its own route-board. Being placed near the main house rather than at the far end of the row is a message, and every regular visitor knows how to read it. Overflow goes down to Merchant Row. The houses are modest and well kept, each with its own frontage, and the boards are in the halls because a guest here checks departures before breakfast. Staff service them between visits. Placement in the row is the estate's quietest instrument, and nobody has ever written the rule down. A guest who has been moved along the row between visits works out why before anyone tells them.

Branch Family Guest Houses.description: Quarters kept for Corsair branch families visiting from elsewhere, some of them occupied for months at a time. Furnishings are family rather than formal. This row carries the compound's real politics: which branches are thin, which are stationed away, and who has not been invited back recently. The houses are larger and plainer than the guest row's, furnished for stays measured in seasons rather than nights, with children's things left in them between visits. The row is quiet for months and then entirely full, and the household knows which it is going to be long before anything is announced. Branch families come for council sessions, for schooling, for work in the city, or because there is nowhere else to be.

Staff and Service Quarters.description: Living and working space for the household staff who keep a compound this size functioning: kitchens, stores, laundry, and the supply entrance. Long-serving staff know more about the family's rhythms than most of the family does. They are also the people guests forget are standing in the room. This is the working half of the compound, with the kitchens running from before dawn and deliveries coming up from the working quarters, and the pace here is steadier than anywhere else on the estate. The kitchens know who is in the house well before the council room does. Work here is organised around the family's schedule and reorganised around it again without comment whenever the schedule changes.

Security Wing.description: House security's base: watch rotations, access records, the gate and landing logs, and Korriven Corsair's standing arrangements. Unshowy and permanently staffed. The compound is not a fortress and is not meant to become one, but everything that enters it is written down somewhere in this wing. It is a plain set of rooms near the vault and the landing terrace, with watch displays and a duty desk that is never empty. The wing is deliberately undersized for a compound this large, because the estate is protected by being needed rather than by being defended, and the staff are courteous to guests and precise about names.

Private Landing Terrace.description: An open terrace on the high west edge where family and invited fliers arrive directly, bypassing the approach up from the working quarters. Wind screens, marker lights, and a clean drop to the terraces below. Who lands here rather than walking up is itself a statement, and the household notices every time. The surfacing is open composite with the screens along the inner edge and the lights set low, and the wind comes across it unbroken off the river. The landing log is kept in the security wing, so the fastest approach to the estate is also the most thoroughly recorded one. Family and invited fliers set down directly onto it; everyone else walks up through the working quarters and arrives having seen them.

Bankside Care Hall.name: Bankside Care Hall
Bankside Care Hall.basicInfo: Helvyra's independent care institution, wide and plain and chronically busy, with intake doors sized for a crane-injured rigger on a powered stretcher. It stands on the First Terrace, deliberately close to the working levels, with an emergency lift running straight down to the Barge Quays, so a serious accident at the waterline arrives here before the news of it does. It takes crush injuries off the quays, blade wounds from both sword schools and whatever travellers arrive carrying. There are no house colours anywhere in the building, and that is deliberate. The palette inside is neutral to the point of being a statement: pale composite, even working light, and plain signage rather than the bright route colour-codes that label everything else in the city. It is not Corsair, not house-run and not for sale, and its neutrality is treated as a civic asset by people who agree on very little else. Anyone who cannot pay is treated anyway. Dock crews, riggers, barge families, students from both banks and travellers wait in the same court and behave, because the custom is older than any current grievance and the staff enforce it without raising their voices. It is never quiet, and it has never finished being busy.
Bankside Care Hall.hiddenInfo: Meya Orlin is chief physician and has been logging an injury pattern that matches no known blade style, which puts her in quiet correspondence with Daxor Veltrax's forensic question on the other bank. Neither of them has said so publicly. The hall's neutrality is fierce and defended: students from Rux's school and the Redcourt wait in the same court and behave, Bank Wardens deliver river casualties without jurisdictional argument, and staff will refuse to confirm that a patient is here at all, to anyone, including a house. That refusal is currently being tested. Anyone who cannot pay is treated anyway, which means the hall sees the city's failures before any ledger does: the injuries that come in during a bad season tell you which trades are being pushed. The Morvane family supplies its botanicals, and the emergency lift runs straight down to the Barge Quays, so a serious quay accident arrives before the news of it does.

Intake Hall.description: Doors wide enough for a powered stretcher with a rigger still strapped to a load frame. Triage happens standing up in the doorway, with the injury logged before the name. Floor markings route arrivals by severity rather than by who brought them, which is the first thing the hall makes clear to anyone wearing a house crest. The hall is wide, low and stripped of anything that cannot be washed down, lit evenly so that nothing depends on where a person happens to be standing. Wardens bring river casualties in from one side and the emergency lift from the quays opens on the other. Staff call across the space in a shorthand of grades and bay numbers that visitors find alarming and that never rises in pitch.

Trauma Bays.description: Curtained bays with articulated tables and overhead systems that come down to the patient rather than the other way round. Crush and cable injuries, drops, blade wounds. Staff work fast and talk quietly, and the only raised voice is usually somebody's escort being walked back out to the waiting court. The bays run off a single corridor so equipment and staff can be pulled from one to the next without anyone leaving the working side, and the curtains are for dignity rather than secrecy: everything is audible and nobody comments. The systems overhead are entirely modern and entirely unglamorous. Dock injuries and training wounds are handled in adjacent bays as a matter of routine.

Recovery Ward.description: Rows of beds for people who cannot yet go back down the terraces, flight balconies shuttered, and a strict rule about visitors bringing work in with them. Barge crew recover beside Redcourt students. Conversations across the aisle are how a surprising amount of the city's cross-bank gossip actually travels. The shutters stay closed because a patient who can see a balcony begins calculating how soon they could use it, and there are no route-boards on these walls at all. Crews visit in numbers and are asked to come in fewer; families bring food up from the market halls. A factor arriving with a contract for a patient to sign is walked straight back out.

Physician's Office.description: Meya Orlin's room: a desk buried in case records, wall charts of injury patterns sorted by trade, and two chairs for the arguments she has with instructors from both sword schools. She wins those by outlasting them. One chart on the wall has no trade heading, and she offers no explanation for it. The room is small for its function and has never been reorganised, records stacked in an order only she can navigate, a single window onto the working side rather than the view. The charts are the office's real furniture: injuries by trade, by season, by school, each one an argument she has assembled rather than an opinion she holds. She keeps the door open by default, which makes the arguments semi-public.

Dispensary.description: A counter and a wall of locked cabinets stocked from Morvane botanicals and manufactured preparations, with a keeper who checks a grading seal before dispensing anything. Preparation happens behind a glass screen in full view. The ledger tracks what went where, not who paid, because frequently nobody did. Stock arrives from the market stall on the river's schedule and from manufactured suppliers on contract, and the keeper reconciles the two daily against what the wards have used. The seal check is not a formality: a grading mark that cannot be verified means the preparation does not leave the counter, whoever is waiting for it. Cabinets are locked, logged, and opened one at a time.

Quiet Room.description: A small plain room off the corridor for conversations that should not happen in a ward: a death, a diagnosis, a refusal to name a patient to someone who badly wants the name. Soft light, no window onto the hall, and a door that closes properly. Staff book it more often than they would like to. The furnishing is deliberately unmemorable, a few chairs and a water point and nothing to read, because the room is meant to be the least interesting place in the building. It is the only space in the hall where the working noise cannot be heard, and the silence lands harder than people expect. House representatives asking after a patient are received here, sitting down, and refused politely.

Waiting Court.description: An open courtyard where families, crews and escorts wait, with benches, a water point and a route-board nobody is really reading. Students from Rux's school and the Redcourt sit here at the same time and behave, because the custom is older than either school's grudge and the staff enforce it without raising their voices. The court is open to the sky and planted along one edge, which makes it the only part of the hall pleasant to sit in, and the benches are worn smooth where they face the intake doors. Crews come up from a shift still in working gear and wait through the evening, with food carried over from the market halls. Nobody is asked to leave at any hour.

The Emberward.name: The Emberward
The Emberward.basicInfo: The Emberward is Ignivex's central civic district and the city's public political floor: government halls opening onto heat-lit plazas, thermal fountains, fire sculptures and Volen banners standing in the open. Citizens from every district come here to gather, argue, celebrate and settle public matters where everyone can watch. The ground is worked in basalt-black stone with copper-bronze fittings, opened wide rather than built tall, so that sound carries and nothing said in the middle of a plaza stays there. The heat is engineered and deliberate, drawn off the geothermal network that keeps Ignivex independent of Contair-managed supply, and it comes off the sculptures and the fountain basins in steady waves residents stop registering and outsiders never quite do. Civic business runs from early shift: officials crossing between halls, families cutting through on errands, delegations walking under escort, newcomers stopping on the stairs because the scale and the air arrive together. Both family districts bring their business onto the same stones, which is why a repair count and the surrender argument get aired within earshot of each other. What the district refuses is privacy, and a grievance raised in the open is finished in the open. Ceremonies and civic announcements happen in front of a crowd, not behind a door.
The Emberward.hiddenInfo: Both family districts reach the Emberward, and that is the pressure in it. House Caldris arrives from the walls with repair counts and evacuation needs; House Meravil arrives from the record halls with casualty lists and ration forecasts, and the surrender argument gets aired on the same stones where Volen banners hang. Delegations from off-world are received here under watch, because Ignivex is connected but not widely open, and every visiting party is read for Dravon leanings before it reaches the Delegation Rooms. The Family Houses along the district's residential edge are ordinary civic housing and are not attributed to any House — the private Volen family seat is simply not part of the public district, and people who come looking for it in the Emberward do not find it. A challenge brought to the Challenge Ground is genuinely public: refusing it in front of the plaza costs more than losing it.

The Civic Halls.description: Ignivex's government halls front the plaza in basalt and copper, their interiors cooled by channelled heat rather than sealed against it. Civic business, hearings and administrative work run through them from early shift onward. Inside, the halls run high and plain, their floors worn pale along the lines people actually walk and their copper rails rubbed thin at every turn. Aides carry word between chambers while petitioners wait on benches against the walls, and a board at the entrance lists what is being heard that day and what has been deferred. The deferred list is read more closely than the other one. The tall doors are left open on purpose, so anyone standing outside can hear what is being decided inside.

The Ember Plaza.description: The district's great open floor, paved in dark stone with ember lines worked into the seams so the ground itself glows faintly at dusk. Crowds assemble here for ceremonies, arguments and celebrations, often all three in one evening. Underfoot the paving is dark, close-fitted and slightly uneven where generations of crowds have worn it, and the ember lines in the seams throw just enough light to cross by once the plaza fills. Nothing permanent stands on it, so the space stays open for whatever the city needs it for that evening: a ceremony, a hearing that spilled outdoors, a family shouting itself back into agreement. Ignivex citizens shout in public without shame, and the plaza is built wide enough to hold the noise.

The Fire Sculpture Walk.description: A colonnade of public fire sculptures, each a worked metal armature carrying restrained, shaped flame fed from the city's thermal supply. Citizens walk it slowly, and artisans maintain the pieces as a civic commission. Each armature is anchored into the paving and fed by its own regulated line, and the flame shapes differ from piece to piece, some held steady, some worked into a slow turning motion that catches the eye from across the plaza. Maintenance happens in the open, artisans crouched at a base checking fittings while people pass close enough to speak to them. Children are told not to touch the armatures and touch them anyway. The heat comes off them in even waves, warm enough to feel on the face but tuned never to scorch a passerby.

The Thermal Fountains.description: Geothermally fed fountains push steaming water through bronze basins at the plaza's edges, cooling it in stages before it runs out clean. People meet at them, rinse ash from their hands and talk where the noise of the water covers a conversation. The basins step down in stages, bronze darkened by mineral deposit at every rim, and the water goes from steaming to merely warm across the run. The ground around them stays damp and the noise is constant, which is why the fountains are where people bring the conversations they do not want carried across the open paving. Rinsing ash from hands and forearms before eating is ordinary manners here rather than ceremony. On cold nights the steam stands in columns high enough to be seen from the far side of the district.

The Family Houses.description: Ordinary civic housing built into the Emberward's inner blocks, sharing the district's heat supply and opening onto small stepped courts. Families here live above the city's political floor and hear every argument that happens on it. The blocks are close-built and stepped, with narrow stairs, shared landings and doors left open for the air, and every household draws its cooking and living heat from the same district supply. Laundry, argument and the smell of a meal move between floors without much resistance. Residents complain about the noise off the plaza in the same breath as they refuse to live anywhere quieter. No House emblem hangs over these doors; they are simply where Emberward residents live, work and raise children.

The Banner Stair.description: A broad ceremonial stair rising to the Civic Halls, hung with Volen banners because Volen leads the city and civic emblems default to Volen outside a family district. Processions form here before ceremonies. The steps are broad and shallow, cut from dark stone and worn smooth down the centre, wide enough for a procession to form across rather than in a column. Banner crews work the stair on ordinary mornings with poles and ties, checking cloth for scorch damage and rehanging whatever needs it. Citizens sit on the lower steps to eat and watch the plaza, and nobody moves them along unless a ceremony is forming. The cloth is heat-treated and hangs heavy, and replacing a scorched banner is a routine job nobody treats as symbolic.

The Announcement Step.description: A raised speaking step of dark stone set where the plaza narrows, used for civic announcements and public notices. Officials climb it, say the thing plainly and take the reaction. It is a plain block of dark stone with no rail and no shelter, deliberately unimpressive, so that whoever climbs it stands there with nothing to stand behind. The plaza narrows enough at that point for an unamplified voice to reach the back of a crowd. A notice frame beside the step carries the written version, and people gather to read it after the speaker has gone. Bad news is delivered from the same step as good news, and the crowd's habit of answering back is tolerated as normal Ignivex civic life.

The Challenge Ground.description: A marked circle of hardened flooring where public challenges are brought and answered in front of witnesses. It is civic rather than martial — the point is that the challenge and the response both happen in the open. The flooring inside the circle is hardened and a shade darker than the paving around it, and the boundary is cut into the stone rather than painted, so it cannot be scuffed away in the middle of a dispute. Challenges brought here are civic as often as personal: a broken agreement, a public insult, a question someone wants answered where witnesses can hear the answer. Onlookers ring the edge closely enough that stepping out of the circle is visible to everyone present.

The Delegation Rooms.description: Reception rooms off the Civic Halls where visiting delegations are received, cooled somewhat for guests unused to Ignivex conditions. Talks about trade, movement and standing pressure happen here across bronze tables. The rooms are low-ceilinged and screened, served by their own cooling channels, with bronze tables, water within reach and seating arranged so that no side takes the head of the room. Aides wait in the corridor while civic staff carry messages in and out. Visiting parties are read for Dravon leanings long before they reach these doors, and the reading does not stop once they are seated. The comfort is deliberate hospitality, and everyone in the room knows it is also a measurement of who needs it.

The Arrival Steps.description: The wide entry stair where newcomers first set foot in the civic district, arriving inward from the transit system. Guides, officials and relatives wait at the top. The stair is deliberately wide and shallow, with landings where someone can stop without blocking the flow, and civic staff keep water at the top for arrivals who need it. Guides sort newcomers by where they are going and by how well they are handling the air, which is information gathered by watching rather than by asking. Residents meeting family stand where they can be seen from below. First-time visitors usually stop halfway up, because the heat and the open scale of the plaza land at the same moment and both take getting used to.

The Crucible Yard.name: The Crucible Yard
The Crucible Yard.basicInfo: The Crucible Yard is Ignivex's training and discipline ground — not a tournament arena but a survival school, with floors and rings held at deliberately punishing temperatures. What is taught here is pain tolerance, hand-to-hand offense, breath control and restraint, all of it at once. The Yard is a working ground rather than a built showpiece: open floors, marked rings, sealed chambers and plain halls in basalt-black stone, with copper-bronze fittings and ember-line markings at the boundaries that matter. The heat is engineered and held high on purpose, fed from the same geothermal supply that runs the rest of the city, and the air above the working surfaces moves visibly. Sessions run in rotations from early morning, instructors calling corrections across the floor, students queueing at the water points, attendants pulling the ones who have stopped answering properly. A local tolerance for heat is not an affinity, and nobody on this ground confuses the two. Outsiders may watch from the edges with permission and are not invited onto the floors, because the conditioning temperatures that make the training work would make an unadapted visitor a casualty. Maeryn Volen instructs, and her standard is control rather than power.
The Crucible Yard.hiddenInfo: Korrvane trains people to win a match; the Crucible Yard trains people to keep moving after they have already been hit, because Ignivex expects to be attacked. That difference shows in who struggles here. Kaivor Volen's raw surges outrun his control, and the Restraint Trials exist precisely for students like him — Maeryn has little patience for anyone who confuses anger with strength, and she will fail a trainee for winning badly. Tessan Caldris trains alongside the Volen students, admires Oryn and wants to prove himself, which is its own hazard in a place where the instructors are watching for exactly that impulse. Trainees who overrun the heat end up at the Cooling Steps to recover; that is a routine functional relationship, not a scandal, though some students treat needing it as a defeat. The First Flame Ground is the ceremonial ground for the coming-of-age rite, and the rite tests the same qualities the Yard drills daily: controlled power, discipline, restraint.

The Heat Floor.description: The Yard's main working floor, a broad surface held at conditioning temperatures that outsiders cannot stand for long. Drills run across it in rotating groups from dawn. The surface is laid in dark heat-rated stone, marked out in ember lines for drill spacing and worn shiny along the routes the rotations take. Water points stand at the edges and are used constantly. Instructors work the floor rather than watch it, moving between groups, correcting a stance with a hand and a short word, pulling anyone whose colour or gait has changed. The air above it shimmers visibly, and instructors judge a trainee's state by their breathing long before the trainee is willing to admit anything is wrong.

The Breath Chambers.description: Sealed chambers where breath control is trained under regulated heat and thin, dry air. Students learn to pace lungs that want to panic, one session at a time. Each chamber is small and dark-walled, lined with plain benching, its heat and air regulated from a panel outside where an instructor watches the session through a narrow port. Students enter in small groups and leave in the same order. Sessions are ended from outside rather than from within, which is the part trainees find hardest to accept and the part they are told is not open to argument. The doors are heavy and the silence inside is total, which is why several trainees find these rooms harder than the Heat Floor despite nobody hitting them.

The Pain Line.description: A marked run of graded surfaces where pain tolerance is trained deliberately and in measured increments. Trainees cross it, stop, and cross it again. The run is a line of graded surfaces set into the floor, each harder to cross than the last, bounded in ember marking and worked in materials that hold their heat evenly. Instructors stand along it and ask questions, a name, a count, an instruction, listening for whether the answers still come back clean. Students who stop are walked off, treated, and put back on the first grade the following day. Nobody pretends it is pleasant; the instructors' only interest is whether a student can still think clearly and act at the far end of it.

Maeryn’s Instruction Ring.description: Maeryn Volen's own ring, smaller and harder-floored than the duel rings, where she takes students one and two at a time. Her corrections are short and physical. The ring is small enough that there is nowhere to retreat to, floored harder than the duel rings and bare of anything decorative. Maeryn works from inside it rather than from the edge, and the students waiting their turn stand close enough to hear every correction she gives. Her own expression of fire is precision, heat held exactly where she puts it, and she treats that as a standard to teach toward rather than a thing to display. A trainee who lands a wild, furious hit here is stopped immediately and made to repeat it slowly, because control is the only thing she grades.

The Duel Rings.description: A row of controlled sparring rings with reinforced boundaries and raised edges, used for supervised duels between trainees. Matches are stopped early and often. The rings sit in a row with raised reinforced edges and floors that run hot, each overseen by an instructor who stops bouts on breath and stance rather than on damage. Trainees queue along the boundary and call the next pairing among themselves. Argument about a stopped match is permitted, loudly, and changes the ruling almost never. The rings run hot enough that a bout ending on the floor ends fast, which teaches footwork more efficiently than any lecture does.

The First Flame Ground.description: The Yard's ceremonial ground for the First Flame coming-of-age rite, kept clear and unused between ceremonies. It tests controlled power, discipline and restraint — the qualities drilled everywhere else in this district. The ground is kept swept and empty between ceremonies, a plain marked circle with a low surround where families stand, and nothing about it is dressed for the occasion. Preparation is practical: the surface checked, the surround cleared, the order of candidates set. A candidate who produces something spectacular without holding it is understood by everyone present to have failed. Families ring the ground on the day, and the silence before a candidate begins is the loudest thing in the Yard.

The Restraint Trials.description: Purpose-built trials where trainees are pressured, provoked and measured on what they do not do. Stopping short, pulling a strike and standing down all score. The trial spaces are enclosed and deliberately awkward, with instructors and senior students running provocation in relays, insults, feints, interruptions, unfair calls, while the trainee under test is scored on what they hold back. Sessions are short and repeated often. What is recorded is stops, pulled strikes and stand-downs, and a trainee's file here counts toward readiness as much as anything on the Heat Floor. Students who have spent years being praised for aggression find this the most humiliating ground in the city, which is exactly the intent behind it.

Student Quarters.description: Plain shared lodging for trainees, with cooled sleeping alcoves, equipment lockers and a communal wash line. Injuries, rivalries and homesickness all come back here at the end of the day. The quarters are plain and close-packed: alcoves cooled just enough for sleep, lockers scratched with the marks of everyone who has used them, and a wash line where gear is scrubbed of ash and blood in the same bucket. Students eat communally and cook almost nothing. Visitors are family or nobody, and the day's injuries are compared across the alcoves with more pride than sense. The walls are thin enough that a student crying after a bad session is heard, and the Yard's unwritten rule is that nobody mentions it.

The Instructors’ Hall.description: The instructors' working hall, where training rotations are set, trainee records kept and arguments about a student's readiness settled among themselves. Bronze-framed boards track each cohort. The hall is a working room with a long table, bronze-framed boards down one wall and a heat source at the centre that gets used for meals as much as for anything else. Rotations, injuries, ceremonies and equipment are all settled here in the same conversation. Instructors disagree openly about students, and the disagreement is usually over whether a trainee is dangerous to others or only to themselves. Instructors eat here between sessions, and a name spoken twice in one week over that table usually means someone is about to be pulled from the floor.

Caldris Wallworks.name: Caldris Wallworks
Caldris Wallworks.basicInfo:
Caldris Wallworks is House Caldris's district and Ignivex's defensive infrastructure quarter, built along fortified interior wall routes, emergency response lanes, firebreak gates and reinforced maintenance corridors. Basalt-black walls carry copper-bronze reinforcement, muted red lights, heavy thermal shutters and ember-line markings, with Caldris emblems on gates and armor racks. The district is built to be held. Fortified interior wall routes run through it, firebreak gates stand at the joins between what can be sealed and what cannot, and reinforced corridors let crews and residents move under cover between depots, gates and shelters. An ordinary day is inventory, drills, breach repair and patrol preparation: response crews turning out from the depots, wall-runners moving fast along the elevated routes, wardens timing shelter access against real capacity, patrols forming up for the contested outer territory. The house's business is civilian protection, and it holds that surrender is not strategy but infection. The memorial stones naming defenders who died holding breach points stand in the corridors people walk every day rather than in any hall built for the purpose. Drills, repairs, staging and readiness are the ordinary business of the day.

Work on offer here: House Volen — Through the Heat (ask Varessa Volen).
Caldris Wallworks.hiddenInfo: The Wallworks exists because Ignivex is attacked often enough that defense has become architecture — this is not ceremony like the Emberward or training pride like the Crucible Yard. Davor Caldris personally held a breach gate during a Dravon raid, and the house's position follows from that: loyal to Volen, and certain that surrender is not strategy but infection. Rava Caldris runs emergency response with no patience for pride when civilians are at risk, which puts her at odds with Volen aggression more often than either side advertises. Maedra Caldris designs the firebreak gates and is deliberately not Contair-trained, keeping the city's defenses locally sourced in the same spirit as its power. Orvak Caldris's patrols stage from here into the Dravon-Contested Outer Territory, whose position and extent are undefined; Tessan trains at the Crucible Yard and wants to prove himself, which is watched closely here. Lysa Caldris coordinates the civilian shield out into the Hearth Rows.

Caldris Family Halls.description: The house's own halls, functional rather than grand, where Davor Caldris holds the family's business and its arguments. Emblems mark the doors without fanfare. Inside they are solid and low-lit, laid out for work: a long table, boards carrying gate states and repair counts, gear stacked along one wall and living quarters behind. Davor is broad, quiet and hard to provoke, and the family's habit of disagreeing with him in front of witnesses is treated as ordinary rather than as a challenge. Visitors expecting a noble seat find a working command building with people eating at the same tables they plan from.

Emergency Response Depots.description: Depots holding Rava Caldris's response equipment, staged for immediate deployment and checked constantly. Crews turn out from here at speed. The depots are wide-doored and plainly built, gear staged in fixed positions on marked floor, lockers loaded to a standing list, and nothing parked where it would have to be moved to clear a turnout. Rava Caldris runs them and checks them constantly. Crews sleep in rotation on site during pressure, and a responder who leaves a piece of kit out of place hears about it from whoever trips on it at the next alert. The depot floor is kept clear to a standard that looks obsessive until the first alert of the day makes the reason obvious.

Firebreak Gate Control Rooms.description: Control rooms governing the firebreak gates that can seal a district's heat and fire away from its neighbours. Operators monitor gate states continuously. The rooms are small, reinforced and dim, with gate-state boards, manual releases and sightlines or feeds covering each gate's approach, and they are staffed continuously rather than only during alerts. Operators track heat and pressure together. The procedure is written down and the operators still argue about it in the quiet hours, because no written version describes every way a district can be losing. Closing a gate protects one side and traps the other, and the people in these rooms are the ones who have to make that call in seconds.

Breach Repair Yards.description: Working yards where breached wall sections are rebuilt and reinforced materials are cut, fitted and staged for the next repair. Work runs at all hours after a raid. The yards are open and heavily stocked, with cutting stations, material racks, staging bays for prepared sections and lifting gear for anything too heavy to carry. Work runs in shifts through the night after a raid, and the noise off them is one of the ways the district measures how bad the last one was. Crews finish a repair and then rehearse fitting it faster than they just did. The yards keep damaged sections on display as references, and crews know each one by which attack produced it.

Civilian Shelter Access Points.description: Hardened access points where civilians enter the protected shelter network during an alert, marked with ember-line guidance and wide enough for crowds. Wardens direct the flow. The access points are hardened openings with heat-sealed doors and wide approaches, ember-line guidance running into them from every direction a crowd might arrive from. Wardens stand at each one during an alert and at every drill. Households are counted through by assignment, and a warden who finishes a count short holds the next group at the door until the shortfall has been chased. Drills here are timed against real capacity, and a route that fails its timing gets rebuilt rather than excused.

Wall-Runner Routes.description: Narrow elevated routes along the interior wall network, used by wall-runners moving fast between positions with minimal gear. Young scouts like Tessan Caldris work them. They run with handholds, staged rest points and gear caches set where a runner can reach them without descending, and they are checked after every raid for damage that would not be visible from below. Runners carry messages, spot damage and move ahead of the crews. Tessan works them, admiring Oryn Volen and wanting the kind of proof that only real fighting gives, which the house keeps trying to redirect into survival. The routes are unforgiving of showing off, which is precisely why the house lets its ambitious young run them.

Patrol Staging Platforms.description: Staging platforms where patrols form up, load and depart, including Orvak Caldris's patrols into the contested outer territory. Kit checks are done aloud and twice. The platforms are open staging decks with load racks, water and equipment stations, marked out so that one patrol can form, kit and depart without crossing another. Orvak Caldris's crews go out into the contested territory from here and come back to the same boards. He knows the difference between a real attack, a probe and bait, and the briefings he gives on these decks are built around telling the three apart. What comes back from those patrols in the way of information is passed on carefully, since the border's extent is not something anyone here can state.

Heat-Resistant Supply Lockers.description: Banks of heat-resistant lockers holding protective gear, consumables and emergency stock for both responders and civilians. Contents are rotated and logged. The lockers stand in banks along the corridors and inside the depots, marked by contents, sealed, and opened against a log anyone on shift may read. Protective gear, consumables and civilian emergency stock share the same rotation. A locker is restocked the moment it is drawn from rather than at the end of a shift, a rule written after a night when the second crew found what the first crew had left. A locker found short during a check is a serious matter in this district, treated as a failure of the house rather than of an individual.

Fortified Neighborhood Corridors.description: Reinforced corridors threading through the district's built fabric, letting crews and residents move under cover between gates, depots and shelters. They carry the daily traffic of the Wallworks. The corridors run broad enough for two crews to pass with a stretcher between them, roofed, reinforced and lined with the district's emblems and posted guidance. Daily traffic moves through them constantly: shift changes, deliveries, families taking a covered route between errands. They are swept and inspected the way a wall is inspected, because that is what they are. Thermal shutters punctuate them at intervals, and the muted red lighting never quite goes out.

Defender Memorial Stones.description: Set memorial stones naming defenders who died holding breach points, placed along the corridors where people pass them daily rather than in a dedicated hall. Names are added with little ceremony. The stones are set flush into the corridor walls at head height, cut plainly with names and nothing else, sited where the district's daily traffic passes them rather than in any dedicated hall. New names are added by the same crews who repair the gates. The house's philosophy is that the wall remembers who stood there, and these stones are how the wall does it. Responders touch or pass them without comment, and the habit is taught to new crews by example.

Maedra’s Gate Workshop.description: Maedra Caldris's design workshop, where firebreak gate mechanisms are drafted, modelled and tested against local conditions. Her work is deliberately not Contair-trained. The workshop is part drafting room and part test floor, drawings pinned in layers, component stock racked by size, and a rig built into the far wall where mechanisms are cycled against local conditions until they fail. Maedra Caldris works late and alone by preference. Her gates are heavier and rougher than Contair designs and she says so first, before anyone else gets the chance. Prototype gate sections stand along one wall in various states of failure, kept as evidence of what she has already ruled out.

The Armor Racks.description: Racks of maintained defensive gear standing ready near the depots and halls, each set marked with the Caldris emblem. Crews draw from them at the start of a shift. They stand in the open rather than in a store, sets hung by size with maintenance benches alongside and a log for damage and repair kept where anyone drawing gear can read it. Ignivex's standardized sets are fitted, treated and maintained locally, and a piece that comes back damaged is on a bench before the responder who wore it has finished reporting. Armor here is repaired and reissued rather than retired, and a well-scarred set is considered better than a new one.

Meravil Ash Hall.name: Meravil Ash Hall
Meravil Ash Hall.basicInfo:
Meravil Ash Hall is House Meravil's district and Ignivex's civic-administrative quarter, handling casualty records, continuity planning, ration forecasting and political meetings. Ash-gray stone, black glass, muted bronze and pale ember lighting give it a cooler, more controlled feel than the Volen and Caldris districts, helped by cooling channels that make it easier on outsiders. The district is built low and screened, lit in a pale ember light that never reaches the brightness of a Volen plaza, and its cooling channels give a relief outsiders notice within a few steps. Its ordinary business is paperwork with consequences: casualty records consulted daily by families searching for a name, continuity offices planning what still runs after a bad week, ration and displacement scenarios modelled against damage reports, archive vaults holding proceedings sent on from across the city. The thin red ring and pale ash spiral of the Meravil emblem mark record halls, archive doors and administrative seals, while public Volen emblems still stand in the district's city-facing spaces. The district does not feel cowardly; it feels exhausted, and the suspicion attached to it is about its politics and its Dravon ties rather than its comfort. Where Volen districts shout and Caldris districts brace, Meravil calculates.

Work on offer here: Ignivex — Rows After the Raid (ask Ilvara Meravil).
Meravil Ash Hall.hiddenInfo: The district does not feel cowardly; it feels exhausted. House Meravil's surrender-leaning politics come from casualty lists, grieving families, damaged homes, civilian exhaustion and ration forecasts rather than from treachery by default — and the house is not a monolith. Seralyne Meravil leads it as a mother afraid resistance will kill her child. Vennik Meravil operates politically. Auralis Meravil dissents against surrender from inside the house, which makes the Controlled Meeting Rooms genuinely contested ground rather than a rubber stamp. Caevan Meravil's marriage to Nyssara Dravon makes the whole district a living pressure point, and suspicion in Ignivex attaches to exactly that tie and to Meravil's politics — not to the district's physical comfort, whatever people say in the Emberward. Ilvara Meravil keeps the casualty records and the civic continuity function, so families searching for a name come here, and the numbers they are given become the argument.

Meravil Family Hall.description: The house's principal hall in ash-gray stone and black glass, where Seralyne Meravil receives and the family's formal business is conducted. Public Volen emblems still appear in its city-facing spaces. The hall is broad and low, its ash-gray walls broken by panels of black glass, seating arranged for conversation rather than for audience and no raised position anywhere in the room. Seralyne receives here and is careful in public. Staff move quietly out of habit, and guests are offered water and cooled seating before anybody asks what they have come about. The room is deliberately calm, and the calm is doing considerable work for a family under this much strain.

Casualty Record Chambers.description: Chambers holding Ignivex's casualty records, maintained under Ilvara Meravil's authority and consulted daily. Families come to search for a name. The chambers are lined with record cases in muted bronze, palely lit and kept cool, reading tables set apart from one another so that nobody searching has to do it beside a stranger. Requests are made at a counter and fetched rather than browsed. Ilvara Meravil's people keep the ordering exact, because the only thing worse than a family finding a name is a family being told to come back tomorrow. Staff have learned to hand over a record and then simply wait, because there is nothing useful to say in the interval that follows.

Civic Continuity Offices.description: Offices planning for the city's continued function through siege, raid and loss — services, staffing, replacement and succession of civic roles. The work is unglamorous and relentless. The offices are plain working rooms with wall boards tracking services, staffing and the succession of civic roles, and they are busiest in the days after a raid rather than during one. Officers work in pairs and check each other's assumptions out loud. The planning is deliberately unheroic, and the phrase these rooms use is not victory but what still runs. Continuity officers think in terms of what still runs after a bad week, which colours how they hear every Volen speech.

Ration And Displacement Planning Rooms.description: Planning rooms where ration forecasts and displacement scenarios are modelled against damage and population figures. Projections cover the walls in pale ember light. The rooms are large, screened and quiet, with working tables and stacks of damage reports cross-checked against housing records before anything is modelled at all. Planners argue over assumptions at length and in detail, and treat an unexamined assumption as worse than a bad one. Volen visitors read the same figures and reach different conclusions from them, and the planners have stopped expecting that to change. These numbers are the raw material of the surrender argument, which is why people from outside the house ask to see them and are rarely refused.

Quiet Negotiation Salons.description: Cooled salons furnished for small, careful conversations that are not meetings of record. Talks happen here that could not happen in the Emberward. The salons are small cooled rooms with soft seating and screened doors, arranged so that two or three people can talk without any of them facing an audience. Water and food arrive without being asked for. Nothing said here is minuted, which is what the rooms are for, and everyone who uses them understands that the absence of a record protects both sides of a conversation equally. The comfort is calculated hospitality — an outsider relaxing in a Meravil salon is a person slightly easier to read.

Heat-Moderated Interior Courtyards.description: Interior courts served by the district's cooling channels, planted and shaded, noticeably kinder than core Volen areas. Staff take meals in them. The courts are enclosed and planted, with low walls to sit on and shade across most of the paving, and the air in them is the kindest in the district. Clerks, planners and record staff take their meals out here in shifts, and families waiting on a record are directed to them rather than left standing in a corridor. The planting is kept by the house's own staff and is the one thing in the district nobody has ever argued about. Visitors from other districts enjoy the relief and then feel obliged to make a joke about it, which residents have heard many times.

Archive Vaults.description: The city's archive vaults, holding records, proceedings and rulings sent on from across Ignivex including the Smoke Court's. Access is controlled and logged. The vaults are sealed rooms behind bronze-fitted doors, cooler and drier than anywhere else in the district, cases stacked floor to ceiling with narrow aisles between them. Nothing leaves without a signature and a stated reason. Clerks retrieve on request while the requester waits outside, and the waiting is where most people first understand how much of this city is written down in here. The vaults are the reason people say the house that counts the dead also holds everything anyone has ever said under pressure.

Memorial Record Walls.description: Walls carrying the recorded names of the city's losses, thin red ring motifs marking the entries by year. Families come to stand rather than to search. The hall exists for nothing else: ash-gray stone faced smooth, the names cut in rather than posted, lit palely and cooled like the record chambers, with no seating, no attendant and no ceremony attached to coming. Families arrive and stand, sometimes for a long time, and the district's staff have learned to take the long way round rather than pass behind them. The walls have been extended more than once, and the joins are visible enough that people count them.

Controlled Meeting Rooms.description: Formal meeting rooms for political business, sealed and minuted, where the surrender question is argued inside the house and with the city. Auralis Meravil dissents in these rooms. The rooms are sealed and plain, a table, a clerk's position and doors that close properly, and everything said in them is minuted as a matter of course. Sessions are scheduled and run long. Auralis Meravil dissents against surrender from inside her own house in these rooms, which is tolerated, recorded, and quietly used by both sides of the wider argument as evidence that House Meravil is not a monolith. Sessions run long, and the arguments made here are calculated rather than shouted.

Intermediary Corridors.description: Discreet corridors used by political intermediaries moving between salons, meeting rooms and the family hall without crossing public space. Traffic through them is quiet and constant. They are narrow, dim and unmarked, finished plainly and lit only enough to walk by, turning often enough that a corridor is never visible along its whole length, and no door along any of them cannot be closed. Ordinary staff use them for ordinary errands as well, which is the cover that makes them usable at all. Nobody keeps a record of who passes through. Being seen entering one is information in itself, which is why some people take the long way instead.

Ilvara’s Record Desk.description: Ilvara Meravil's own desk, where casualty records and civic continuity work meet in one set of ledgers. She works methodically and late. The desk is heavy and bronze-fitted, covered in open ledgers kept in an order only she maintains, set where she can see both the chamber doors and the people waiting at them. Casualty records and continuity work meet on the same surface because to her they are one piece of work. She does not hate House Volen; she hates funerals becoming ordinary, and she says so to anyone who asks her which side she is on. People who come expecting a clerk find someone who can recite what the city has lost from memory, and would rather not have to.

The Ash Spiral Court.description: The district's central court, its floor laid in an ash-gray spiral with thin red rings worked through it, cooled and unhurried. Everything in Meravil Ash Hall opens off it. It is broad and open, wide enough that crossing it takes a moment, and the pale ember light falls evenly over every part of the pattern. Staff, families and visitors all cross it, and the district's halls and offices open off it on every side. There is nothing posted on its walls and nowhere provided to sit down, and both of those are decisions. Crossing it, people lower their voices without being asked, which is the clearest statement the district makes about itself.

The Red Forges.name: The Red Forges
The Red Forges.basicInfo:
The Red Forges is Ignivex's forge and craft district, and it is culturally prestigious rather than merely industrial. Metalwork houses, thermal crafting lines and heat-channel machinery run advanced thermal engineering at district scale, turning out shaped weapons, treated armor and fine craft work. The district is built around its heat rather than merely subjected to it: heat-channel machinery runs beneath and through the workshops, thermal crafting lines hold temperatures no hand can judge, and the metalwork houses stand tall-roofed under extraction hoods and shielding. Basalt-black walls carry copper-bronze bracing, the light is the working light of open metal, and the noise is constant and layered. An ordinary day is masters, journeymen and apprentices sharing floors by rotation, masters taking on apprentices by word and handshake, buyers arriving for commissions, and rare material released only on a master's say-so. Local fitting, thermal craft and armor treatment happen here, which is what gives Ignivex's standardized sets their working identity. The district's standing tension is that when a piece fails nobody can prove whether it was rivalry, a Dravon hand or plain bad work, and all three get said aloud. Guild standing, apprenticeships and family workshops set the social order here.

Work on offer here: Ignivex — Keep the Fires Lit; Ignivex — The Remade Commission (ask Tavren Halessin).
The Red Forges.hiddenInfo: When a piece fails in the Red Forges, nobody can tell immediately whether the cause was a rival, a Dravon agent or simply bad work — and all three accusations get made, often the same day. That ambiguity is the district's live tension: standing Dravon pressure targets systems rather than open walls, so sabotage is a real possibility, but so is wounded pride looking for somewhere to land. The Rivalry Yard is where those arguments surface publicly; the Rare Materials Store is where they get expensive. Inside the Halessin workshop the same pattern runs in miniature. Maeron, Nessa and Tavren Halessin make window panes for the trade and take one commission at a time for pride, and a ruined commission is being quietly remade after hours. All three hold competing private theories about whose fault the ruin was, and none of them has said theirs aloud — which is the only reason the family is still working smoothly.

Metalwork Houses.description: The district's core workshops, tall-roofed halls where metal is worked at scale under extraction hoods and heat shielding. Masters, journeymen and apprentices share the floor by rotation. The halls run high and open, roofed for extraction, furnaces banked along one side and working floors laid in heat-rated stone that stays warm through the night. Overhead rigging carries pieces too heavy to lift by hand. Water, salt and somewhere to sit are kept at every entrance, because heat adaptation is not immunity and the houses gave up pretending otherwise a long time ago. The noise is constant and layered, and craftspeople here read a piece's readiness by colour and sound long before an instrument confirms it.

Thermal Crafting Lines.description: Engineered production lines that hold precise temperatures across a whole run, used for work that cannot tolerate variation. Operators watch readouts as closely as they watch the metal. The lines are enclosed runs with instrumented stages, fed from the district's heat channels and monitored from standing positions along their length where operators watch the readouts and the metal in the same glance. Nothing on a line is hurried and nothing is left unattended. A stoppage is logged with the name of whoever called it, which makes calling one a small act of courage for an operator still building standing. A line that drifts even slightly is shut down immediately, because in this district a flawed batch is never allowed to be only a technical problem.

The Heat-Channel Machinery.description: The machinery that routes and regulates working heat through the district — channels, regulators and transfer assemblies threaded under and through the workshops. Engineers service it constantly. The assemblies run under the workshop floors and up through the walls in copper-bronze runs, with valves, regulators and transfer housings reachable from maintenance gratings that people cross a dozen times a shift without looking down. Engineers service them in rotation and keep their own separate log. The machinery is local work, locally maintained, and the district says so often enough that visitors notice the emphasis. Standing on the maintenance gratings, the throb of the channels comes up through the soles of the boots before it is audible.

The Artisan Guild Halls.description: The guild halls where craft standing is recorded, apprenticeships are registered and masters argue over standards. Commissions are brokered here as well as judged. The halls are formal in a plain way, long tables, record walls, bronze-framed boards listing registered apprentices and open commissions, and the doors stay open to the district's noise rather than shutting it out. Masters attend because absence is read as a position. Rulings are posted where anyone can read them, and the crowd that gathers around a contested one is larger than the crowd that sat through the hearing. A guild ruling on whether a failed piece was bad work or bad luck carries real weight, which is why the arguments in these halls are rarely calm.

Weapon Shaping Floors.description: Open floors dedicated to shaping weapons, with anchored forms, shaping presses and quench assemblies set in the stone. The work is methodical and unhurried. The floors are anchored heavily, forms set into the stone, shaping presses standing in line and quench assemblies plumbed straight into the district's supply. The work is done by pairs and small teams who have worked together long enough not to need to speak. Pieces are tested before they leave, and a smith who declines to test in front of a buyer has effectively withdrawn the commission. Ignivex weaponry is expected to survive being used badly, and a smith who cannot explain their tolerances does not get a second commission.

Armor Treatment Baths.description: Treatment baths where armor is heat-cycled and finished, sunk into a shielded floor and worked with long bronze rigging. Pieces come out darkened and hard. The air above them shimmers even by this district's standards, and the floor around each one is kept clear and dry as a matter of standing discipline. Treatment runs in cycles that cannot be interrupted, so crews work in shifts and hand over mid-process. Ignivex's standardized sets come through here for fitting and finishing, and local treatment is what gives equipment obtained from Contair its Ignivex working identity. The chemical smell carries further than the heat does, and armorers claim they can tell a good batch by that smell alone.

Family-Run Workshops.description: The district's smaller family shops, each with its own furnace, bench line and household living space behind or above the work floor. Skills pass down inside these walls. Each shop is a single working room with the household's rooms adjoining it, furnace at one end, bench line down the side, and a door onto the lane that stands open whenever work is on. Children grow up on the floor and are given real tasks early. Meals happen at the bench as often as at a table, and a household's entire standing rests on work that leaves by that one door. Custody of a family's technique matters more here than guild rank, and a workshop losing its last trained child is a quiet local tragedy.

The Apprentice Benches.description: Long shared benches where apprentices do repetitive work under supervision until their hands stop arguing with them. Failures are kept and displayed. The benches run long and shared under plain light, the day's repetitive work set out in quantity: forms to be matched, fittings to be finished, the same joint made again until the hands stop arguing. Supervisors walk the line and say very little. Water is compulsory and taken at a called interval, which is one of the few rules in this district nobody treats as negotiable. Being allowed to take a bench nearest the working floor is the district's first real promotion, and everyone at the benches knows the order exactly.

The Rare Materials Store.description: A secured store holding rare and difficult materials, issued against guild authorisation and logged on release. Buyers wait while a request is checked. The store is a secured room with a counter, a logbook and shelving behind a grille, kept cooler than the workshops so that what it holds behaves predictably. Requests are made in writing against guild authorisation and checked before anything crosses the counter. The keeper releases by weight and signature and does not care whose commission is waiting, which makes this simultaneously the most orderly and the most resented room in the district. When a commission fails, the first argument is almost always about what came out of this store and who signed for it.

The Halessin Workshop.description: The Halessin glasswright shop: window panes for the trade by day, one pride commission at a time on the side. Maeron, Nessa and Tavren work it as a family. The shop is small and scrupulously clean, panes racked by size, the working bench set under the best light and a kiln line at the back running off the district's heat supply. Trade work pays for the room; the pride commission sits under cloth whenever there are customers in it. Maeron, Nessa and Tavren speak to one another in a shorthand nobody else in the lane can follow. A ruined commission is being quietly remade after hours, and the three of them keep three competing theories about whose fault the ruin was, none of them spoken.

The Rivalry Yard.description: An open yard between the larger workshops where competing craftspeople settle standing in public — comparisons, accusations and the occasional formal wager over quality. Work gets carried out and laid side by side. The yard is open, hard-floored and deliberately public, with benches and a set of trestles anyone may claim for laying work out. Comparisons are made piece against piece in the open rather than by argument alone. The district treats this as legitimate and even useful, and the guild halls quietly prefer a rivalry settled out here to one that arrives on their tables. A sabotage accusation made in this yard is heard by the whole district within the hour.

Geothermal Core Facilities.name: Geothermal Core Facilities
Geothermal Core Facilities.basicInfo:
The Geothermal Core Facilities are the player-facing access point to Ignivex's geothermal power network — heat tunnels, pressure chambers, thermal conduits, turbine halls and maintenance routes built into and beneath the city. This is local power, heat regulation, defensive pressure systems, transit support and emergency infrastructure, maintained by Ignivex crews. What can be reached here is the accessible face of a larger distributed system, and the rest stays as it is: the network's extent, depth, capacity and interconnections are not published, not drawn, and not discussed with people who have no business knowing them. The accessible portions are shored in heat-rated material and lit in low amber, marked at every junction with posted limits that crews treat as absolute, and loud enough in the turbine halls to force hand signals. Work is continuous: inspection rotations, conduit checks logged twice, pressure readings taken by gauge and by feel, repair teams living in the maintenance routes for the duration of a fault. Rated gear is mandatory and heat adaptation is no substitute for it. This is also the city's largest single exposure, which is why an unexplained pressure drop is treated as a possible act before it is treated as a fault. Tharen Volen oversees major parts of the network.

Work on offer here: Ignivex — Heat Below the Streets (ask Tharen Volen).
Geothermal Core Facilities.hiddenInfo: This is why Ignivex can refuse Contair-managed infrastructure and refuse Dravon in the same breath, and the city's pride in that self-sufficiency is real — resilience under siege is built into the design. It is also the city's largest single exposure. Geothermal sabotage can threaten entire districts, and standing Dravon pressure targets systems rather than open walls, which is why the Sabotage Watch Points exist and why a cracked conduit is investigated as a possible act before it is written off as wear. Tharen Volen's battlefield is underground: heat tunnels, pressure chambers, thermal gates, sabotage points and geothermal engines that would kill most outsiders in minutes. Caldris Wallworks connects here, tying the power network directly to the city's defense. What a player can reach is the accessible face of the network, not the network — its plant count, topology, depth, capacity and full underground extent are undefined, and parts of the system stay hidden.

The Heat Tunnels.description: The main working tunnels driven into the geothermal formation, shored in heat-rated material and lit in low amber. Crews move through them in rated gear on fixed rotations. The tunnels run rough-walled and shored, wide enough for two crew in gear and no wider, cable and conduit bracketed overhead and the amber lighting set low enough that a crew's own lamps do most of the work. Air moves through them constantly and dries everything it touches. Rotations are called in at the head of the tunnel and called out again on return, and a crew running late generates a response before anyone asks whether it was necessary. Time limits are posted at every junction, and nobody down here treats them as advisory.

The Pressure Chambers.description: Chambers where working pressure is held, stepped and released, walled in reinforced shielding and instrumented at every seam. Engineers read them by gauge and by feel. The chambers are heavily shielded rooms with stepped inlets, relief assemblies and instrument clusters at every seam, entered through doors that take two people to work. Readings are taken standing at the gauges rather than remotely, because the remote feed is the second opinion and never the first. Nothing in here is adjusted alone, and the rule holds for the engineers who have worked the chambers longest. The chambers make a deep irregular knocking as they cycle, and crews learn the healthy rhythm within a week.

The Thermal Conduits.description: The conduit runs distributing heat out to the districts, the forges and the transit system, inspected on a continuous schedule. A cracked conduit is a citywide problem. The runs are bracketed housings that shift and settle as they load, following the walls and roofs of the service ways where crews can reach them. Inspectors walk them section by section with lamps and instruments, checking seams, brackets and shielding. A section under repair is isolated and announced, because a district losing supply without warning is a civic incident and not merely an engineering one. Inspectors photograph and log every fault twice, because the second record is the one asked for when sabotage is suspected.

The Turbine Halls.description: Halls of geothermal turbines converting the city's underground heat into usable power, loud enough that crews work by hand signal. Output boards line the walls. The halls are the loudest rooms in Ignivex, machinery standing in ranks beneath gantries, the air moving hard and the floor carrying a vibration that never stops. Crews wear ear protection and speak by hand, and any conversation that needs words happens in the sealed side rooms. The boards are read at a glance by people who have read them for years and can tell from a single needle that something upstream has changed. This is the machinery Ignivex points to when anyone suggests it accept Contair-managed infrastructure instead.

The Maintenance Routes.description: Service routes threading between the halls, chambers and conduits, narrow and heavily marked. Repair teams live in them during a fault. They are narrow enough that two crew pass sideways, marked at every branch with colour, symbol and posted limits, with kit, water and rated gear cached along them at intervals and a call point wherever a branch could be taken wrongly. The relays work around the clock and sleep where they stop, and food carried down from the surface arrives cold and is warm by the time anyone opens it. The routes are mapped in detail for crews and deliberately not published anywhere else, which is a choice rather than an oversight.

The Emergency Access Paths.description: Dangerous emergency paths running through the facility, kept passable for reaching failures fast when the ordinary routes are compromised. They are genuinely hazardous. The paths run where nothing else does, alongside live runs, through sections that are not shut down for anybody, past shielding that is rated rather than generous. They are marked and maintained and never made comfortable. Crews train on them in full gear and in sequence, which is the reason they get used correctly by people who are frightened at the time. Crews are trained on them anyway, because the alternative is losing a district while waiting for a safer way in.

The Thermal Gates.description: Heavy gates isolating sections of the network so a failure in one part can be cut off from the rest. Operating one commits the crews on the far side. The gates are massive shielded assemblies set at section boundaries, worked from control positions beside them and from the overseer station, with a manual backup that takes two crews and a great deal of time. Indicators above each one show its state to anyone passing. Closing a gate isolates a failure and seals in whatever is on the wrong side of it, and the crews on both sides know exactly what a changing indicator means. The decision is taken quickly and argued about afterwards, sometimes for years.

The Geothermal Engines.description: The core engines of the accessible network, massive and locally maintained, running the heat regulation and defensive pressure systems the city depends on. Their sound carries through the rock. They sit deep in the accessible portion, built into the rock and serviced from platforms that ring them, with instrument positions set close enough that a reading can be taken by hand. Everything about them is local: local maintenance, local parts, local crews, and no imported power anywhere in the arrangement.
