Entry is free and the gallery is open to the city, so school parties and visiting families use it as often as students do.

Academy Affinity and Combat Campus.name: Academy Affinity and Combat Campus
Academy Affinity and Combat Campus.basicInfo: The Academy's training campus for affinity control, combat disciplines and formal student competition, built so students meet counters and techniques their home cities never taught them. Sparring forums, aerial volumes and control chambers run from early morning to closed examinations at night. It is demanding, highly visible and driven by reputation. The halls are broad and low-shouldered, floored in dark sand-coloured resin over star-metal frames, with older energy conduits carried openly along the ceilings and repurposed to feed the chambers that absorb what students cannot yet aim. Little of it is decorative: the colour comes from lane markings, equipment racks and the amber safety lamps that hold steady while a floor is live. Corelight reaches the interior through high slots and is read as a clock, brightening through the teaching periods and dimming across the maintenance window when the control chambers are recalibrated and the aerial nets are checked. Combat is one field among many here, and strength without control, ethics, recovery or judgment is treated as an incomplete education. Floor time is booked, paid for and rationed; a student who misses a slot waits days for another. Instructors, examiners, clinicians, equipment assessors and visiting teachers from several traditions work the same corridors, and the noise of a scheduled match carries through most of them.
Academy Affinity and Combat Campus.hiddenInfo: The campus fights a constant institutional battle not to become a smaller Korrvane. Its faculty teach that strength without control, ethics, recovery or judgment is an incomplete education, and they enforce that through the Ethics Chamber and the Recovery Wing as hard as through the ring. Not everyone agrees: house instructors are pressured to advance sponsored students, and at least one is currently weighing an offer that would cost a rival student a ranking. Illegal betting has attached itself to the student match calendar, which is why the Closed Examination Floor exists and why bookmakers keep finding ways onto the observation gallery anyway. A celebrated prodigy lost publicly here recently and has not returned to the sparring forum since. A second student is hiding an injury from the Recovery and Return Wing to protect a ranking, and a third — powerful enough that their house considers the matter settled — wants to leave combat training entirely for another campus. Cross-house technique rooms regularly expose the cultural assumptions behind a family style, and the accusation that someone reproduced a protected tradition without permission is never far away.

Central Sparring Forum.description: The campus's open heart: a reinforced floor under a high canopy where formal supervised combat and public demonstrations take place, tiered seating on three sides. Matches run on a posted schedule that half the Academy follows. The floor is resurfaced nightly and still carries scoring from the previous term. The canopy is ribbed star-metal with clear panels that drop the Corelight straight down onto the mat, so the fighters work in bright light and the seating stays in shade. Entry to watch is free to Academy members and charged to the public on ranked days, which fills the upper tiers with people who have paid to be there. The fourth side is left open for equipment carts, clinicians and the stretcher route to the recovery wing.

Affinity Control Chambers.description: Sealed, individually tuned environments for safe practice of control, precision, stamina and recovery, each chamber able to absorb an output its student cannot yet aim. Instruction here is slow and unglamorous. Students who arrived famous for raw power tend to spend their worst weeks in these rooms. The chambers are small and windowless, lined in grey absorbent panel, entered through a double door with an amber lamp above it that holds while the room is live. Sessions are booked singly and charged by the hour, and the waiting list is longest in the weeks before examinations. An instructor watches from a recessed station and speaks only when necessary. The corridor outside is lined with benches where students sit afterward, wrung out, waiting for the shaking in their hands to stop.

Aerial Combat Volume.description: A protected vertical space, netted with soft-field boundaries, given over to flight, pursuit and three-dimensional tactics. Instructors call manoeuvres from suspended platforms while students learn how quickly altitude stops being an advantage. Falls are caught, but the catch is deliberately uncomfortable. The volume is a hollow shaft of ribbed star-metal with marked bands at intervals so a student can be told exactly where they went wrong, and the soft-field boundaries hum audibly when they take a body. Sessions are supervised and capped, and nobody flies here without a clearance mark from the recovery wing. Spectators stand behind glazing at the mid bands. The floor of the volume is padded, swept and inspected before every session by a deck crew who are unmoved by anybody's ranking.

Grounded Counter Court.description: A low-ceilinged court built specifically to strip aerial and high-mobility specialists of their one advantage and make them fight without it. Students who dominate the volume above lose here weekly. Instructors consider that the point and say so, loudly, from the edge of the floor. The ceiling is close enough that a full extension touches it, the surface is bare packed resin with no give, and the walls are marked with the same bands used in the volume so a student can see the height they have lost. There is no seating, only a rail. Sessions are short, repeated and run in pairs drawn by the instructor rather than chosen. The court is booked solid through the cycle, and the sound of people hitting the floor is audible from the corridor.

Power Restraint Hall.description: A hall of graded targets and collapsing structures for controlled-output practice and collateral prevention, where the passing standard is damage not done. Public protector candidates train here constantly. It is the only room on campus where a perfect score looks, to a spectator, like almost nothing happening. The structures are rebuilt between runs from standard components that the campus buys in quantity and the students are charged for breaking, a cost that concentrates attention better than any lecture. Targets are graded by fragility and set among mannequins standing in for bystanders. Assessors score from a raised walk with a tally board visible to everyone on the floor. The hall smells of dust and resin, and the sweeping between runs is done by whoever failed the last one.

Cross-House Technique Rooms.description: Smaller studios where students learn principles drawn from several traditions without claiming mastery of protected family styles. The line between study and appropriation is argued in these rooms every term. Visiting instructors teach what their houses permit and stop, visibly, at the boundary. The studios are plain, matted, and identical to one another so that no tradition can claim the better room, with a single bench and a rack for whatever equipment the visiting teacher has brought. Class sizes are small and places are allocated by application rather than seniority. What may and may not be taught is posted at the door before each block, which is the only reason the arrangement survives. Students take notes by hand because recording is not permitted in these rooms.

Weapon and Wayline Court.description: Comparative sword, staff and weapon disciplines share a long court with racked training arms and measured lanes, including visiting Helvyran instruction. What is taught stops well short of Rux Corsair's complete protected Wayline tradition, a limit the instructors state at the start of every cycle. The court is long and narrow, lit evenly along its length, with the lanes cut into a floor of dark composite and the racks locked between sessions. Training arms are signed out and signed back, and a missing piece stops the class until it is found. Weapons may be carried to this court along an approved route and nowhere else on campus. Visitors may watch from the end wall, where a worn notice explains, in unglamorous detail, what a training blade can still do.

Magical Practice Chamber.description: A shielded room for controlled instruction in legal magical practice, often led by visiting Open Circle specialists. Magic stays firmly distinct from biological Starian affinity here, and remains uncommon enough that the gallery outside fills with curious students and a reliable share of open skeptics. The chamber is lined in dull grey shielding with a single sealed door, and its supply runs off an isolated conduit so that nothing practised inside touches the campus systems. Attendance is capped and booked in advance, and observers are held behind glazing rather than admitted to the floor. Sessions run on the visiting specialist's terms and stop when they say so. The teaching notice by the door states the distinction between practice and affinity in the first line, every time.

Public Challenge Ring.description: An open ring where approved student challenges, rankings and demonstrations are fought in front of anyone who wants to watch, including people with no connection to the Academy. Results move student standing immediately. The crowd noise is the reason several students refuse to compete here at all. The ring is a raised disc of dark resin ringed by a low barrier and standing room, with no seating and no shelter, so the crowd presses close and the officials work with their backs to it. Challenges require approved conditions, witnesses and a named official before they are posted. Betting is prohibited on the ground and conducted energetically beyond it. The board beside the ring carries the day's approved matches and a much longer list of requests that were refused.

Instructor Observation Gallery.description: A raised gallery of analysis stations overlooking the main floors, where faculty score technique, log injuries and quietly mark who is improving. Assessment recordings are reviewed frame by frame. Bookmakers have twice been removed from these seats, which says everything about how good the sightlines are. The gallery is a narrow run of angled glass and padded stools above the forum and the challenge ring, reached by a stair that requires a faculty mark, with the analysis stations wired into housings older than the campus. Instructors work through a session in near silence and then argue about it at length. Injury logs written here follow a student to the recovery wing before the student arrives. The stools are worn through at the front edge from people leaning forward.

Recovery and Return Wing.description: Medical clearance, rehabilitation and supervised return to training, staffed in partnership with city clinicians. No student resumes contact work without a signature from this wing. Its corridor notices spell out, in plain words, what hiding an injury costs — a message aimed at specific students every term. The wing is quiet and warm, lit low, with treatment rooms off a corridor that is deliberately wide enough for a stretcher and a walking patient to pass. Care is covered for enrolled students and billed to anyone else. Clinicians here also run the graded return programmes, which are unhurried by design and resented accordingly. A worn bench by the clearance desk holds the students waiting to be told whether they can compete, and their friends, who are usually more nervous than they are.

Equipment Testing Court.description: Legal training equipment, protection systems and safety gear are tested to destruction in a bunkered court with its own assessors. Manufacturers and student inventors both submit designs. Half the interesting failures end up cited in a lecture on the research campus within the month. The court is sunk below the surrounding floors behind a heavy door, with rigs bolted into a star-metal deck and a viewing slot rather than a window. Submissions are queued, charged for and tested in the order they were filed, and no submission jumps the queue regardless of who funded it. Results are posted publicly whether or not the maker likes them. The wall of failed samples beside the door is the most persuasive teaching aid on the campus and is never tidied.

Team Coordination Arena.description: A large mixed-terrain arena for group exercises that force combat students to work with medics, engineers and civic trainees who cannot fight at all. Objectives are written so no single powerful student can carry the exercise. The debriefs are more brutal than the exercises. The terrain is modular: broken slabs, a collapsed frame, a water channel and a narrow stair, rebuilt into new arrangements between blocks by a crew who take some pleasure in it. Teams are assigned across campuses rather than chosen, and the assignment lists are posted the evening before. Exercises are supervised from a control walk and stopped without warning when a team does something unsafe. The debrief room off the arena has one long table and no comfortable seats.

Professional Protector Track.description: Training for public protection and emergency response: crowd handling, rescue in collapsed structures, restraint under civic law and coordination with the city's protectors. Students here graduate into real posts across Relstaris, and their instructors mostly held those posts first. The track occupies a plain block of classrooms and a rigged practice structure that can be made to fail in several controlled ways, its stairwells deliberately awkward and its lighting deliberately poor. Candidates are screened before entry and reviewed throughout. Placement into civic service carries a Capitol Service term that is respected, politically useful and occasionally used as inexpensive labour. The kit room stocks real equipment, worn hard, and a board of past incidents referred to by case number.

Combat Ethics Chamber.description: A seminar chamber where force, consent, public responsibility and the consequences of power are examined through real cases, several of them involving students in the room. Attendance is required for every combat track. Arguments here follow students into the ring for years afterward. The chamber is a shallow bowl of benches around an open floor, deliberately plain, with the only display being a case summary projected where everyone must look at it. Sessions are led by an instructor and carried by the students, and nobody is permitted to sit out an entire block. Cases are anonymized and the anonymization regularly fails. What is said here is not minuted, which is the single concession that makes the room work at all.

Closed Examination Floor.description: High-level assessments run on a sealed floor with no spectators, no recordings released and no advance schedule, specifically to keep examiners away from spectators and bookmakers. Students enter alone. What happens inside is known only from results posted hours later on the administration boards. The floor is reached through a controlled corridor with a single staffed door, and the rooms beyond it are stripped: bare surfaces, fixed lighting, no gallery and no seating for anyone but the examiners. Candidates surrender personal effects at the door and collect them on the way out. Examiners are drawn from outside the candidate's own school wherever possible. The corridor bench outside is where students wait, without company, for a door to open.

Academy Research and Applied Sciences Ca.name: Academy Research and Applied Sciences Campus
Academy Research and Applied Sciences Ca.basicInfo:
The Academy's research campus, where Contair-trained engineers, Myralis medical specialists, independent scholars, house-funded programmes and visiting Helvyran magical researchers work along the same corridors. Its institutes cover applied systems, affinity theory, medicine, materials and Core systems history. The tone is intellectual, competitive, experimental and heavily regulated. The buildings are pale composite and green-tinted star-glass set on star-metal frames, connected by covered walks and stacked so that a laboratory sits above a workshop and below an office, with old conduit runs left in place along the ceilings and quietly reused to carry instrument power. Nothing is one colour: each institute has repainted its own frontage over the decades and nobody has ever made them agree. Corelight enters through the green glass as a cool wash and shifts on the city's routing, which the campus reads as its clock, with the deepest instrument work scheduled into the low maintenance window when the supply is steadiest. An ordinary day is bookings, refusals and paperwork: test slots, review filings, subject consents, verification queues. Funding is visible everywhere, since sponsors are named on the bays they pay for, and equipment, materials and chamber time all cost money that somebody has to have raised.

Work on offer here: Study — Readings from the Flooded Foundation (ask Nexis Contair).
Academy Research and Applied Sciences Ca.hiddenInfo: Regulation here is not decoration. The Ethics and Risk Review Court can stop a project outright, and the Contair Verification Annex can refuse a modification no matter who funded it — a refusal currently sitting between a house sponsor and a team that thought approval was a formality. Suppression is the campus's recurring problem: a house is pressing to bury a result that embarrasses it, and a junior scholar's discovery is being reframed in a sponsor's publications as the sponsor's own. The Comparative Magic and Affinity Institute has become unexpectedly political, because a magical method solved a problem that affinity-based work had failed at for two cycles, and the professional resentment is real. A project shelved as a failure years ago has turned out to be commercially valuable, and more than one party has been reading the Failed Project Archive with new interest. A medical ethics dispute involving synthetic-person review is open in the Ethics Court, and an old Core systems theory recovered on this campus contradicts the version of Relstaris history the Republic teaches.

Applied Systems Institute.description: Civic technology, infrastructure, tools and practical engineering, worked out in open bays full of half-assembled transit components and conduit sections. Teams here fix things the city actually uses. Their prototypes tend to end up in a Maker's Reach yard long before they end up in a paper. The bays are high and unglamorous, floored in scarred composite with gantries overhead and cable runs taped down where somebody promised to route them properly. Work here is done to a request from a civic office rather than to a research question, which shapes everything about the schedule. The institute's own lighting is patched off a reused conduit line that fails politely once a cycle, an irony nobody on the floor finds funny any more.

Affinity Theory Laboratories.description: Instrumented rooms studying how Starian biological ability expresses itself, where it fails, and what training can and cannot change. Volunteers are measured rather than tested to exhaustion. Results from these labs quietly underwrite half the teaching on the combat campus. The rooms are small and heavily monitored, walls padded and instrumented, each with an observation station behind glass and a consent notice posted at the door in plain language. Volunteers are recruited, briefed and paid, and may stop a session at any point without explanation. Every protocol passes the ethics court before a single measurement is taken. The labs keep a log of withdrawn sessions alongside the completed ones, on the principle that a refusal is data too, and that log is read more often than anyone admits.

Comparative Magic and Affinity Institute.description: Study of how learned or external magical practice differs from innate Starian affinity, governed by strict rules against treating the two as interchangeable. Its seminars draw sceptics as reliably as students. Conflating the two in a paper here is a professional error nobody lets the author forget. The institute occupies a restored upper floor with a run of small seminar rooms, its shielded practice space partitioned off and fed from a separate supply. Visiting practitioners are hosted rather than employed, and the terms of what they will demonstrate are agreed in advance. The corridor board carries the institute's founding distinction printed at the top of every notice, which visitors find pedantic and the staff consider the entire point.

Open Circle Visiting Research Studio.description: A studio kept for temporary Helvyran faculty and cross-institution projects, arranged for practical magical problem-solving rather than theory. Visiting researchers rotate through on short terms. Their working notes leave with them, which is a standing frustration for the institute next door. The studio is one large room with movable benches, good light and almost no fixed equipment, deliberately arranged so each arriving team can lay it out their own way. Terms are short and the room is stripped and reset between them. Access is by invitation and the visiting party sets the working hours, which rarely match the campus routine. A shelf by the door holds the things successive occupants have left behind, none of it labelled, all of it kept in case somebody comes back for it.

Medical Research Institute.description: Recovery, long-term health, trauma and public medicine, studied in wards and simulation suites rather than lecture halls. Work here feeds directly into city clinics. Researchers argue with clinicians constantly about how fast a finding should become a treatment. The institute is quiet and warm, floored in seamless pale composite, its simulation suites built to resemble real clinic rooms down to the awkward corners. Patient material is handled under rules that are posted, audited and enforced without exception. Study places are limited and applications are competitive. The corridor between the wards and the offices has a bench where clinicians wait to speak to researchers, and the researchers have learned that anyone sitting on it has already tried to resolve the matter by message.

Materials Science Hall.description: Volen thermal materials, Korrvane impact structures, star-metal and advanced construction tested under load in a hall built to survive its own experiments. The floor shakes on a schedule. Fabricators from Maker's Reach come in to see whether a material will behave outside a laboratory. The hall is a single tall volume of exposed star-metal frame with test rigs bolted into a reinforced deck, sample racks along one wall and a viewing walk behind heavy glazing. Test slots are booked, charged and posted so that anyone working nearby knows when the noise is coming. Samples are supplied by the sponsor and destroyed by the test. The far wall carries a display of fracture faces, mounted and labelled, that instructors use for teaching and visiting buyers use to argue about quality.

Gate Systems Classroom.description: Contair-approved instruction in Lunar Gate principles, taught with working models and redacted schematics that stop short of protected designs. Students who want more are told exactly where the line is. Several graduates of this room now work the maintenance annex at the Grand Lunar Gate Hub. The classroom is small, panelled and windowless, with the models set on a central bench and the schematics displayed only while the class is in session. Materials do not leave the room and are counted back at the end of every block. Enrollment is limited and approved individually, and the approval takes longer than students expect. A Contair standards notice is fixed beside the door, worn at the corners from being tapped by instructors making the same point year after year.

Core Systems Theory Wing.description: Academic study of Relstaris power distribution and the systems left by earlier custodial eras, conducted from records rather than access to the Core itself. Old schematics are reconstructed here from fragments. The wing's conclusions occasionally embarrass the official civic history. The wing is housed in the campus's oldest structure, a Genesis foundation with later floors dropped into it, and the reading rooms are lined with drawers of plans that have been copied, corrected and recopied by successive hands. Scholars here work slowly, since the evidence is fragmentary and the corrections matter. A reused conduit runs visibly through the main room, dead for generations, and is the most photographed object on the campus.

Independent Research Offices.description: Small rented offices for two-person teams, visiting scholars and professional specialists who answer to no institute director. Doors are labelled in handwriting. The best work and the least accountable work on the campus both come out of this corridor. The offices are narrow, cheap and always let, arranged along a single corridor with a shared kitchen at one end and a shared instrument room at the other, both maintained by whoever complains loudest. Rent is charged by the term and rises with the campus's reputation, which prices out exactly the people the corridor is meant to serve. Occupants pay separately for chamber time, publication and verification. The corridor board is a tangle of collaboration notices, equipment for sale and one very old advertisement nobody will take down.

House-Funded Project Gallery.description: Research sponsored by major and minor houses, displayed openly with the funder named on every bay — a transparency rule the campus fought for and the houses accepted reluctantly. Recruiters walk it weekly. So do rivals, counting how much money a house is spending and on what. The gallery is a broad lit hall with bays along both sides, each fitted out by its sponsor, so the frontages range from plain panel to polished star-glass and the contrast is the first thing a visitor reads. Bay tenure runs by the cycle and is renewed or withdrawn in public. Researchers staff their own bays on posted hours and are expected to answer questions from anyone. A small plate at the entrance records the rule itself and the year the faculty council carried it.

Ethics and Risk Review Court.description: Review of research subjects, civic danger, synthetic-person questions and anything that could injure people outside the laboratory. The court can halt a project regardless of its funding. Its hearings are open, and the gallery is usually full of the researchers waiting to be next. The court sits in a plain room with a long table, a witness chair and public benches, deliberately unlike the ceremonial chambers elsewhere in the Academy. Filings are made in advance and circulated; a project that arrives unfiled is not heard. Decisions are posted with reasons attached, which is the part that makes them useful to everybody else. The bench outside is long, worn and known for the particular quiet of people rehearsing an answer they have already given twice.

Prototype Testing Chamber.description: A hardened chamber for controlled evaluation of experimental devices, monitored from behind shielding and cleared after every run. Test slots are booked months out and traded like currency. The chamber's failure log is the most honest document on the campus. The chamber itself is a windowless box of layered shielding with a single heavy door, its interior surfaces replaced rather than repaired, entered only when the control station releases it. Every run requires an ethics filing, a safety officer and a fee that small teams feel keenly. Runs are timed and overruns are charged. The control station keeps a handwritten board of the current booking order beside the official one, because the official one has been wrong at least once and nobody has forgotten it.

Research Publishing House.description: Formal publication, peer dispute and the slow manufacture of academic reputation, run from editorial rooms where authorship order is fought over harder than results. Papers are posted publicly on release. So are the corrections, which some authors consider unnecessarily cruel. The house occupies a quiet upper floor of small offices and one long production room, its walls hung with proofs in various stages of argument. Submissions are queued, reviewed by named editors and charged a handling fee that sponsors usually cover and independents usually do not. Disputes over credit are heard here first and escalate only when that fails. A framed retraction notice hangs by the editor's door, its subject long retired, kept as a reminder of what the process is for.

Failed Project Archive.description: A deliberately public archive preserving useful failure instead of hiding it: dead prototypes, abandoned lines of inquiry and the notes explaining why. Students are sent here in their first term. Lately other people have been reading it too, and not for the lessons. The archive is a long low room of open shelving and open crates, with the objects out where they can be handled and the notes filed beside them in plain boxes. Nothing is restricted, nothing is catalogued as well as it should be, and the finding aid is a series of handwritten cards that successive archivists have not agreed on. Access is free to anyone the gate admits, and requests are signed for at the desk. The dust on the older crates makes it obvious which shelves have recently had attention.

Contair Verification Annex.description: Technical review of any claim involving Contair systems, staffed by Contair-standard examiners with the authority to refuse. A rejection here kills a product across the capital's legal market. The waiting room has a reputation for very quiet, very expensive arguments. The annex is a separate block with its own entrance, its own records and a counter rather than an office door, finished in plain grey with none of the campus's sponsor branding anywhere in it. Submissions are logged, charged and examined in order. Examiners are rotated so that no maker deals with the same one twice in succession. The waiting room has hard seating, a water point and a posted notice stating that the outcome will be issued in writing and will not be discussed at the counter.

Myralis Clinical Partnership Floor.description: A shared floor linking Academy research to the Myralis Capitol Clinic and the Myralis Continuum, where clinicians and researchers hold joint review of live cases. Patient material never leaves the floor. Clinical urgency and academic caution collide here on a weekly schedule. The floor is built to clinic standard rather than laboratory standard, quiet and warm, with review rooms around a central station and a controlled door at each end. Attendance is by named permission and the list is checked. The clinic's standards govern everything done here, and the Academy's convenience does not override them. Case reviews run long and end abruptly when a clinician is called away, which happens often enough that the researchers have learned to put their questions first.

Academy Civic, Cultural, and Professiona.name: Academy Civic, Cultural, and Professional Campus
Academy Civic, Cultural, and Professiona.basicInfo: The Academy campus for government, law, education, commerce, arts, food, performance, history and public service, and the clearest proof of Relstaris's claim that anyone may become anything. The strongest student of a generation might study cooking here while a student with no combat promise trains to become a famous teacher or attorney. It is social, ambitious, politically active and creatively competitive. The buildings are warm sandstone and amber star-glass around planted courtyards, a patchwork of eras with a Genesis foundation carrying a Corsair balcony over a Castro-restored colonnade, and the colour changes street by street because each school has decorated its own frontage and none of them match. Old conduits run under the courtyards and are still used, tapped for the kitchens and the studio lighting. Corelight is the campus clock: teaching runs while it is high, rehearsals and public sessions fill the evening shift, and the maintenance window is when the performance halls reset and the newsroom goes to press. A visitor can eat in a student kitchen at posted hours, sit in a mock court, watch a showcase or ask a placement clerk for advice, and much of it is open without charge, while tuition, studio materials and kitchen fees are not.
Academy Civic, Cultural, and Professiona.hiddenInfo: This campus produces more of the capital's working power than the combat campus does, and it knows it. Student journalists out of the Public Media Hall are currently chasing a scandal that reaches past the Academy, and the pressure to have them stopped is being applied through channels, not in public. A law student has taken the defence of someone their own house would rather see convicted, which has made the Arbitration Hall very interesting to watch. The Student Enterprise Incubator has attracted underworld attention — one funding offer arrived with terms too generous to be honest, and the mentor who noticed has not yet decided who to tell. A culinary rivalry between two students has grown more famous across the city than any Academy match this term, to the visible irritation of the affinity campus. And the Practical Failure Seminar Hall is host to the campus's real philosophical fight: whether a public failure should follow a person forever, argued by students who intend to write the laws that decide it.

Civic Administration School.description: Public service, infrastructure management, district planning and governance, taught through real Relstaris casework rather than theory. Students model budget failures and transit collapses. Graduates staff the offices that keep the largest city on Nexara from seizing up, and they know it. The school occupies a plain block of seminar rooms and one large planning hall where a working model of the city's civic systems is laid out and constantly annotated by hand. Casework comes from offices that genuinely want an answer, which means the deadlines are real. The planning hall's correction sheets, pinned over the model in layers, are the closest thing the campus has to a public argument about how the city is run.

Law and Arbitration Hall.description: Relstaris law, house disputes, contracts and civic rights are studied and practised in mock courts that copy the city's real chambers down to the bench height. Student advocates take supervised public cases. The arguments carry, and a few of them have made it into actual civic rulings. The hall is panelled in dark wood over an older star-metal frame, its courts lit evenly and fitted with the same recording rings used elsewhere in the capital. A free advice counter operates on posted hours, staffed by students under supervision, and the queue for it starts outside. Cases are allocated rather than chosen, which occasionally puts a student opposite their own house's interest. The public benches at the back are open to anyone, and the same handful of retired listeners occupy them most days.

Education Institute.description: Teacher training, youth development and public learning, with practice classrooms full of real children from the surrounding districts on scheduled days. Trainees are assessed on patience as much as knowledge. The institute supplies teachers to schools in every section of the city. The building is low and bright, its classrooms fitted out at child height and its corridors hung with work that is changed often and never labelled with a grade. Practice days are booked with the districts a term ahead, and families are told plainly that trainees will be teaching. Observation happens from the back of the room rather than behind glass. A cupboard by the main door holds spare coats and shoes in a range of sizes, contributed over years by staff who stopped waiting for a budget line.

Trade and Logistics School.description: Markets, Waypoints, supply chains, contracts and commercial ethics, taught with live route data piped in from the Waypoint and the Grand Market. Students run simulated shortages until they stop panicking. Corsair instructors visit often and are blunt about what the coursework leaves out. The school is a single long room of shared tables under a wall of route boards that mirror the Commercial Route Gallery, so a change in real conditions interrupts the lesson whether or not the lesson is ready. Students take rotations on actual market and cargo floors as part of the course. Contracts drafted here are reviewed line by line and torn apart in front of their authors. The wall board keeps a record of every simulated shortage the cohort mishandled, updated by the students themselves.

History and Cultural Studies Court.description: House cultures, Relstaris identity, oral history and contested memory, worked through in a court where two accounts of the same event are read side by side. Sessions get heated. Students from houses that disagree about the past are seated together on purpose. The court is a stepped ring of benches around an open floor, in old stone that predates the school built around it, with the reading desks set where everyone can see who is speaking. Oral history sessions are recorded only with consent and the consent is asked at the start of each one. Visiting residents come to give accounts and are paid for their time. The wall cases hold objects lent by families rather than bought, each labelled with the lender's terms, several of which require the object to go home at the end of the cycle.

Arts and Design Studios.description: Visual art, clothing, architecture, public design and cultural production, spread through high studios with north light and permanently occupied worktables. Student work goes up in public galleries across the city. Commissions arrive from houses who then try to dictate the result. The studios are the untidiest rooms on the campus, floors spattered past cleaning, racks of stretched work and half-built models crowding the walkways, the whole block smelling of solvent and hot resin. Materials are bought by the student and the costs are a standing grievance. Studio space is allocated by application and held jealously once won. A commission board by the stair lists current offers with the terms attached, and somebody has annotated most of them with an opinion.

Performance Conservatory.description: Music, stage, public speaking and the entertainment professions, rehearsed in soundproofed halls that leak anyway. Conservatory students perform publicly from their first term. Recruiters from the Grand Performance Hall and the entertainment district attend the showcases openly. The conservatory is a stack of rehearsal rooms around a single working stage, its corridors lined with cue sheets and sign-up boards, the stage itself rigged and re-rigged so often that no two showcases look alike. Rooms are booked in short blocks and overrunning is a serious social offence. Showcases are free to attend and fill early. The stage door opens onto a small yard where performers wait before a call, and the wall beside it is covered in the names of people who waited there first.

Culinary Institute.description: Regional cuisine, public hospitality, food systems and restaurant management, taught in working kitchens that serve real customers at posted hours. Students cook dishes from cities they have never visited under instructors who have. Its graduates open half the notable kitchens in the capital. The kitchens are hot, loud and fitted with equipment from several cities, the service counters opening onto a dining room that anyone may book and pay in. Ingredients arrive from the Regional Food Exchange each morning and the day's teaching follows what actually turned up. Service is assessed as strictly as cooking, and a student who plates well and speaks badly to a customer fails the block. The complaints book is kept on the pass, open, where the whole brigade can read it.

Public Media Hall.description: Reporting, city news, reputation and information ethics, run as a functioning newsroom with a student edition that genuinely circulates. Investigations start at these desks. The hall's independence is defended in policy and tested, roughly once a term, in practice. The newsroom is one open floor of shared desks and pinned corrections, with a small broadcast room at one end and an editor's office that has a door nobody closes. Sources are protected under a written policy that students are taught to recite before they are allowed to file. Publication decisions are made by students and reviewed afterward rather than before. A framed copy of the first edition the Academy tried to withdraw hangs where every new reporter is shown it in their first week.

Professional Mediation Rooms.description: Small neutral rooms for conflict resolution and mixed-house communication, where trainees mediate genuine disputes under supervision. Parties come from the Academy and from the districts nearby. The rooms are deliberately plain so nobody can read advantage into the furniture. Each room holds one round table, identical chairs and a water jug, with no house markings anywhere and separate entrances so parties need not meet in the corridor. Sessions are free and booked through a single desk. Supervisors watch from a corner seat and intervene rarely. The booking clerk keeps a simple rule that has survived every attempt to formalise it: whoever asked for the session first chooses the room, and nobody is told who that was.

Student Enterprise Incubator.description: Workspace, small funding and mentorship for student businesses, new services and professions that do not yet have names. Ventures launch and collapse within a term. The public pitch nights draw investors, curious faculty and at least one person every cycle who should not be there. The incubator is a wide floor divided by movable partitions, benches and storage cages, rearranged so often that the layout is argued over more than the funding. Space is allocated by application and comes with a term limit that is enforced. Small grants are made and accounted for publicly, and a venture that fails must still file its accounts. The pitch night board records every venture the incubator has hosted, successful or not, with the term it ran and nothing else.

Public Service Placement Office.description: Careers inside Relstaris institutions: the Citadel's administrative floors, the Protection District, the clinics, the transit authority and the schools. Placement staff know which offices treat new graduates well. They say so quietly, and they are usually right. The office is two rooms with a counter, a wall of current vacancies and a row of chairs that is full through the placement season and empty for the rest of the cycle. Interviews are arranged here and often held here, in the back room, with the employer travelling to the campus rather than the reverse. Capitol Service terms are advertised alongside permanent posts and explained honestly, including how often they are used as inexpensive labour. The vacancy wall is updated by hand every morning.

Cultural Translation Forum.description: A seminar forum helping students read customs from other cities and houses before they give offence rather than afterward. Sessions are run by students from the cultures in question. Visitors from the Arrival Ward sometimes sit in, for entirely practical reasons. The forum is a single carpeted room with seating in a loose circle and no raised position for a teacher, which is itself part of the method. Sessions cover greetings, hospitality, weapon expectations, mourning, gift-giving and the things visitors from different cities each assume are normal. Attendance is open and free, and the room is regularly fuller than its seating. A board by the door lists which cultures are covered in the coming cycle and which are not, because nobody has volunteered to speak for them.
paths: Magic, Affinity, and Public Life Seminar

Magic, Affinity, and Public Life Seminar.description: Examines why Helvyra accepts visible magical practice while many Starians remain unfamiliar with it, and how magical specialists actually operate in shared civic space. Visiting practitioners answer questions that are sometimes rude. The reading list changes faster than any other on campus. The seminar meets in a small tiered room with a single demonstration bench that is used sparingly, since the point of the course is civic life rather than technique. Places are limited and allocated by application, and the applications are read. Practitioners who attend are paid and briefed beforehand about what kind of questions they will face. The reading list is pinned to the door in successive layers, and nobody has removed the older sheets underneath.

Practical Failure Seminar Hall.description: Courses built entirely around failed businesses, lost cases, damaged reputations and how people rebuilt afterward, taught in part by the people who failed. Attendance is voluntary and the hall is always full. It is the most quietly famous room on the campus. The hall is plain and steeply raked, with a lectern nobody uses and a single chair on the floor that speakers sit in while they tell it. Sessions are not recorded and the audience is asked to keep names out of the corridor afterward, a request that mostly holds. Speakers are paid and are under no obligation to give a happy ending. The standing room at the back fills first, because it is the part of the hall where a listener cannot be seen from the floor.
paths: Magic, Affinity, and Public Life Seminar

Academy Residential City.name: Academy Residential City
Academy Residential City.basicInfo: The Academy's residential district, large enough to hold several completely different ways of living: supervised first-cycle housing, independent towers, house-sponsored residences and low-cost rooms for unsponsored students. Faculty live here too, a few streets and a large social distance away. It is busy, social, chaotic and emotionally immediate at all hours. The district is built tall and close in pale stone and star-glass, its towers linked by suspended bridges and public lifts, with older star-metal frames carrying newer floors and reused conduits threaded up the stairwells to feed rooms that were never in the original plan. Colour is not uniform: sponsored streets keep their frontages restored, the independent blocks are painted by their residents, and nobody has ever imposed a single scheme. Corelight sets the rhythm even here, with the towers waking as it rises toward the teaching hours and the food walk coming alive after it drops, and residents learn to expect the water pressure to fall through the maintenance window. Rent, deposits, meals and laundry all cost money, and the difference between a sponsored room and an unsponsored one is visible in the stairwell before anyone opens a door.
Academy Residential City.hiddenInfo: Housing here maps wealth, sponsorship and house politics onto physical streets, and everyone living in it can read the map. The Resident Mediation Office is currently handling a case it cannot solve with rules: a Dravon student and a Castro student assigned to the same mixed-house dormitory, both refusing to request a transfer for reasons of pride. Several students are hiding academic failure from families who are still paying, and the Recovery House shelters at least one who has been publicly humiliated and has not left the building in days. The Empty Bed Office is tracking a withdrawal that does not add up — a student who stopped attending without notice, whose contacts in the residence all give slightly different accounts. Underworld recruitment reaches the Academy through this district rather than the campuses, arriving as a friendly neighbour with a small favour to ask and a job that pays too well. Food theft from the communal kitchens, meanwhile, is prosecuted socially with a seriousness that visiting parents find genuinely alarming.

First-Cycle Residences.description: Closely supervised housing for new arrivals, with staffed entries, shared study rooms and a curfew nobody admits to respecting. Most students meet their first friends and their first rival in these corridors. The walls carry a decade of names scratched near the door frames. The buildings are plain and solidly built, rooms shared in pairs along corridors wide enough for the traffic of arrival day, with a common room on every floor that is never quiet and never properly cleaned. Staff hold a desk at the entrance through the night and log who comes in. Rooms come furnished, charged by the term, and the charge is the same whether or not a student uses the room. Arrival day fills the stairs with crates, relatives and people learning that the lifts are already broken.

Advanced Student Towers.description: More independent apartments for experienced students, with private kitchens and no supervision beyond the building systems. Rooms here are won by seniority and traded at the end of every cycle. The upper floors have a view of the Grand Forum that the residents pretend not to care about. The towers are narrow and high, faced in pale stone with star-glass balconies, reached by lifts that are reliable except when the district's maintenance window takes them out together. Apartments are let individually and cost noticeably more than supervised housing, which sorts who applies. Residents arrange their own cleaning, their own food and their own disputes. The trading of rooms at the end of a cycle is conducted through a board in the lobby and a great deal of private negotiation nobody records.

Mixed-House Dormitories.description: Students from different houses living together, some assigned and some by choice, in halls designed to make avoidance impossible. Shared washrooms have settled more cultural disputes than any seminar. Long friendships and permanent grudges both start on these landings. The halls are built around open landings rather than corridors, so every door faces the same shared space and nobody enters or leaves unobserved. Assignment is made by the residential office and appeals are heard but rarely granted. House markings are permitted on doors and not on shared walls, a rule tested every cycle. The landings collect furniture nobody owns, a rota nobody follows and the particular quiet of two people who have agreed not to discuss something.

House-Sponsored Residences.description: Privately funded housing where the quality of the rooms and the weight of the expectations both depend on the sponsoring house. Some offer cultural support and a cook from home; others offer surveillance. Students who lose a sponsorship move out within the week. The residences sit behind their own gates with their own staff, restored and maintained to whatever standard the house considers appropriate, and the frontages are the most obviously expensive thing in the district. Residents are not charged rent and are expected to attend house functions. The gate staff record arrivals and departures for the house rather than for the Academy. Each residence keeps a room ready for a visiting representative, and the students know exactly which room it is and what it means when it is occupied.

Independent Student Housing.description: Lower-cost residences for unsponsored students, cheaply built and fiercely defended by the people in them. Rent is posted publicly so nobody can be quietly overcharged. There is a permanent waiting list and a culture of leaving useful things behind on moving out. The blocks are older and plainer than anything around them, painted by residents in whatever colour was cheapest, their stairwells fitted with reused conduit that the district has repaired rather than replaced. Rooms are small, single and unfurnished beyond a bed and a shelf. The residents run their own noticeboard for work, tutoring and shared meals. The cupboard by each entrance holds the things left behind by people who have moved on, and taking from it carries no shame at all.

Faculty Housing Court.description: Homes for instructors, researchers and visiting faculty around a walled court with old trees, a short walk and a considerable social distance from the student blocks. Students come here for supervision meetings and leave quickly. Faculty gossip here is the fastest information network on campus. The houses are old, restored more than once, their frontages carrying the marks of several custodial eras and their interiors rebuilt around whatever the current occupant needs. Tenancy comes with the post and ends with it, which makes the court's politics quietly vicious. Visiting faculty are lodged at the far side on short terms. The court gate is closed but not locked, and the bench beside it is where students wait, visibly, for an appointment they were told not to be early for.

Communal Kitchens.description: Long shared kitchens where culinary experiments, social conflict, stolen food and late-night friendships all happen at once. Regional dishes get cooked badly by homesick students and corrected by strangers. The theft board by the door is taken extremely seriously by everyone except the faculty. The kitchens are tiled, hard-lit and fitted with equipment from several different eras of purchasing, half of it labelled with the block that paid for it. Cupboards are assigned and locked; the cold store is shared and is the source of most of the trouble. Cleaning is rostered and enforced by other residents rather than by staff. The notice above the sink about what happens to unwashed pans has been rewritten by successive residents into something considerably less polite than it started.

Rooftop Study Gardens.description: Planted roof terraces used for quiet work, dates, arguments and informal training at hours when nobody official is watching. The city glow makes reading possible past midnight. Every garden has an unofficial owner group and a negotiated arrangement about the good corner. The terraces are laid over the tower roofs in raised beds and gravel, planted by residents and watered from a line that the district charges for, which is why half the beds are thriving and half are not. Access is open to the building's residents and closed to everyone else by a door that is propped anyway. Furniture arrives by stages and is never removed. The best corner on each roof has a mismatched set of chairs and an understanding about who sits there that nobody has ever written down.

Student Laundry Court.description: A mundane hall of shared machines and folding tables where house prestige provides no protection at all from lost clothing. Students wait out cycles doing coursework on the benches. More cross-house conversation happens here than in any organized cultural programme. The hall is warm, damp and loud, floored in scuffed composite, its machines paid for by the cycle and its drying racks claimed by anyone quick enough. Two of the machines have been out of service long enough that their notices have faded. Attendants are on duty at posted hours only, which is not when most students come. The lost property rail by the door carries a season's worth of unclaimed clothing, and the rule that anything left past the cycle's end goes to the independent blocks is universally accepted.

Resident Mediation Office.description: Handles roommates, cultural misunderstandings, noise, property and harassment, with the authority to reassign housing and a strong preference for not using it. The staff hear the same six disputes in endless variation. Some of what walks through the door is much worse than that. The office is a counter and two closed rooms on the ground floor of a residential block, deliberately placed where residents can enter without crossing an open court. Appointments are free and can be made without naming the other party. Staff can move a student the same day in a serious case and will say plainly when a matter belongs with the review court instead. A worn card on the counter lists what the office cannot do, which is the first thing most visitors read.

Late-Night Food Walk.description: A run of affordable stalls and small counters serving students long after formal dining closes, lit in warm strips against the pale district stone. Vendors know which students are eating properly and which are not. Some of them say something about it. The walk is a narrow street between two tower blocks, roofed in places, its counters fitted into ground-floor units that were storage before somebody saw the opportunity. Stalls pay a pitch fee to the district and open on their own hours, which means the walk thins and thickens through the night. Prices are low and posted, and the portions are sized for people who have not eaten since morning. Somebody is always sitting on the step at the far end, eating slowly and not going home yet.

Dormitory Flight Court.description: An open court with marked landing rings for safe arrivals and movement practice, used equally for reckless shortcuts between towers at speed. Traffic rules are posted and routinely ignored. The Arrival Ward's flight instructors quietly describe it as a bad influence. The court is a paved square between the tower blocks with the rings picked out in worn paint, a soft-surface strip along one side and a rail where people sit to watch. Fast flight is restricted across the district and the restriction stops at the court's edge, which is precisely why it is used as it is. Residents land here with shopping, with luggage, and occasionally with each other. The repair notice on the lamp standard at the corner has been replaced so often that the bracket is wider than the post.

Family Visit Residences.description: Temporary lodging for visiting relatives, furnished for comfort and arranged so a family can stay a week without living inside a dormitory. Rooms fill at graduation and at term start. Some visits are celebration; some are an intervention arriving without warning. The building is quiet and plainly comfortable, rooms let by the night at a rate families find high and pay anyway, with a common room where relatives from several cities wait out an afternoon together. Bookings are made through the residential office and the best rooms go months in advance. Staff are used to arrivals who have not told the student they are coming. A shelf in the entrance holds district guidance in several forms, and the most-handled sheet is the one explaining how the transit rings work.

Academic Recovery House.description: A quiet residence for students returning after injury, breakdown, scandal or long absence, with staff trained to manage a return rather than hurry one. Nobody is asked why they are here. Residents come and go by a side entrance for reasons the house understands perfectly. The house is low and plain behind a planted screen, its rooms single and its corridors carpeted so that movement is not announced, and the common room is arranged in small separated groups rather than one table. Placement is arranged through the Academy and the residence is not charged to the student. Clinicians and counsellors visit on a posted schedule. The kitchen keeps food available at any hour, which is the detail most residents mention afterward as the one that mattered.

The Empty Bed Office.description: A small office that follows up on students who disappear, withdraw or simply stop attending, contacting families and tracing last known movements. Most cases end in a quiet withdrawal form. A few do not, and those files stay open on the wall behind the desk. The office is one room at the end of a residential corridor with a single desk, a filing wall and a window onto the flight court, and it is staffed by people who are also doing other jobs. Referrals come from tutors, residence staff and friends, and anyone may make one. The office works by asking rather than by authority, which means it depends entirely on people being willing to answer. The open files are turned face out, a decision the staff made deliberately and have never reversed.

Academy Commons.name: Academy Commons
Academy Commons.basicInfo: The student commercial and social district where formal Academy education spills into ordinary life: cheap food, clubs, resale stalls, tutors, rumours and small businesses run out of temporary units. It is one of the fastest-changing parts of Relstaris, loud and affordable and never quite the same two terms running. Shops fail, clubs split, and reputations are made and destroyed between cycles. The Commons is built low and dense against the campus edge, older star-metal frames filled in with cheap panel and star-glass, unit fronts repainted by every successive tenant so that the streets carry a dozen colours and no agreement between them. Reused conduit runs along the eaves feeding sign strips that were never in any plan. Corelight reaches the narrow lanes late and leaves them early, so the Commons runs on its own lamps for much of the day and comes properly alive on the evening shift, when classes end and the night counters open. Everything here is transactional and cheap rather than free: pitch fees, term leases, tutoring rates, a charge for the room a club books. Turnover is the one constant, and the empty units between tenants never stay empty long.
Academy Commons.hiddenInfo: The Commons is where the Academy's official structures lose their grip. Recruitment Lane hosts major houses, public institutions and underworld scouts working the same crowd, and the scouts are better at it — a current offer circulating among unsponsored students is dressed as ordinary employment and is nothing of the kind. The Questionable Assignment Service is investigated every term and reopens every term, and this cycle the Student News Office has an editor who intends to prove why. A rumour running through the Commons has already damaged one student faster than any evidence can repair, and the target is not the person who started it. A house society is attempting to take effective control of a public space here, booking it out permanently through a friendly club registration, which the Commons manager has noticed and not yet challenged. Meanwhile a student business has exploded in popularity, and its owners are being approached with investment terms that would quietly take it away from them.

Student Market.description: Supplies, clothing, inexpensive tools, art and student-made goods sold from tight rows of stalls that change hands constantly. Prices are argued openly and the good sellers are known by name. A quarter of the stock is somebody's coursework being sold to cover next term's rent. The rows are covered by mismatched awnings strung between the unit fronts, and the aisles are narrow enough that a loaded stall blocks traffic and is told so immediately. Pitches are let by the term and the fee rises where the footfall is best. Sellers set out before the teaching hours and pack down when the light shifts. The board at the entrance lists current pitch holders in chalk, amended so often that the surface has worn shiny where the same few names keep reappearing.

Club Registration Hall.description: House clubs, professional societies, cultural groups and organizations of dubious purpose all file here for recognition, room bookings and funding. The clerks approve almost everything. The wall of current registrations is the single best map of student politics in the city. The hall is a plain room with a counter down one side and the registration wall down the other, its panels replaced piecemeal so the newest ones are a different colour from the rest. Registration carries a small fee and a named officer who is answerable for the club's conduct. The ledger of refused registrations is kept under the counter and shown to anyone who asks, which is a courtesy the clerks extend because being refused is usually more interesting than being approved.

Academy Food Court.description: Affordable cuisine from cities across Nexara served under one long roof, from Ignivex heat to Helvyran travel food, at prices students can survive. Queues form by reputation rather than signage. Arguments about whose regional cooking is being done badly are effectively permanent. The court is one high span of reused star-metal trusses over a floor of shared tables, the counters ranged along both sides and vented into a common flue that makes the whole building smell of everything at once. Counters pay rent by the term and a share of takings. Tables are shared without ceremony and holding one for an absent friend is a recognized offence. The counter at the end that keeps changing hands has had its sign repainted so many times that the old lettering shows through underneath.

Used Equipment Row.description: Legal resale, repair and trade in training gear, instruments, tools and protective systems, much of it on its third owner. Sellers test equipment in front of buyers because nobody trusts a description. Graduating students dump their whole kit here every cycle and prices drop overnight. The row is a run of deep narrow units with the stock hung from the ceiling and the workbenches at the back, so a repair and a sale happen within arm's reach of each other. Sellers are required to display safety ratings and are checked on it, irregularly. Trade-ins are valued on the spot and argued about at length. A sign on the busiest unit lists the items it will not take, and the list has grown by hand over several cycles.

Student Performance Steps.description: Wide public steps used for music, comedy, debate, open challenges and protest, with no booking system beyond arriving early. Conservatory students test material on the harshest audience available. A performance that works here tends to be in a real venue within a month. The steps face a small paved square and are backed by unit frontages whose owners have long since given up objecting to the noise. There is no amplification and no permission required; the acoustics of the square do the work. Performers put out a box and take what the crowd gives. The worn patch at the centre of the third step is where everyone stands, and stepping off it to address the square from the side is a choice the regulars will notice.

Recruitment Lane.description: Major houses, businesses and public institutions hold hiring tables along a covered lane, beside underworld scouts putting considerable effort into not looking like underworld scouts. Offers are made on the spot. The difference between the two kinds of table is rarely visible on the day. The lane is roofed in panel and lit along its length, tables set in numbered bays that are booked and paid for by the day. Bay holders are registered and the register is public, which is a genuine protection and an easily satisfied one. Traffic peaks at term end and at any point when a cohort is anxious. The notice at the lane entrance advising students to have an offer reviewed before signing is read by fewer people than the tables beside it.

Study Café Terrace.description: A terrace café of smart brewing heads, a long collaborative table and a quieter reading edge behind acoustic dividers, with a small arrival space that keeps flying students from descending over hot drinks. Cyrra comes light or concentrated. Tutoring, group work, dates disguised as tutoring and pure academic panic share the tables. The terrace is raised a half level above the lane, floored in warm tile with planted troughs along the rail, and the dividers are moved through the day as the balance between noise and work shifts. Seats are held by purchase and the staff enforce it politely at the busiest hours. The collaborative table carries a permanent scatter of borrowed chargers and abandoned notes, and the corner seats behind the dividers are occupied by the same people every cycle.

Student News Office.description: A cramped newsroom of shared desks and pinned corrections where student reporting, rumour, investigation and reputation warfare are produced on a punishing schedule. The edition circulates across the whole Academy. Subjects of its stories learn about them at the same time as everyone else. The office is an upper unit reached by an outside stair, its windows papered over with layouts and its single door propped open for the heat of the press equipment below. Copies are printed cheaply and distributed free, funded by advertisements the editors dislike selling. Anyone may walk in with a story and many do. The corrections board by the door is kept deliberately at eye height, and a long-standing rule holds that a correction runs at the same size as the error.

House Debate Rooms.description: Bookable rooms for student-led political and cultural argument, scheduled back to back and often overrunning. Motions range from house reform to who should control the Commons itself. The rooms are soundproofed, which everyone agrees is the only reason the building survives. Each room holds a ring of benches, a speaker's floor and a clock that is visible from every seat and ignored by every speaker. Bookings are made through the registration hall, charged at a small hourly rate, and contested when two societies want the same evening. Audiences are open unless a society closes the session. The corridor outside carries a board of upcoming motions, and the annotations other societies add to it are half the reason anybody attends.

Night Commons.description: The late social district that wakes when classes end: open counters, small venues, benches full of people who should be asleep. It is affordable, crowded and much safer than the entertainment district across the city. Most of what happens here is friendship conducted at unwise hours. The lanes are lit in strung colour rather than civic light, each frontage choosing its own, so the whole district reads as a patchwork after the Corelight drops. Counters and venues pay for late trading and the permission is checked. Fast flight is restricted through the lanes and the restriction is largely self-enforcing, since nobody can get up any speed in the crowd. The bench outside the closed lecture annex is where the night reliably ends, in groups that break up slowly and reform the following evening.

Independent Tutor Hall.description: Legitimate private tutors work from partitioned booths alongside several services operating very near the edge of academic misconduct. Credentials are displayed; some of them are real. Students who cannot afford the Academy's own support end up here, and most of them do fine. The hall is one large floor divided into booths by shoulder-high panels, lit evenly and loud with a dozen quiet conversations, with a booking desk at the entrance that takes a cut of every session. Rates are posted at each booth and negotiated inside it. Tutors rent by the hour and the good ones keep the same booth for years. The complaints file at the desk is open for inspection, and students who check it before booking are notably rarer than students who consult it afterward.

Questionable Assignment Service.description: A shopfront that publicly claims to provide editing support, is investigated every term, and has never once been closed. Its staff are unfailingly cooperative with investigators. Students who use it tend to stop admitting so around the time the disciplinary notices go up. The shopfront is clean, well lit and deliberately unmemorable, with a counter, a price list for editing services and a back room whose door is always shut. Payment is taken in advance and no records are kept beyond what the law requires. The staff answer questions with the same patient script every time. The frontage has been repainted twice in recent cycles, both times in the same colour, which the neighbouring units regard as its most honest feature.

Student Enterprise Arcade.description: Temporary shopfronts and services launched through the professional campus incubator, leased by the term and rebuilt constantly. Half fail before the lease ends and the other half outgrow the arcade. The signage is changed so often the frames are permanently fitted for it. The arcade is a single covered run of small units with shared services and thin partitions, built cheaply on an older foundation and altered by every tenant who can afford to. Leases are short, deposits are real, and the terms are posted at the entrance. Tenants trade through the day and rebuild through the night. The end unit has been empty for two cycles because its previous tenant left the fittings in place and nobody has decided who owns them.

Public Match Viewing Hall.description: A hall of shared displays showing Academy competitions and major Nexaran events to a crowd that pays nothing and reacts to everything. Seats fill hours before a ranked match. Betting is prohibited inside and conducted energetically on the steps outside. The hall is a wide shed of a room with banked benches and displays hung from a reused truss frame, its walls bare because anything hung on them gets damaged on a big night. Entry is free and unmanaged until the room fills, at which point the doors are simply held. Food is not sold inside and arrives anyway. The floor is swept between events, and the count of broken bench slats after a close match is the district's informal measure of how good it was.

Lost Sponsorship Office.description: Support and appeals for students whose house or private patron withdraws funding mid-cycle, offering emergency housing referrals and blunt advice about what comes next. The office is small and constantly busy. Nobody who walks in here is having a good week. It occupies two rooms above a food counter, reached by a stair that makes discretion impossible, with a waiting bench on the landing and a door that is kept closed. Appointments are free and given the same day where possible. Staff can argue a fee deferral, find a bed in the independent blocks and explain exactly how much time a student has. The card taped inside the door lists the offices to try in order, and it has been amended in three different hands.

The Open Circuit.name: The Open Circuit
The Open Circuit.basicInfo: A public and commercial training district that exists entirely outside the Academy, serving residents who are not students, professionals after specialized instruction, visitors testing unfamiliar techniques and anyone who cannot or will not enter house-controlled training. Private instructors, rental gear and open floors are available to whoever can pay the daily rate. It is active, competitive and occasionally exploitative. The district is a run of converted halls in grey-green stone and dulled star-glass, older star-metal structures reroofed and subdivided by successive owners, with reused conduit feeding the lighting rigs and the soft-field boundaries that make the volumes usable. Frontages are painted by whoever holds the lease, so the street reads as a row of competing claims rather than one district identity. Corelight crosses the halls through clerestory slots and marks the trading day, the floors busiest as it rises toward the working hours and again after it drops for the evening, with the cheapest rates in the maintenance window. Everything is priced and posted: floor time, instruction, rental, certification, recovery programmes. The district asks for money rather than a house name, which is exactly why people come to it.
The Open Circuit.hiddenInfo: The Circuit's openness is its strength and its weakness: anyone may teach here, and the False Master Investigation Office exists because of what that permits. It is currently building a case against an instructor whose fabricated record has already cost two clients serious injuries, and the man has moved halls twice to stay ahead of it. The Unlicensed Door has reopened under new ownership again, with the same equipment and a different name over it. Challenge Broker Hall arranges legal contests, but at least one current arrangement is a cover for something else entirely, and the broker involved may not know it. A disgraced Academy student is rebuilding out here where nobody checks transcripts, training beside a minor-house instructor whose reputation is climbing fast enough to attract house attention. Begin Again Court keeps the district honest about what it sells, since most of the people crossing it are proof that talent and a career are different things.

Public Training Floors.description: Wide affordable floors for general physical and affinity work, open from before dawn to late, with a day rate anyone can meet. Dock workers train beside retirees and off-duty protectors. The floors are scuffed past repair and the district considers that a selling point. The halls are high and plain, matted in sections with equipment racked along the walls and no seating for anybody watching. Day passes are bought at a counter by the door and nobody asks for anything else. Attendants circulate to reset equipment and to stop what should be stopped. The board by the counter lists the floor rules in short lines, the last of which was clearly added after an incident and has never been explained to anyone who asks.

Private Instructor Row.description: A run of small rented halls where independent specialists teach on their own terms, reputations ranging from excellent to actively dangerous. Rates are posted at the door and negotiated inside. Students compare instructors in the corridor, which is how most of them choose. The halls are identical boxes behind different frontages, each instructor fitting out their own with whatever equipment and decoration they can afford, so the row runs from bare mats to polished floors within a few doors. Leases are short, and certification is displayed where it exists and conspicuously absent where it does not. The corridor bench between the doors is the row's real institution, occupied by people waiting for a session and willing to tell a stranger exactly what they think of the hall behind them.

Cross-Discipline Hall.description: A hall built for mixed methods and counter-training, where a flier learns what a grounded fighter does to them and a striker learns why precision work matters. Sessions pair strangers deliberately. Cross-house technique disputes surface here without any of the Academy's supervision. The hall is one long floor with mixed surfaces along its length, mats at one end and hard composite at the other, lit unevenly by a rig that has been extended twice. Sessions are booked by the hour and pairings are drawn at the door. Instructors here work by rotation rather than by contract, which means the quality of a session depends on who turned up. The argument about whose tradition a technique belongs to happens at least once a session, and the house rule is that it stops when the timer does.

Aerial Practice Volume.description: Public flight and movement instruction in a netted volume open to anyone from nervous adults to couriers shaving seconds off a route. Beginners keep to the lower third. The upper levels are where professionals practise things the city's traffic rules do not permit outdoors. The volume is a tall converted shaft with netting strung at intervals and marked bands on the walls, its lower floor padded and its upper reaches deliberately unlit except where a session is running.
