Time is sold in blocks and the popular evening blocks go early. An attendant holds the floor and will ground anyone flying beyond their booked band. The beginners' corner keeps a rail to hold and a row of chairs for the people who came with them and have not yet left.

Controlled Impact Court.description: A reinforced court for combat and durability training, floor and walls built to absorb what the Public Training Floors cannot. Bookings are hourly and supervised. The noise carries across the district and residents nearby long ago stopped noticing it. The court is sunk below the street behind a double door, its surfaces layered composite over star-metal and replaced in panels as they fail, with a supervisor's station set into the wall behind armoured glazing. Bookings require a certification check and a deposit against damage. Sessions are timed and cleared strictly, because the next booking is already waiting. The replacement panels on the far wall are a different shade from the originals, and there are enough of them now to read as a map of where people aim.

Precision Studio.description: Quiet rooms for timing, control, balance and low-output technique, used by surgeons, fabricators, performers and fighters who have realized that force is not their problem. Sessions are slow and exacting. It is the least dramatic room in the district and the hardest to book. The rooms are small, softly lit and acoustically dead, fitted with graded apparatus that is calibrated between sessions and never moved otherwise. Booking is by the hour at a rate above the general floors, and the list runs well ahead. Instructors take one client at a time and keep written records of progress that clients may take with them. The waiting corridor is furnished with a single bench and no display of anything, which the regulars say is the first part of the training.

Professional Certification Office.description: Credentials for public protectors, trainers, instructors and specialists, issued after examinations run by assessors who are not paid by the schools. A certificate from this office is accepted across the capital. Refusals are posted, which is how several careers have ended publicly. The office is a plain civic-standard suite with a counter, examination rooms behind it and a public board beside the door where results are displayed until the next cycle replaces them. Examination fees are charged and are not refunded on a failure. Assessors rotate and their names are published with each result. The appeals notice on the board is worn illegible at the fold, which tells its own story about how often people read it before they need it.

Recovery House.description: Legitimate rehabilitation and conditioning, staffed by clinicians who coordinate with the city's clinics and will refuse a client who should not be training. Programmes run for months. Its waiting room mixes injured professionals with people recovering from work nobody calls dangerous. The house is warm and low-lit, its treatment rooms opening off a corridor floored in something quiet, with a conditioning hall at the back that is deliberately visible from the waiting room. Programmes are paid for in blocks and some are supported through referral arrangements that the staff will explain if asked. Clinicians here write to a client's own physician as a matter of course. The noticeboard carries no advertisements, only a list of what the house does not treat and where to go instead.

Equipment Rental Exchange.description: Legal training tools, protective systems and testing gear rented by the hour or the season, inspected on return by staff who log every fault. Losing a deposit here is a minor local tragedy. The exchange is also where people quietly learn which gear is being sold as something it is not. The exchange is a long counter backed by racked stock under hard light, with an inspection bench at one end where returns are opened and checked in front of the person returning them. Deposits are taken against every item and the schedule of charges is posted. Staff mark faults on a card that stays with the item for its working life. The rack of withdrawn gear behind the counter is kept visible on purpose, each piece tagged with the reason it will not be rented again.

Public Demonstration Stage.description: An open stage where instructors market themselves through demonstrations, some genuinely instructive and some pure advertisement. Crowds gather free of charge and judge loudly. A good showing here fills a hall for a season; a bad one is remembered for years. The stage is a raised platform of worn composite at the district's widest point, backed by a blank wall and faced by standing room with no seating at all. Slots are booked through the district office and paid for by the instructor. Demonstrations run through the day and cluster around the evening shift when the working crowd arrives. The rail along the front is bent outward at the centre from years of people leaning on it, and the district has straightened it twice rather than replace it.

Challenge Broker Hall.description: Arranges legal private contests and training matches between clients, with terms written down, witnesses required and outcomes recorded. Brokers take a fee and a reputation risk. Most arrangements are exactly what they appear to be, which is what makes the others work. The hall is a room of small tables with a records counter at the back, plain and well lit, where two parties and a broker can sit without being overheard by the next table. Contests require approved conditions, a named venue and responsibility for damage agreed in advance. The recorded outcomes are available to anyone who asks. The terms board on the wall lists the standard conditions a broker will not vary, and a client who wants them varied is directed, politely, to the door.

False Master Investigation Office.description: Handles dangerous instructors, fabricated records and abusive schools, working from client complaints and its own quiet observation. Its findings can strip a certification. Investigators are not popular in the district and are quietly relied on by almost everyone in it. The office is two rooms above the certification suite, reached by an internal stair so that a complainant need not be seen entering from the street. Complaints can be made in person or in writing and are accepted without a fee. Investigators attend sessions unannounced and are usually recognized. The wall behind the desk carries the current open matters in numbered form only, and the number of cards on it is the district's most accurate measure of its own condition.

Unlicensed Door.description: A training hall that has been closed repeatedly and keeps reopening under new ownership, the same mats and the same clientele behind a fresh name. No certification, no records, cash arrangements. Some of the instruction inside is genuinely good, which is the whole problem. The hall sits behind an unmarked frontage at the end of a side lane, its interior a single matted room with equipment that is older than any of the ownerships and better maintained than the paperwork. Sessions are arranged by word of mouth and paid for on arrival. Nobody signs anything, which suits both sides until it does not. The closure notices from previous administrations are still fixed to the door frame, layered over one another, and nobody has ever bothered to scrape them off.

Begin Again Court.description: Programmes for failed contenders, injured professionals and people changing disciplines entirely, run in a plain court where nobody's previous ranking is mentioned. Sessions are cheap and attendance is unremarkable. A surprising number of the district's best instructors started here. The court is an open floor with a rail and a few benches, lit plainly, with equipment that is functional and unglamorous and a clock nobody watches closely. Sessions are paid for singly rather than in blocks, so a person can stop without explaining. The instructors are drawn from the district and are paid modestly by the court itself. The sign-in sheet asks for a name and nothing else, and there is a quiet convention that names on it are not repeated outside the room.

Grand Lunar Gate Hub.name: Grand Lunar Gate Hub
Grand Lunar Gate Hub.basicInfo: The largest shared public passenger interchange in the Nexaran capitol, connecting Relstaris to every major approved planetary destination through dedicated city gate platforms. Arrivals, departures, student intake, delegation movement and citywide transfers all pass through its concourses, which never fully close. It is vast, precise, overwhelming and in constant motion. The complex is built in pale stone and star-glass on an older star-metal frame, with Dravon-era security corridors still running behind the operations floors and later restoration visible wherever a ceiling meets a wall, and the whole of it is threaded with reused conduit feeding guidance light in the blue the Hub has used for generations. The gates themselves are Contair-built and technically distinct from everything around them, drawing on civic power and support infrastructure without belonging to it. Corelight carries through the high glazing and marks the working periods for the staff more reliably than any rota, dropping through the maintenance window when calibration runs. The Hub moves people; the adjacent Waypoint moves goods. Baggage handling, orientation services and food all cost money here, and the queues are longest where the cheapest options are.
Grand Lunar Gate Hub.hiddenInfo: The Hub moves people; the Waypoint moves goods, and the two are careful not to blur. Routes here are political as much as technical: the Quilrath platform runs under capitol restriction with enhanced review and traveler protections, and operating it grants Dravon no access to unrelated Contair technology or support. Restricted Movement Control is currently managing a closure that has not been publicly explained, and the Platform Dispute Desk is absorbing the anger from it. The Dustfall route has degraded again — component shortages on the far side mean delayed arrivals, which is how the capital first learns that Dustfall is short of something. A traveler flagged at Security Review is being held on grounds the Records Office cannot fully document, and Dravon travelers are meeting a mix of justified scrutiny and plain discrimination at the same desks. Academy Arrival Hall has a student listed as arriving who never reached the housing directions desk, and the Contair Maintenance Annex has an open calibration fault on a platform that is still scheduled.

Solvraxis Gate.description: A controlled direct platform serving House Castro's cultural city, one of only three confirmed Solvraxis connections anywhere. Passage is checked carefully at both ends and the queue is short by design. Travelers arriving from it are usually expected by someone specific. The platform is quiet and restrained, finished in plain pale stone with none of the commercial signage that crowds the rest of the Hub, and the waiting area holds seating for far fewer people than the concourse outside. Passage is booked in advance and confirmed against the receiving city's own checks. Arriving travelers are frequently carrying awkward personal luggage, since what may accompany a passenger is limited, and the handling bench beside the arch is used more here than its size suggests.

Korrvane Gate.description: A high-traffic platform feeding Korrvane's distributed gate plazas, swollen around tournaments, training intakes and public events. Fighters, coaches, families and merchandise sellers arrive in the same waves. The platform staff can predict the crowd from the Korrvane event calendar alone. The platform is built wide with a deep holding apron and a rail line of barriers that can be reconfigured for a surge, its surfaces hard-wearing and repainted often. Equipment cases are common and are checked at a dedicated bench, since training gear may be carried lawfully to approved destinations and is inspected accordingly. The floor markings at the apron have been relaid in a slightly different arrangement each time, and the old lines show through where the traffic is heaviest.

Quilrath Gate.description: A politically sensitive public route governed by capitol restrictions, traveler protections and enhanced review, staffed accordingly. Its operation grants Dravon no access to unrelated Contair technology or support, a point the posted notices repeat. Passage is legal, slow and closely watched. The platform sits behind its own barrier line with a review hall beside it, finished plainly and lit harder than the neighbouring gates so that nothing happens in shadow. Protections are posted in plain language beside the queue, including the right to have a refusal explained and recorded. Staff rotate off this platform more often than elsewhere in the Hub, and the rota board in the corridor behind it shows exactly how short those rotations are.

Vexorath Gate.description: Technical and professional traffic routed into Vexorath's diagnostic and authentication systems under strict Contair standards, with verification beginning before the traveler steps off the platform. Engineers pass through constantly. The platform is the cleanest and quietest in the Hub. It is finished in smooth grey composite with recessed lighting and no advertising at all, its benches few and its floor kept clear for equipment trolleys. The authentication desks work fast because the documentation is usually correct, and the rare failure is handled out of sight in a side room. A worn strip of floor runs from the arch to the transit exchange, marking the path taken by people who have made this journey often enough to stop looking up.

Helvyra Gate.description: The Hub's busiest platform, carrying high-volume passenger, hospitality and commercial traffic between the capital and Nexara's movement and Waypoint centre. Arrivals here have usually travelled before and behave like it. Route notices update faster on this platform than anywhere else. The platform is the largest in the Hub, a broad span of pale stone under a run of route boards, with separate lanes for travelers carrying bounded courier consignments and a handling bench that is busy at every hour. Staff manage the flow by voice as much as by barrier. Traders, hospitality workers and returning residents move through in overlapping waves. The bench at the side of the arch carries a permanent scatter of route cards and timing notes left behind by people who no longer need them.

Ignivex Gate.description: A heat-armored direct platform built to survive what arrives through it; Relstaris and Dustfall are Ignivex's only confirmed Lunar Gate connections. The air near the arch runs warm even between cycles. Thermal materials and forge goods come through alongside the passengers. The platform is armoured in dark plate over its star-metal frame, with a standing clearance area in front of the arch that nobody is permitted to cross while a transit is live. Handling here is specialized and charged accordingly. Travelers arrive in working clothing and are used to the procedure. The floor plates immediately before the arch are replaced on a schedule rather than on failure, and the stack of retired plates against the side wall is the most persuasive safety notice in the building.

Dustfall Gate.description: A smaller and less reliable route tied to Dustfall's patched local gate infrastructure, vulnerable to component shortages and intermittent restriction. Delays here are routine and informative. The platform's waiting benches are worn smoother than any others in the Hub. The platform is modest, tucked at the end of a run, its finishes plainer and its board smaller than those of the major routes, with a status light that the regulars watch more closely than the schedule. Departures are confirmed only shortly before they run. Travelers here carry their own baggage and expect to wait, and the counter sells nothing but water and hot food. The list of held departures posted beside the arch is written by hand, and the staff update it whether or not there is anything new to say.

Regional Transfer Gates.description: A bank of rotating connections to approved smaller settlements and local networks, reassigned on a published schedule that changes more often than travelers like. Destinations appear and vanish seasonally. Nobody who uses these platforms relies on finding the same one twice. The bank is a row of identical arches with reassignable boards above them, built plainly and lit evenly so that no platform in the row looks more important than another. Assignments are posted in the departure hall and again at the head of the row. Travelers gather at the boards rather than at the arches. A standing desk at the entrance to the row exists solely to tell people which platform their destination has moved to, and the person staffing it repeats the same three answers all day.

Main Arrival Concourse.description: An immense hall of pale stone and blue guidance light where the majority of travelers first stand in Relstaris, gate platforms feeding it from every side. The scale stops people where they enter. Concourse staff are trained to spot the ones who have stopped for too long. The ceiling is carried on star-metal ribs older than the current finishes, and the guidance light is routed through conduit that has been reused so many times that its housings are a catalogue of previous city eras. Free water points, public seating and district guidance are available without charge; everything else on the concourse is sold. Fast flight is forbidden across the floor and the restriction is enforced. The worn stone inside the main entrance arches is polished pale in two broad tracks, one inbound and one out.

Grand Departure Hall.description: Scheduling, permit processing, waiting and travel notices for everyone leaving the capital, under a board that rewrites itself continually. Departures are called in several languages and one universal chime. The hall empties and refills on a rhythm the staff feel rather than read. The hall is long and high, glazed along one side so the Corelight crosses the floor through the working periods, with booking counters down one wall and banked seating in the centre that is never quite sufficient. Bookings are made here and missed cycles are argued here. The chime is generated from an old fixture that has been repaired rather than replaced, and its slight flatness is the sound most residents associate with leaving.

Diplomatic Transit Court.description: Secure, separate movement for Republic representatives and official delegations, with its own approach and its own authorization chain. Delegations pass through without touching the public concourse. Reporters wait outside the court's exit anyway, and occasionally it works. The court is a restrained hall of dark star-metal and restored stone, its approach running through a corridor that was cut for security in an earlier era and never removed. Access is by authorization only and the authorizations are checked twice. Delegation staff, escorts and baggage handlers outnumber the representatives themselves. The bench in the public passage outside the exit has no other purpose and is never removed, which the Hub's staff consider an accurate description of the arrangement.

Academy Arrival Hall.description: Student intake, housing directions and family waiting, calm most of the year and complete chaos at term start when several cities' worth of new students land within days. Academy staff work from folding desks. The luggage volume alone has its own dedicated handling crew. The hall is a plain annex off the concourse with a high ceiling and poor acoustics, fitted with barriers that are stored for most of the cycle and deployed for the intake weeks. Directions, transit advice and housing lists are given without charge; storage, portering and onward transport are not. Families wait along the side wall and are asked, repeatedly, to keep the lane clear. The floor markings laid down for the intake surge are never fully removed, and the faded lines are visible through the rest of the year.

Visitor Orientation Center.description: City law, transit, housing, work and district guidance delivered free to anyone who asks, in sessions that run continuously through the day. The advice is practical and unromantic. Half of what it teaches is which offices will help and which will simply take up an afternoon. The centre is a suite of plain rooms off the concourse with a standing counter at the front and seating behind it, papered with district maps that are amended in ink faster than they are reprinted. Sessions are short and repeated. Printed guidance is free; anything the centre arranges on a visitor's behalf is not. The corner shelf of leaflets about work contracts is restocked more often than any other and is the one thing staff will physically press into a newcomer's hands.

Family Reception Court.description: An open court for reunions and departures, ringed with benches and sightlines to the arrival gates. Reunions, arguments and relatives arriving entirely unannounced all happen here in full public view. Hub staff intervene only when someone is clearly not glad to be met. The court is paved in pale stone with a low rail separating it from the concourse traffic, its benches set in facing pairs and its light kept warmer than the guidance blue everywhere else. There is no charge to wait and no limit on how long. Vendors are kept outside the rail, which does not stop them working the entrance. The floor immediately inside the rail is worn in a broad arc where people stand rather than sit, watching the arch and refusing to be seated until they see who they came for.

Lost Property Hall.description: Personal items, luggage and documents recovered from platforms and concourses, shelved by day and claimed against description. A back section holds several objects nobody has ever admitted owning. Staff have a standing policy of not asking why a claim took a year. The hall is a long room of racking behind a counter, lit flatly, with the day's recoveries laid out at the front and everything older moved back by stages until it reaches the far wall. Claims are free; storage beyond a period is charged, and the charge is waived more often than the rules allow. Documents are held separately and released only against identification. The ledger at the counter records every item's journey down the racks, and the entries at the back of it are written in several retired hands.

Emergency Medical Station.description: Treatment for arrival injuries, gate sickness, trauma and urgent transfers, positioned so a stretcher can reach any platform quickly. Cases range from dehydration to genuine emergencies. Its staff see more first-day-in-the-capital collapses than any clinic in the city. The station is a compact clinical suite with a wide door onto the concourse and a cleared route behind the barriers that is kept clear by habit rather than by signage. Stabilization is given first and questions about payment come afterward, with onward referral arranged by patient choice and clinical judgment where the transfer is safe. Clinicians work in short rotations because the pace does not let up. The chairs immediately outside are occupied at all hours by people who are not ill and will not leave.

City Transit Exchange.description: The direct handover from planetary travel to local transit rings and district routes, a layered interchange of platforms, lifts and marked flight lanes. Most travelers reach it within minutes of arriving. Getting it wrong is how newcomers see districts they never intended to visit. The exchange is stacked vertically, older star-metal galleries carrying newer platforms, with the flight lanes marked overhead and a lift bank that is the single most complained-about mechanism in the Hub. Fares are paid at the barrier and cost the same whether or not the traveler ends up in the right district. Staff stand at the junctions through the busy periods and point. The lane markings on the upper deck are repainted constantly and are still the thing first-time fliers misread.

Public Waiting Gardens.description: Planted terraces held deliberately quiet inside the Hub's constant movement, with water, shade and seating that is not designed to move people along. Long-delay travelers sleep here. It is the only part of the facility where the noise genuinely drops. The terraces are stepped in shallow levels behind a screen of planting, floored in something soft underfoot, and lit low enough that the Corelight through the glazing above is the brightest thing in the space. Entry is free and unrestricted, and nobody is asked to prove they are travelling. Water points are public and the food carried in comes from the concourse outside. The gardeners work early, before the first heavy departures, and the residents who use the terraces as an ordinary public garden know exactly when that is.

Restricted Movement Control.description: Gate scheduling, emergency closure and route authorization, run from a controlled floor with live status for every platform in the Hub. Decisions made here strand thousands within minutes. The staff are calm in a way that becomes unsettling during an actual incident. The floor is reached through a security corridor inherited from an older era and never rebuilt, and the room itself is dark except for the status wall, which carries every platform, every hold and every authorization in progress. Access is by post rather than by rank and the list is short. Decisions are logged with the name of the controller who made them. The handwritten card taped below the status wall lists the sequence for a full closure, and it has been rewritten exactly once in living memory.

Contair Maintenance Annex.description: Calibration, safety inspection, repair and technical oversight of the gate systems, staffed to Contair standards with authority to pull a platform out of service. Their sign-off is not negotiable. Schedulers and engineers argue here more or less continuously, and the engineers win. The annex is a workshop and records suite behind the platforms, finished to a technical standard that makes the rest of the Hub look decorative, with test benches, sealed component stores and a door that requires its own authorization. The gates are Contair-built and remain technically distinct from the civic systems that support them. The fault board by the door lists open items by platform, and nobody is permitted to erase one without a signature.

Security Review Court.description: Relstaris law enforcement inside the Hub, structured to check specific concerns without treating every traveler as hostile. Reviews are recorded and time-limited. How well that principle holds depends heavily on which city the traveler came through, and everyone here knows it. The court is a plain suite of interview rooms and a waiting area with fixed seating, lit evenly, with a public counter where a traveler's companion can ask what is happening and receive an answer. Reviews have a posted time limit and an obligation to state the grounds. Officers work in pairs and their names are recorded on the file. The notice board in the waiting area carries the traveler protections in several languages, and the panel in the most-read language is the most faded.

Emergency Isolation Platforms.description: Sealed platforms held in reserve for gate failure, contamination or violent arrival, kept empty and tested weekly. Entry is one-way until control releases it. Most of the Hub's staff have never seen them used, and the ones who have do not discuss it casually. The platforms sit behind heavy doors at the end of a service corridor, finished in bare sealed surfaces with drainage in the floor and nothing that could be picked up and thrown. Tests are run on schedule and logged. Release is controlled from the movement floor and cannot be overridden locally, a design decision that has been questioned and never changed. The corridor outside holds a rack of sealed kit that is inventoried after every test, and the inventory sheet is the most carefully completed document in the building.

Worker Shift Hall.description: Staff coordination for a facility that never fully closes: rotas, briefings, lockers, hot food at every hour. Handovers happen four times a day and carry more accurate route information than any public board. Many of the workers live a short walk away in the service terraces. The hall is a wide low room with long tables, a food counter along one wall and a locker bank along another, its walls hung with rotas, safety notices and a labour association board that management has learned not to touch. Meals are cheap and subsidized through the staff arrangement rather than free. Briefings are given standing, at the change of each shift. The table nearest the counter belongs, by unbroken convention, to whichever crew has just come off the platforms.

Gate Records Office.description: Authorized arrival and departure records, held under civic rules about who may request them and why. Searches are logged. Families looking for someone and investigators building a case use the same counter and receive noticeably different levels of cooperation. The office is a narrow room with a counter, a wall of sealed storage behind it and two clerks who have worked here long enough to recognise a request that will not survive review. Requests are made in writing, charged a handling fee and answered in order. What may be released and to whom is posted beside the counter in the exact wording of the civic rule. The bench outside is occupied most often by people who have already been told no once and have come back with a different question.

Platform Dispute Desk.description: Delays, denied passage, house restrictions and traveler complaints all land at one long counter staffed by people with limited authority and considerable patience. Most disputes are about money. The ones that are not tend to end up filed toward the Security Review Court. The desk runs along one side of the departure hall, unglamorous and permanently busy, with a numbered ticket dispenser and seating that fills before the hall does. Refunds, rebookings and written explanations are all issued here, and the schedule of what can and cannot be refunded is posted where the queue can read it while waiting. Staff work fixed rotations for the sake of their tempers. The complaints register at the end of the counter is public, and travelers read it while they wait.

South Arrival Ward.name: South Arrival Ward
South Arrival Ward.basicInfo: The newcomer district built for people who have reached Relstaris but have not yet found their permanent place in it: short-term rooms, employment intake, orientation schooling and cheap food at every hour. Some residents leave within days; others stay for years because temporary housing turned into the first community that accepted them. It is hopeful, unstable, crowded and culturally mixed. The ward is built close and vertical in ochre stone and grey panel over an older star-metal frame, stacked blocks linked by external stairs and public lifts, with reused conduit running up the outside walls to feed rooms that were added long after the buildings were finished. The colour is nobody's plan: frontages have been repainted by successive owners and the ward reads as a patchwork from any angle. Corelight reaches the lower lanes late and thin, so the ward keeps its own lamps burning through the working periods and fills at the evening shift when the gate crews change. Nothing here is free except advice: rooms, meals, storage, lessons and passage all carry a price, and the gap between what a newcomer was promised and what a room actually costs is the ward's defining fact.
South Arrival Ward.hiddenInfo: The Ward runs on promises, and a measurable share of them are false. Independent Recruiter Row puts honest small employers at the same tables as operators who take a placement fee for a job that does not exist, and the No Sponsor Desk is currently working through a cluster of arrivals who all named the same promised patron and all found nobody waiting. Underworld figures move through the ward offering faster solutions than the public offices can, and their terms are clearer and their money arrives first. A family in the Short-Term Residence Towers is coming apart over whether to stay in the capital at all, one half already working and the other half counting passage costs at the Return Passage Office. Long-term residents who run the First Week Court do more real orientation than the school does, and they have started warning newcomers about specific recruiters by name — which has made the court itself a target for complaints nobody will put their name to.

New Arrival Housing.description: Short-term public and private rooms let by the night or the week, small and clean and stacked in narrow blocks near the transit lines. Most residents arrive with one bag and a name to find. The corridors carry cooking smells from eight cities at once. The blocks are plain and well used, their stairwells lit at all hours and their entry desks staffed by people who have seen every possible version of a first day. Rooms are let against payment in advance with no requirement to show a local record, which is the whole point of the place. Bedding is provided and laundry is charged. The board in every entrance carries the same three notices in several languages: the rate, the rules and where to go if the job a resident came for does not exist.

Employment Intake Hall.description: Entry-level jobs, apprenticeships, public contracts and referrals handled from a long hall of numbered desks with a queue that starts before opening. Most placements are real and poorly paid. The staff know which employers to steer people away from and are not permitted to say so aloud. The hall is a single wide room under a reused truss roof, floored in hard composite, with the desks ranged along one side and benches filling the rest of the space. Registration is free and a placement carries no fee to the worker, a rule posted at the door and broken outside it. Interviews are held at the desk in front of everyone waiting. The chalk board above the desks lists the morning's openings and is wiped and rewritten as they go, which is why the queue forms so early.

Short-Term Residence Towers.description: Affordable towers with rapid turnover, shared washrooms and rent set by the fortnight. Families crowd into rooms meant for two and make it work. Half the doors on any floor change occupants within a season, and the neighbours have long since stopped learning names. The towers are narrow and tall, built cheaply onto an older foundation, their lifts unreliable and their stairwells the real thoroughfare of the building. Rent is collected in advance and a missed payment is answered quickly. Water and power are charged separately and the charge is the thing residents argue about most. The landing on each floor holds a shared cooking point, a drying rail and a rota that is honoured until the fortnight's arrivals change everything again.

Family Reception Center.description: Support for relocated families and dependents: school placement, childcare referral, documentation and the practical business of moving several people into one unfamiliar city. Staff work in whatever language the family brought. Children are given something to do while the adults are told hard things. The centre is a low building with a carpeted waiting room, a corner of worn toys and a run of small offices where a family can sit together without being overheard. Services are free and referrals are made the same day where they can be. Placement into district schools depends on capacity and the capacity is not always there. The wall by the door carries a map of the city with the transit rings marked, and the same three districts have been pointed at so often that the finish is worn through.

Public Orientation School.description: Free classes in city systems, district culture, law, transit and practical survival, taught in short cycles so a newcomer can finish before their first job starts. Attendance is voluntary and heavy. The most valuable session is the one on which contracts not to sign. The school is two classrooms and a hall in a converted block, fitted with benches rather than desks and a display wall that is redrawn for each cycle. Teaching is done by ward staff and by long-term residents who are paid a little for it. Classes run early, late and between shifts so that people in work can attend. The attendance sheet is kept for the ward's own records and for nothing else, a point the teachers make at the start of every cycle because somebody always asks.

Cheap Food Terrace.description: Open terraces of low-cost counters serving every shift, from pre-dawn gate workers to people coming off a night at the Market. Portions are large, prices are posted, and nobody comments on how long a customer sits. Regional cooking here is the unglamorous, accurate kind. The terraces are stepped above the lane behind a rail, roofed in panel along their length, with long shared tables and counters that pay a pitch fee to the ward. Counters open and close on their own hours, so something is always being served. Water is free and refills are not questioned. The end table nearest the stair is where the ward's long-term residents sit, and newcomers work out within a few days that it is the most useful seat in the district.

Independent Recruiter Row.description: A row of hiring tables where legitimate employers work alongside operators charging fees for work that will never materialize. Both look identical at the start of a conversation. Experienced residents walk newcomers along it and translate what the offers actually mean. The row runs down one side of a covered lane with numbered pitches that are registered and paid for by the day, which establishes who was there and almost nothing else. Offers are made verbally and written down only if the applicant insists. The ward posts a notice at each end advising that no lawful employer charges a worker to be hired. The notice has been torn down and replaced often enough that the ward now fixes it with metal rather than paste.

Arrival Services Clinic.description: Basic medical care and referral for people without established records: gate sickness, untreated injuries, pregnancy care and the conditions that travel badly. No proof of residence is required. The clinic is the first place in the capital many arrivals are asked how they are actually doing. The building is small and plainly clinical, waiting benches along one wall and consulting rooms along the other, kept warm and lit steadily through the night. Charges are modest and reduced through an access arrangement that the desk explains without being asked. Referral onward follows patient choice and clinical judgment where transport is safe. The card rack by the door holds contacts for clinics, childcare and the No Sponsor Desk, and the staff restock it by hand every morning.

Temporary Storage Hall.description: Racked lockers and crated storage for residents without stable housing, rented cheaply and audited rarely. Whole lives sit in these cages for months. Staff have a quiet protocol for what happens when a locker goes unpaid and unclaimed for a full season. The hall is a converted service floor with cages stacked in rows, lit by strip lamps and watched by an attendant at the single door. Rentals are paid by the fortnight and a lapsed rental is held before it is cleared. Residents may access their cage during posted hours and are not asked what is in it. The list of unclaimed cages is posted by number at the door, and the numbers stay on it far longer than the rules require because nobody wants to be the one to clear them.

Newcomer Flight Lessons.description: Instruction in Relstaris traffic etiquette and dense-city movement for people who learned to fly over open ground and are now facing suspended bridges and public corridors. Lessons run in a marked practice lane. The first rule taught is where fast flight is forbidden and why. The lane is a netted run above a cleared yard, marked with the same lane symbols used across the city, with a low platform where the instructor stands and a rail of chairs for people waiting their turn. Lessons are cheap and booked in short blocks, and the ward subsidises places for residents in registered work. Instructors are certified and say so. The practice lane's markings are repainted after every civic change, and the older symbols underneath are used to explain why the rules are what they are.

House Contact Office.description: Helps residents locate relatives or house support without requiring either, holding directories for minor houses and a discreet referral system for people who would rather not be found. Some searches end in a reunion. Others end with a clerk explaining that the house has not replied. The office is two rooms with a counter and one closed interview room, deliberately quiet, its directories held in bound volumes that are updated by hand as corrections arrive. Enquiries are free and a resident may ask that their own name be withheld from any reply. Clerks make contact on the resident's behalf rather than passing details on. The volume for the smallest houses is the most heavily annotated in the room, and no two clerks agree on whose handwriting is which.

No Sponsor Desk.description: Assistance for people whose promised support never appeared: the patron who stopped answering, the job that was withdrawn, the relative who moved cities. Staff handle it without moralizing. They keep an unofficial list of names that come up repeatedly and share it carefully. The desk is a counter and two chairs at the end of the intake hall, positioned so that a conversation there is not conducted in front of the whole queue. Help is free and immediate where it can be: a bed for the night, a referral, an argument with an employer made on the resident's behalf. What the desk cannot do is conjure the support that was promised, and it says so early. The unofficial list is kept in a drawer, written in pencil, and has never been photographed or copied.

Return Passage Office.description: Arranges and part-funds passage home, deliberately framed so that leaving Relstaris is a decision rather than a disgrace. Counsellors ask what the person wants, not what their family expects. A quarter of those who book passage here cancel it and stay anyway. The office is a small suite with a private room and a window onto the lane, furnished plainly and without any of the ward's usual noticeboards. Passage is arranged through the Gate Hub and the office covers the costs around it against a means assessment that is handled discreetly. Bookings can be cancelled without penalty. The shelf behind the counsellor's chair holds a handful of returned items left by people who changed their minds, kept in case they come back for them.

First Week Court.description: An open gathering court run largely by long-term residents rather than the city, where newcomers are fed, advised, warned and occasionally found work by people who arrived the same way. There is no official programme. It is the most effective institution in the ward. The court is a paved square with a covered edge, a water point, benches nobody owns and a cooking point that residents supply between them. Nothing is charged and nothing is recorded. The people who run it hold no post and would not accept one. The board propped against the wall carries hand-written warnings about specific recruiters and specific rooms, rewritten whenever it is taken down, and it is the first thing an experienced resident points a newcomer toward.

Relstaris Grand Market.name: Relstaris Grand Market
Relstaris Grand Market.basicInfo: The broadest legal consumer market on Nexara, where almost anything legally available anywhere on the planet can be found through an official seller, specialist importer, family stall or house gallery. Minor houses and independent makers use it to build influence without holding any political power at all. It is dense, colourful, competitive and socially layered from the salvage courts to the luxury galleries. The Market is a roofed and half-roofed sprawl of stone arcades, star-glass galleries and open courts laid over a much older star-metal frame, with Corsair balconies overhanging lanes that were cut long after they were built and old conduits reused to carry lane lighting and cold storage. No two lanes share a palette: each has been painted, hung and re-signed by the sellers who hold it, and the contrast between a salvage court and a luxury gallery is the first thing a visitor reads. Corelight crosses the open courts and sets the trading day, the food halls busiest before it reaches full daytime intensity and the galleries filling as it drops. Leases, pitch fees, verification charges and mediation costs are all real, and every rung of the Market is contested by somebody already standing on the one below.
Relstaris Grand Market.hiddenInfo: The Market is one of the few ladders in Relstaris that does not require a house behind you, which makes every rung contested. A minor-house product has become famous fast enough that larger sellers are trying to buy, copy or discredit it, and the Rising Name Promenade slot it holds expires soon. Counterfeit Contair-standard equipment is circulating through legal sellers who believe their paperwork is genuine, and the Vexorath Verification Desk has started rejecting whole consignments. A recent business collapse has turned into a property war over the lease, fought through the Mediation Court and the Failure Auction Floor at once. Dustfall salvage brought in stolen cargo that the Waypoint has been quietly looking for, and the seller cannot explain the chain of ownership. A public boycott is building against one gallery over a cultural claim it made about a regional product, and underworld goods are entering the Market through at least one seller who thinks they are simply getting a very good price.

Hundred-House Market.description: Stalls and shops run by minor houses from across Nexara, each flying its own small banner along crowded aisles. Families trade here for generations and treat a good pitch as inheritance. It is the most direct place in the capital to discover which small houses are rising. The aisles are narrow and roofed in mismatched panel, every frontage decorated to its own house's taste, so the lane changes colour every few paces and nobody has ever tried to standardise it. Pitches are leased through the contract hall and transferred within families as often as the rules allow. Trade runs from early, with the aisles cleared and swept at the close of the day. The corner pitches at each junction cost noticeably more, and the argument about who holds them is older than most of the sellers.

Luxury Trade Gallery.description: High-value art, materials, clothing, equipment and private service, sold in quiet rooms behind star-glass where prices are never displayed. Major-house buyers shop by appointment. The gallery's discretion is part of the product and its provenance records are genuinely excellent. The gallery is a restored arcade of polished stone and dark star-metal, lit low and evenly, with rooms rather than shopfronts and staff who open a door rather than call from it. Appointments are made in advance and casual visitors are received politely and briefly. Provenance is documented for every significant piece and the documentation travels with it. The visitors' book at the arcade entrance is signed by everyone who enters, which is the gallery's oldest security arrangement and its most effective one.

Independent Artisan Rows.description: Makers, designers, repair specialists and outright experimenters working from open-fronted units where the workshop is the shop. Customers watch things being finished. Many of these artisans keep a second bench over in Maker's Reach and sell the results here. The rows are lit from above through old star-glass panels, floors littered with offcuts, benches pushed close enough to the front that a customer can be handed a piece while it is still warm. Units are leased by the season and the good ones pass by recommendation rather than by advertisement. Commissions are taken with a deposit and a date that is usually optimistic. The chalked board at the end of the row lists which makers are taking work this season and which are not, and it is updated by the makers themselves.

Regional Food Exchange.description: Ingredients and prepared food from every major city, traded in a hall of cold rooms, heat cabinets and arguments about freshness. Chefs from across Relstaris buy here at dawn. The Culinary Institute sends students to learn what an honest supplier looks like. The hall is high and hard-surfaced, its cold rooms running off reused conduit that the Market has maintained rather than replaced, the whole of it smelling of everything at once and rinsed down at the close of each day. Trade is done in bulk before the Corelight reaches full daytime intensity and in small quantities afterward. Stock depends entirely on what the routes delivered. The board at the entrance lists which cities' goods arrived this cycle, and a blank line on it moves prices across the hall before anyone announces anything.

Training Goods Hall.description: Legal training equipment, clothing, protection systems and instruction materials sold under posted safety ratings, with testing rigs on the floor for buyers who insist. Open Circuit instructors kit out entire halls here. The counterfeit problem is worst in this room and everybody knows it. The hall is a broad space of racked stock under hard light, the rigs set in a cleared centre where a demonstration draws a crowd within moments. Sellers are required to display ratings and to permit a test on request. Equipment may be carried lawfully from here to approved schools and secured events, and the route restrictions are posted beside the door. The wall of withdrawn items behind the inspection bench is kept on display, each piece labelled with what it was sold as and what it actually was.

Dustfall Salvage Court.description: Recovered, repaired, repurposed and occasionally disputed goods from the independent mixed-house frontier, sold from open crates by traders of no single house identity. Everything here has had a previous life. Buyers hunt for parts nobody manufactures any more, and sometimes find more than that. The court is open to the air on three sides, floored in worn stone, its crates stacked on pallets and its lighting strung between poles because nothing here is permanent enough to justify fixed fittings. Ownership is asserted rather than documented, and a buyer who wants a chain of title is directed to the mediation court. The tarpaulins over the crates are patched in a dozen colours, and the patches are the most Dustfall thing in the Market.

Ignivex Materials Lane.description: Thermal materials, forge work, cooking systems and heat-resistant products, sold down a lane that stays several degrees warmer than the rest of the Market. Demonstrations involve real flame under real supervision. Ignivex sellers bargain loudly and consider silence rude. The lane is narrow, vented overhead and floored in plate rather than stone, its frontages dark with use and its stock stacked heavily enough that the Market inspects the loading annually. Demonstration bays are licensed and separated from the stock by a clear standing space. Prices are argued at volume and settled with a handshake that is expected to hold. The soot mark above each demonstration bay is cleaned on a schedule and back within days, and the sellers treat it as advertising.

Korrvane Competition Market.description: Tournament goods, training brands, fighter merchandise and match-analysis tools, arranged around display screens running recent bouts. Academy students and Open Circuit trainees shop side by side. Fan culture and equipment retail are entirely indistinguishable here. The stalls are bright and loud, hung with house and fighter colours in combinations nobody would choose for a building, and the screens are angled so that a crowd forms in the aisle and has to be moved on. Stock follows the Korrvane calendar and is discounted brutally when a favourite loses. The rack of last season's merchandise at the back of the market is the cheapest clothing in the district and is bought steadily by people with no interest in the sport at all.

Solvraxis Cultural Exhibition.description: Refined clothing, art, educational goods and protected-city products presented with more restraint than anything around them. Stock is limited by what Solvraxis permits to leave. Buyers are given the cultural context whether or not they asked for it. The gallery is a quiet run of pale rooms with wide spacing between pieces, lit softly and deliberately unlike the lanes on either side of it, its frontage the only one in the arcade without a sign in more than one colour. Stock arrives in small consignments and sells slowly. Staff explain provenance and intended use at length, and a purchase takes longer here than anywhere else in the Market. The bench opposite the entrance is used by people waiting for companions who have been inside considerably longer than they expected.

Quilrath Equipment Row.description: Dravon-region manufactured goods, widely regarded as inferior to Contair standards and still bought steadily for price, availability, compatibility or political loyalty. Sellers make the case plainly. Customers who argue the quality point get a shrug and the number on the tag. The row is plain and practical, stock stacked in crates with the prices chalked on the side, its lighting adequate and its frontages undecorated beyond a painted name. Nothing here is sold as something it is not, which the sellers regard as their only real advantage. The verification desk is a short walk away and the row's sellers point customers toward it without being asked, because the alternative is worse for everyone.

Vexorath Verification Desk.description: Confirms legitimate Contair standards and rejects counterfeit claims, testing items brought in by sellers, buyers and inspectors alike. A rejection slip is public. The queue lengthens noticeably whenever a fake consignment reaches the Market, which is how the Market learns one has. The desk is a counter and a testing bay in a plain bay off the main arcade, finished to technical standard and kept deliberately unwelcoming to conversation. Tests are charged and run in order, with no allowance for who is waiting. Results are issued in writing and posted by item rather than by seller. The board of current rejections beside the counter is read by every buyer in the Training Goods Hall before a major purchase, and by every seller in it the moment a new slip goes up.

Helvyra Trade Arcade.description: Corsair goods, travel supplies, alcohol, route-dependent stock, legal magical tools and specialized sword equipment under one long arcade. What is available depends entirely on which routes are running. Traders here have the best current information on route conditions in the district. The arcade is long and roofed in star-glass, its frontages hung with goods rather than signs, and the whole of it smells of oil, packing straw and whatever came in this cycle. Stock turns over fast and prices move with the routes rather than with the season. Magical tools are sold legally and openly and draw as many sightseers as buyers. The route board at the arcade's centre is copied from the Waypoint's own gallery and is annotated by traders who disagree with it.

Public Contract Hall.description: Vendor agreements, market leases and event contracts are registered and witnessed here, with standard terms posted on the wall for anyone negotiating alone. New sellers sign their first lease at these tables. So do the people about to lose one. The hall is a plain civic room of long tables and a registration counter, lit evenly, its walls carrying the standard terms in large plain lettering that has been repainted rather than reworded. Registration carries a fee and a witness is provided without charge. Clerks will read a document aloud on request, which is a service used more often than the Market admits. The bench along the back wall is where people sit to read what they are about to sign, and the hall keeps it deliberately far from the tables.

Market Mediation Court.description: Customer, landlord, counterfeit and commercial disputes are heard by mediators with authority to suspend a trading licence on the spot. Hearings are fast and public. A seller who loses twice in a season generally finds their lease is not renewed. The court sits in an open-fronted chamber where anyone passing can stop and listen, which is a deliberate arrangement and does more work than the penalties do. Filings are cheap and heard within days. Mediators rotate and are drawn from outside the trade in question. The bell above the chamber entrance is rung at the start of each hearing, and sellers in the surrounding lanes can tell from the number of rings what kind of dispute is being heard.

Failure Auction Floor.description: Legal sale of inventory, equipment and leases from closed businesses, conducted in the open so that nothing disappears quietly into a rival's hands. Bidders include vultures and old friends. The former owner is entitled to attend, and some of them do. The floor is a plain hall with a raised block, banked standing room and a side table where lots are laid out for inspection before the sale. Lots are catalogued publicly in advance and the catalogue names the business. Payment is immediate and collection is the buyer's problem. The chairs set aside at the front for the former owner are kept there whether or not anyone uses them, a practice the auction officers have maintained for longer than any of them can account for.

Rising Name Promenade.description: Premium frontage awarded temporarily to small businesses gaining public attention, allocated by a committee whose decisions are argued over across the whole Market. A season here can make a maker's career. Losing the slot at the end of it has ended a few as well. The promenade is a wide paved run with star-glass frontages and the best light in the Market, its units fitted out to a standard the Market maintains rather than the tenant. Slots are granted for a set term and cannot be extended, and the rent is nominal precisely so that the award means something. Committee decisions are posted with reasons. The plaque list at the promenade's entrance records every business that has held a slot, and the names nobody recognises outnumber the ones they do.

Grand Waypoint and Cargo Exchange.name: Grand Waypoint and Cargo Exchange
Grand Waypoint and Cargo Exchange.basicInfo: The largest Corsair logistics site outside Helvyra's flagship network centre, handling cargo, delivery, commercial routing, emergency supply and the disputes that follow all four. The Lunar Gates move travelers; this complex moves the capital's material life. It is fast, tightly organized, extremely loud and socially chaotic at every hour of the shift cycle. The site is built for load rather than for looking at: star-metal decks and ramp halls under a roof of ribbed panel, floors painted in route colours that are relaid as the handling arrangements change, with older conduit runs reused to carry deck lighting and the cold stores. Its bones are older than its function, and a Genesis foundation, a Dravon service corridor and a Corsair-built gantry all carry traffic in the same building. Corelight enters through high slots and marks the shift pattern, the heaviest movement running before it reaches full daytime intensity and again on the evening change, with maintenance taken in the low window. Everything is charged: shipping, storage, priority, insurance, the locker a small trader keeps stock in. What arrives here is visible in the Grand Market within days, and what fails to arrive is visible faster.
Grand Waypoint and Cargo Exchange.hiddenInfo: Everything the city consumes is legible from these floors before it is visible anywhere else. Route conditions posted in the Commercial Route Gallery are already showing a supply line under strain, and cargo workers in the Commons have worked out what it means several days ahead of any representative. A consignment of emergency medical cargo has gone missing between manifest and pickup, and the Lost Parcel Department's file on it is thinner than it should be. Private house shipments have been misdelivered to the wrong compound twice this season, which is either incompetence or a very cheap way to read a rival's supplies. The Quiet Reroute Office is the site's real vulnerability: legitimate emergency rerouting authority, minimal oversight, and the single access smugglers most want. A legal route has become politically impossible to run, and the workaround being arranged is legal in only the narrowest sense. Xyren interests have again approached the site about modifying or removing the Grand Xyren Sign, and the request was refused in terms nobody bothered to soften.

Grand Relstaris Waypoint.description: The public commercial counter and network hub of the whole complex, a high hall of live route boards, booking desks and Corsair staff working several conversations at once. Anyone can ship from here. The noise is constant and the queue moves faster than it looks. The hall is wide and hard-floored, its ceiling carried on a Corsair gantry that still takes load, with the booking desks ranged under the boards and a weighing and handling line running down one side. Rates are posted by route and class and change with conditions. Consignments are checked, labelled and taken at the counter, and nothing leaves without a manifest. The floor paint at the head of the queue has been worn down to bare deck and repainted so many times that the current line does not quite match the one beneath it.

House Cargo Exchange.description: Major-house and institutional shipments handled on separate floors with their own manifests, seals and handling crews. Volume here dwarfs the public counter. Rival houses' cargo passes within metres of each other, which is why the routing is deliberately opaque. The floors are reached by their own ramps and worked by crews who are assigned rather than chosen, under lighting brighter than the public hall so that seals can be checked at a glance. Contracts are negotiated in offices above the deck and the rates are not published. Handling is charged by weight, class and priority, with a premium for discretion. The seal store behind the supervisor's office is inventoried at every shift change, and a discrepancy in it stops the floor until it is resolved.

Courier Flight Deck.description: Launch and return for priority local delivery, an exposed deck of marked lanes where couriers drop in, load and are gone inside a minute. Flight discipline is absolute and enforced by the deck crew. Couriers rank each other informally and viciously on turnaround times. The deck is a broad plate platform with numbered bays, screens along the outer edge and a crew station at the centre that controls every movement onto it. Couriers are registered, insured and paid by the consignment. Loads are handed over at the bay and signed for on the spot, since nothing is left standing on the deck. The bay numbering was changed once, years ago, and half the couriers still use the old numbers, which the crew have long since stopped correcting.

Diplomatic Shipment Hall.description: Protected Republic, Citadel and representative cargo, moved under seal with a documented chain of custody and its own secure dock. Contents are not declared to handlers. The hall's paperwork survives longer than most of the governments that generate it. The hall is plain and controlled, a short run of deck behind a barrier with its own dock door and a records office that never has more than two people in it. Access is by authorization and the authorization is checked against a list that is updated daily. Handlers move sealed units and are not told what they contain. The custody register is kept in bound volumes rather than only in the systems, a redundancy introduced after an incident that the current staff know about only from the volumes themselves.

Independent Cargo Lockers.description: Small-business and individual storage in racked units rented by the month, from a single crate to a whole bay. Traders stage Market stock here. The lockers are the cheapest legitimate way to hold goods in the capital and are consequently always full. The store is a deep hall of caged racking under strip lighting, reached from the public hall by a ramp worn smooth by handcarts, with an attendant at the entrance who checks every departure against a ticket. Rentals are paid in advance and access runs through posted hours. Insurance is offered, declined by most and regretted by some. The waiting list is kept at the attendant's desk on a clipboard, and everyone who asks is told the same estimate regardless of how long it actually takes.

Emergency Supply Office.description: Medical, infrastructure and disaster-priority routing, with standing authority to bump commercial cargo off a route without negotiation. During a crisis this office effectively runs the site. Between crises it maintains reserves and argues with everyone about storage space. The office is a control room and a reserve store on the same level, the room plainly fitted with a status wall and the store kept locked, stocked and rotated on a schedule that nobody is permitted to defer. Priority is granted against criteria that are published, which does not stop the arguments. Bumped consignments are recorded and compensated under the site's own rules. The reserve store's rotation log hangs inside the door, and the initials on the last line are checked by the next person before anything is moved.

Premium Delivery Hall.description: High-value speed and security contracts, handled by vetted crews in a hall with its own access control and insurance desk. Clients pay for guaranteed timing and mostly get it. Failures here are expensive enough that the Damaged Cargo Court keeps a dedicated list. The hall is smaller and cleaner than the general floors, finished to a standard clients can see, with its own dock, its own scales and an insurance desk that is part of the sale rather than an afterthought. Crews are vetted, named on the contract and rotated to prevent familiarity with any one client. Timing guarantees carry penalties that are actually paid. The client waiting room has a window onto the dock, deliberately, so that a nervous shipper can watch their own consignment being loaded.

Lost Parcel Department.description: Misrouted, disputed, unidentified and politically inconvenient packages accumulate on deep shelving under numbered claims. Investigators work the backlog steadily. A few items have sat here long enough that their original senders no longer exist in any registry. The department is a long room of shelving behind a counter, lit unevenly, its aisles arranged by the date an item arrived rather than by anything useful. Claims are made against description and a handling charge, and a disputed claim is referred to the cargo court. Investigators trace routes backward through manifests that are frequently incomplete. The oldest aisle at the back is not swept as often as the others, and the dust on it is the department's most honest measure of its own backlog.

Damaged Cargo Court.description: Inspection, responsibility, insurance and compensation decided in a court with the goods present as evidence, crates opened in front of both parties. Verdicts are quick. Carriers, senders and insurers all lose here often enough to keep taking the process seriously. The court is a hard-floored chamber with an inspection bench, a drain and a public bench along one wall, built so that a damaged consignment can be brought straight in from the deck. Filing costs little and the court hears it quickly. Assessors are drawn from the site and from outside it, and their reports are given to both parties in writing. The bench is scarred from decades of crates being levered open on it, and nobody has ever proposed replacing it with something more dignified.

Commercial Route Gallery.description: Live route conditions and supply risk displayed across a long wall of boards, updated as fast as reports arrive from every city on the planet. Merchants read it like weather. A route going amber here moves prices in the Grand Market within a day. The gallery is a raised walk facing the board wall, with standing room, a rail and a row of desks where traders work directly from the display. Access is free and the gallery is busiest at the shift changes. The boards carry conditions and risk rather than promises, and the distinction is stated in the heading of every column. The chalk ledge below the boards is used by traders to keep their own running notes, and the site cleans it once a cycle and never more often than that.

Restricted Goods Review.description: Legal review of controlled materials before they move, staffed by inspectors with the authority to hold a consignment indefinitely. Documentation is checked against the goods themselves. Most holds are paperwork failures; a small and memorable minority are not. The review floor is a sealed bay with an inspection table, a secure hold and an office where the paperwork is worked through line by line while the shipper waits outside. Reviews are charged and scheduled, and a consignment that arrives without its documentation simply waits. Inspectors work in pairs and sign jointly. The hold cage at the back carries items that have been there long enough to acquire their own file numbers, and the inspectors refer to some of them by those numbers alone.

Cargo Worker Commons.description: Shift meals, labour organization and route gossip in a wide canteen that never empties, tables claimed by crew and held across generations. The food is heavy and cheap. More is accurately known about the capital's supply situation in this room than in the Republic Forum. The commons is a low hall with a serving counter along one end, long tables, a wall of lockers and a labour association board that management has learned not to interfere with. Meals are subsidized through the site's own arrangement rather than free. Crews come in at the change of every shift and leave in the same groups they arrived with. The table nearest the door belongs to the deck crews by an arrangement nobody wrote down and nobody has successfully challenged.

Grand Xyren Sign.description: The most formal and devastating anti-Xyren sign on Nexara, mounted where every arriving crew must pass it, displayed as a civic requirement nobody can remember officially approving. Its wording is precise and merciless. Attempts to alter or remove it are made and refused with some regularity. The sign is cut into dark star-metal and set at the head of the main handling approach, lit from above so that it is legible at every hour of the shift cycle. It is cleaned as part of the site's routine maintenance and has been recast at least once, in the same wording. Crews pass it without comment and visitors stop in front of it. The stone beneath the mounting is worn in a shallow arc where people have stood to read the whole of it.

Quiet Reroute Office.description: Legitimate emergency rerouting, handled discreetly so that a diverted shipment does not become a public incident. The authority is real and the oversight is thin. It is, by common agreement across the underworld, the single access at this site most worth acquiring. The office is two rooms off a service corridor, unmarked except by a number, with a desk, a terminal and a filing cabinet that is not the site's main record system. Reroutes are authorized by a single officer on duty and logged afterward rather than before. The work is genuinely necessary and genuinely difficult to audit. The corridor outside carries no traffic except people going to this door, which is the one detail that makes the office hard to visit unnoticed.

Public Pickup Hall.description: Crowded civilian parcel collection, a hall of numbered windows and a queue that reaches the doors on delivery days. Families, students and small traders collect here in person. The staff have heard every possible explanation for a missing claim slip. The hall is plain and hard-surfaced with a barrier rail steering the queue past the windows, its noticeboards carrying collection rules that are read while waiting and forgotten at the counter. Items are held for a period and then charged storage. Identification is required and a nominated collector can be registered in advance, which almost nobody does until the first time they need it. The seating at the side is occupied by people waiting for someone else's queue number, and by children who have been told to sit there and stay.

Open Contract Hall.name: Open Contract Hall
Open Contract Hall.basicInfo:
The capital's central place for jobs, apprenticeships, public contracts and independent work, connecting workers, professionals, students, houses, businesses and institutions in one enormous hall. It is one of the clearest expressions of Relstaris's promise that anyone can become anything, and one of the clearest demonstrations of how easily opportunity turns into exploitation. Ambitious, crowded, hopeful and entirely transactional. The building is a single great volume of pale grey stone and star-glass on a star-metal frame, galleries stacked around an open floor, its listing boards mounted on panels that were cut into a Dravon-era corridor wall and never fully disguised. Old conduits carry the board lighting, and the brass rails along the galleries have been polished by hands rather than by staff. Corelight falls through the high glazing onto the public floor and marks the hiring day, the crowd thickest before it reaches full daytime intensity and thinning as it drops, with the immediate queue still standing well into the evening shift. Registration is free and most of what happens here is not: credential checks, contract reviews, arbitration filings and the cost of the days spent waiting.

Work on offer here: Relstaris — The Signed Shift (ask Branna Sol).
Open Contract Hall.hiddenInfo: The Hall's rules are good; enforcement depends on who complains. The Fair Contract Review Office is tracking a contract template circulating on the public floor that is legal, comprehensible and designed to trap the signer in unpaid obligation, and it has already appeared under three different employer names. Sol contractors continue to be offered a disproportionate share of dangerous work through the Sol Contractor Board, and an organizer is building a case out of the Disputed Payment Court's records to prove the pattern rather than the individual incidents. A major house is recruiting a specialist away from a family business that will not survive the loss. Underworld recruiters are copying public listings word for word and running interviews two streets away, which is why the Reputation Verification Desk has started checking employers as well as applicants. The Closed Contract Archive holds the files on failed jobs, injuries and disappearances, and someone has been requesting rather too many of them.

Public Job Floor.description: The Hall's open heart: banks of listings, direct interview booths and a crowd that turns over completely between morning and evening. Work is offered and accepted the same hour. The board refreshes constantly and people watch it the way others watch a match. The floor is a wide stone expanse under the galleries, its listing banks arranged in rows with standing room between them and interview booths built into the side walls. Listing here is free to employers and registration is free to workers, which is why the floor is the busiest room in the district. Terms are shown on the listing and rarely improve in the booth. The rail in front of the central bank has been worn to a different colour at the height where people rest their hands while reading.

Professional Contract Gallery.description: Specialist work in medicine, engineering, law, security, education and administration, posted with real terms and negotiated in private rooms off the gallery. Credentials matter here more than anywhere else in the Hall. Employers court candidates rather than the reverse. The gallery runs above the public floor behind a brass rail, quieter and better finished, its negotiation rooms small and glazed so that a meeting is visible without being audible. Listings carry stated terms and an employer who posts here is expected to honour them. Candidates are checked at the verification desk before a meeting is arranged. The seating along the gallery is comfortable, which is the clearest signal in the building about who the room is designed to keep waiting and who it is not.

Apprenticeship Court.description: Training placements with businesses, houses and independent masters, arranged face to face in a court where the master and the applicant both have to show up. Terms cover years. The court keeps a standing register of masters who have been struck off it. The court is an open square of tables under a lower ceiling than the main floor, set out so that each conversation happens within sight of the clerks. Placements are registered, and the terms, hours and conditions are recorded rather than left to memory. A family member or advocate may sit in and frequently does. The struck-off register hangs by the entrance where every applicant passes it, and the clerks will read out the reasons for any name on it to anyone who asks.

Independent Contractor Hall.description: Short-term work, consulting, protection, investigation and technical service, listed by contractors advertising themselves rather than by employers. Rates are public and undercut openly. Half the capital's freelance professionals keep a permanent listing on this wall. The hall is a long room with the listing wall down one side and a run of hire desks down the other, noisier than the galleries and considerably more direct. A listing carries a term fee and can be amended daily. Contractors are expected to display certification where the work requires it, and the desks check. The most contested space is the eye-level strip at the centre of the wall, which is allocated by a rotation the hall enforces because the alternative was worse.

Civic Service Desk.description: Public jobs supporting Relstaris infrastructure and institutions, from transit maintenance to clinic administration, offered with stable terms and unexciting pay. The desk never runs short of vacancies. Its staff are frank about which posts will still exist in five years. The desk is a plain counter with a vacancy board behind it and a short bench in front, tucked off the main floor where the noise drops enough to hold a conversation. Applications are made here and processed through the institutions themselves, which is slower than the public floor and more reliable. Capitol Service terms are listed alongside permanent posts and explained without varnish. The vacancy board is updated in the morning and again at the shift change, and the older cards are left up until they are filled.
