The chamber is small, plain and controlled, its access corridor kept clear, and the objects inside are unremarkable to look at and impossible to replace. Openings are scheduled long in advance and attended, and the staff describe the arrangement without drama while observing it absolutely. Everything downstream of this chamber would simply agree with a corrupted standard, which is the whole reason for the schedule and the witness.

Seal Issue Office.description: Where certification seals are issued, numbered and recorded against the cargo they cover. The Common Scale seal is the most forged object on Nexara and this office knows it. Issue procedure has been tightened twice this year, and the clerks now check the register before, during and after an issue. It is a counter, a register and a sealing bench, staffed by people who have read every forgery report the Hall has ever put out. A seal is numbered against a specific consignment rather than a merchant, and a request that cannot be matched to a grading is refused however urgent the shipment. A seal means nothing once separated from the cargo it was written for, and the clerks explain that to somebody at the counter most days.

Arbiters' Chambers.description: Working rooms for the minor-house and independent arbiters who staff the Hall, deliberately plain and deliberately not grand. Standards disputes are heard here rather than in any courtroom. An arbiter under pressure has nowhere to hide in a building whose entire value is that it cannot be leaned on. The chambers are a short row of plain rooms with desks, reference shelves and doors opening onto a public corridor rather than a private one. Arbiters are approachable and unhurried and will explain a finding to anybody who asks. None of them is a Corsair, by rule, and the rule is stated aloud often.

Records Vault.description: Sealed storage for grading records, calibration histories and seal registers reaching back further than most houses' own archives. Retrieval is by request and logged. Anyone tracing a forged seal ends up in this room eventually, comparing a register entry against a piece of cargo that should not exist at all. The vault is climate-held, indexed and larger inside than the building's frontage suggests, with retrieval handled by a clerk at a desk rather than by open access. It is quiet enough that a clerk's footsteps are the loudest thing in it, and every retrieval carries the name of whoever asked.

Riverrow.name: Riverrow
Riverrow.basicInfo: Ordinary residential Helvyra, where most of the city actually lives: plain terraced housing in pale composite and rope-tan, worn comfortable, with washing lines strung between flight balconies. Dock crews, clerks, riggers and warehouse keepers pass route-boards on every corner going to and from work. Most people here never touch a sword or a spell. It runs across the mid and lower residential terraces, everything within it a walk or a short flight, with the Underbank directly below it at the waterline. The housing is stepped and close-built on shared stairs, patched across generations and comfortable rather than smart, and even domestic life is scheduled around arrivals, which is why the corner boards matter here as much as they do on a trade floor. Children go to the civic route-school and learn route-reading, weights and measures, contract literacy, flight safety and swim-and-current discipline before they learn much else, and the apprenticeships that follow carry more weight locally than any classroom does. Ordinary civic life governs the district, the Bank Wardens hold the waterline edge and no house claims anything. The neighbourhood supplies labour to the Quays, the Docks and the Waypoint, so whatever happens to the freight system happens here first, in households.
Riverrow.hiddenInfo: Darrow Culle teaches contract literacy early enough that no child's first contract is also their first lesson, and a student's homework, worked on real documents, exposed a genuinely forged manifest. That document has a source, and a school exercise is now evidence in something considerably larger than a school. The neighbourhood supplies labour to the Quays, the Docks and the Waypoint, so a work injury lands here as a household finance problem before it is anything else, and the Neighbourhood Kitchen quietly feeds families in that position without announcing it. The Morvane apothecary household works river-trade botanicals out of these terraces and supplies both the market stall and the Bankside dispensary, which puts them in contact with everything that comes up the river. When something goes wrong here the street closes ranks, fast and without discussion, which is why Bank Wardens working the waterline edge get accurate information about the river and nothing at all about the houses above it.

Civic Route-School.description: The neighbourhood school, teaching route-reading, weights and measures, contract literacy, flight safety and swim-and-current discipline before much else. Darrow Culle runs the contract lessons early enough that no child's first contract is also their first lesson. Homework is done on real manifests, and one of them was forged. The school is a plain building around a shared yard, classrooms opening onto it and a covered area for weather, and the walls carry practice route-boards the children are expected to keep updated themselves. Lessons are practical and noisy. Current discipline is taught at the water and flight safety off the balconies, and neither is treated as an extra.

Terrace Housing.description: Rows of plain stepped housing, shared stairs, flight balconies with washing strung between them, and doors that stay open in warm weather. Families have held the same frontage for generations without anyone calling it an estate. Everyone on a stair knows who is on which shift and who came home injured. The rows step up the slope in pale composite gone rope-tan with age, patched in mismatched repairs nobody minds, with communal drying lines and balconies used as thoroughfares. Windows stand open and conversation crosses between them. The district is quiet at the wrong hours and loud at the right ones, because the shifts have never agreed.

Neighbourhood Kitchen.description: A communal kitchen and eating hall, because shift patterns make cooking alone impractical: fast, hot, portable food and long shared benches. River fish and route-cargo produce in the proudly mongrel Helvyran style. It is also where a family in trouble gets fed without the fact ever being announced. It is a plain hall with a serving counter and a kitchen open to the room, warm at every hour and never entirely empty. A person eating alone is sat down beside somebody without being asked. Work goes on at the tables as well: shifts swapped, children minded, a contract read aloud for whoever wants a second opinion before signing.

Morvane Apothecary House.description: The Morvane family's household and working premises, with drying rooms and preparation benches upstairs from the street, supplying both the market stall and the Care Hall dispensary. River-trade botanicals arrive by barge and are processed fast. Neighbours knock here before they think about crossing to Bankside. The house is an ordinary frontage with a working door and a stair, the drying rooms set where the air moves and the benches behind them, and the whole place smells of its stock. Deliveries come up from the water in the morning and are dealt with the same day. Neighbours are advised for nothing and sold only what they actually need.

The Corner Boards.description: Public route-boards at every junction, showing departures, delays and contract calls for people whose domestic lives are scheduled around arrivals. Neighbours read them together and argue about them. A board that stops refreshing is reported faster than a broken light, because somebody's shift depends on it. The boards stand on plain posts, lit at night, refreshing on the same dawn cycle as every other board in Helvyra and read by people in working gear with a cup in one hand. Small notices accumulate around them: rooms, tools, work, a lost thing. A knot of neighbours in front of one is how household news arrives.

Swim Steps.description: Steps down to the water, where children are taught current discipline as a matter of course and adults swim after a shift. Bank Wardens patrol the edge and pull someone out often enough for it to be routine rather than dramatic. Year-marks cut into the stone show how far the high season has reached. The steps are broad and worn and go straight down into the water, with a rail on one side and nothing on the other, busy in the evening and empty in the cold months. Children are taught in groups by whichever adults are free, and a season is remembered afterwards by which step the water came up to.

The Underbank.name: The Underbank
The Underbank.basicInfo: Water-level cheap rooms cut back into the bank directly below Riverrow, damp in the high season and honest about it. This is where new arrivals land broke and work their way up a terrace at a time, alongside seasonal labour between contracts. Everyone above has either lived here or is one bad season away from it. It sits at the waterline immediately beside the Barge Quays, which is how most residents get work: a walk of minutes from a rented room to a berth where hands are needed. The rooms are low and cheap by the night or by the season, with stone that sweats when the river is high and lamps that stay lit because the daylight down here is borrowed from somewhere else. This is the city's first rung. Arrivals with nothing, seasonal labour between contracts, people between jobs and the ones who have been here longer than they meant to be all live along the same corridors. Room keepers run their own houses, the Bank Wardens hold the water edge and no house claims the district at all. A keeper's ledger records who made it up the terraces and who simply stopped appearing, which is the only continuous account anyone keeps of the city's arrivals.
The Underbank.hiddenInfo: Tam Vessic keeps a ledger of who made it up the terraces and who simply stopped appearing, and three recent tenants are in the second column: gone within a month, rent paid in advance, rooms untouched. Paid-forward rent means whoever arranged it expected them not to need the rooms, which is a very different thing from tenants who ran. Vessic rents to arrivals other keepers turn away, so his rooms are also where people come when they need not to be looked for, and the Shared Wash House circulates that kind of news long before any ledger records it. The Day-Work Board feeds casual labour straight to the Barge Quays and out to the Hauler Yards, which makes it the fastest way in the city to disappear into legitimate work under no particular name. Pell Odran lodges here when the belt is out of season. No house claims the Underbank and the Bank Wardens only hold the water edge, so what happens in the rooms is nobody's jurisdiction at all.

Rented Rooms.description: Low rooms cut back into the bank, cheap by the night or by the season, with stone that sweats when the river is high. A bed, a lamp, a hook for wings. Nobody pretends they are better than that, and the honesty is part of why people come back here rather than somewhere that lies to them. Doors open off a common corridor lit end to end, and the rooms behind them are dry enough in low water and frankly not in high. Rent is taken with no ceremony and no lease. Neighbours hear each other through the stone and mostly pretend otherwise, and a room that goes quiet for a week is noticed on the corridor before it is noticed at the desk.

The Keeper's Desk.description: Tam Vessic's desk at the entrance: the rent ledger, the room keys, and the record of who arrived with nothing and who eventually left going upward. He rents to people other keepers turn away. Three recent entries are paid forward, and those rooms have not been touched since the rent was taken. The desk sits inside the entrance where everyone passing has to go by it, with the key wall behind, a lamp that is never off and a bench for people waiting to be decided about. He takes rent, takes names and asks very little, and people who have made it up a terrace still come back to tell him so. The ledger stays open on the desk, and anybody may read their own line in it.

Waterline Walk.description: The walkway along the river face, wet underfoot in high season and lit by whatever the rooms behind it spill out. Bank Wardens pass along it on the night round. It is the fastest route to the Barge Quays, which is why most residents can be at a berth minutes after hearing there is work. The walk is narrow and unfenced along the water, with the river close enough to be heard from every doorway, and in the high season it is wet the whole length and people take it anyway. It is the district's street, its shortcut and its meeting place, and standing on it at the right hour is how a person hears that a berth is short-handed.

Day-Work Board.description: A posting board of the day's casual labour: quay hands, hauler transfers, warehouse shifts, read before dawn by people who need it filled today. Terms are short and enforceable. Someone reading this board every morning and never taking anything is doing something else, and the regulars notice. The board is plain, weatherproofed and lit well before first light, posted by whoever needs hands and read by people who need the work today rather than this season. Contract literacy is taught in the civic schools, so everybody standing here can parse a posting, and a bad one stays up all morning. A posting that goes unclaimed by mid-morning tells the district something about whoever wrote it.

Shared Wash House.description: A communal wash house with hot water on a schedule, and the one reliably warm place in the Underbank through the cold months. It functions as the district's meeting room entirely by accident. News about who has gone, who has moved up and who should be avoided circulates here before any ledger records it. It is a plain room of stone benches, taps and drying lines, and it fills for an hour and empties again on a schedule everybody in the district knows. People talk because they are waiting and because it is warm. It is where a new arrival learns which keeper is fair and which berth pays late. It is also where somebody learns which terrace can realistically be reached from here, and how long it took the last person who managed it.

Ashglass Market.name: Ashglass Market
Ashglass Market.basicInfo: Ashglass Market is Ignivex's market district, bright and crowded beneath heatproof awnings and the ashglass canopies that are its visual signature. Stalls sell food, clothing, fire-treated materials, heat-resistant tools, spices, thermal devices and Volen ceremonial goods — anything from a meal to a ceremony's regalia. The market is roofed rather than walled: ashglass panes over the central run filter the light into a dim amber that traders steer by, and the outer lanes shelter under heatproof awnings strung on copper frames. Underfoot the lanes are packed hard and swept constantly, because ash settles on everything in this city and a stall that looks dusty does not sell. Trade begins early and runs loud, with stallholders calling, buyers testing, porters shouldering through and cooking heat stacking on top of the city's own along the food counters. The spice rankings and heat waivers attached to the food are less a joke at an outsider's expense than a warning outsiders keep disregarding. What ashglass is made of is not something anyone in the lanes will explain, and the question is turned aside with the same easy courtesy the Corsair post uses when asked where its cargo comes from. Rumor is part of ordinary market business, and festival season brings custom through every row.
Ashglass Market.hiddenInfo: The market runs on merchants and trade families, but the established Corsair trade presence is the part everyone has an opinion about. Which house or crew holds the trade post, what it actually carries, how its goods reach a city under standing Dravon pressure and what arrangement it has with House Volen are all genuinely unsettled — the goods appear, the prices are met, and questions get deflected pleasantly. That uncertainty makes the Rumor Tables valuable: traders, festival organisers and people simply listening trade information here faster than any civic channel moves it. A dispute that cannot be settled at the Dispute Bench becomes the kind of grievance that reaches the Smoke Court, which merchants know and use as leverage well before anyone files anything. Sabotage suspicion from the Red Forges lands here too, since a failed piece is often blamed on materials bought in these rows.

The Ashglass Canopies.description: The market's signature roofing: broad panes of ashglass spanning the central rows, filtering the light into a dim amber that traders navigate by. Everything passes under them. The panes are set in copper-bronze frames overhead, broad enough to roof the whole central run, and the amber light beneath them flattens colour so that cloth and metal both have to be carried out to the lane edge to be judged properly. Buyers do exactly that all day long. Maintenance crews work the frames between trading hours, and a cracked pane is replaced rather than repaired, without any account given of where the replacement came from. The panes tick faintly as they expand through the day, a sound regulars stop hearing within a week of working here.

The Awning Rows.description: Ranks of heatproof awnings over the outer stalls, strung on copper frames and re-tensioned every morning. Clothing, household goods and general trade fill these lanes. The frames are re-tensioned at the start of trade and checked again when the heat peaks, and the cloth is heat-treated, patched, and patched again rather than replaced. Below them the stalls stand close enough that neighbours share a customer's attention whether they want to or not. General goods, household stock and clothing move through these lanes in volume, and the porters who carry for the traders know the row order better than the traders do. Stallholders compete for the deeper shade nearest the canopies, and the pecking order of who holds which pitch is older than most of the traders standing in them.

The Spice Line.description: A dense row of spice traders working from sealed bronze bins, selling the heat-forward seasonings Ignivex cooking is built around. Buyers taste before they commit. The bins stand in ranks, bronze-lidded and labelled by heat grade rather than by name, and the ranking is taken seriously enough that a trader who overstates one loses the row's custom. Tasting spoons, water and a bench for the overambitious are standard equipment at every stall. Cooks from the food rows buy here in bulk before the market has properly filled. The air along this line is thick enough to make an outsider's eyes water, and merchants treat that reaction as a perfectly good opening for a sale.

Fire-Treated Goods Row.description: Stalls dealing in fire-treated materials and finished goods able to take sustained heat — cloth, cord, fittings and sheeting. Buyers from the forges and the Wallworks both source here. The stalls put the material itself on show, stacked by grade, each counter with an open element for demonstration. The forge trade wants tolerance under sustained work; emergency crews want gear that survives being handled badly at speed. Sellers keep their failed samples too, and produce them when a customer asks what the cheaper grade actually does. Sellers demonstrate by holding a sample to an open element, and a product that discolours in front of a customer does not sell twice.

The Tool Stalls.description: Rows of heat-resistant tools laid out on dark benches: tongs, clamps, cutters and hand equipment built for working temperatures. Artisans and apprentices pick through them slowly. The benches are dark and scarred, tools laid out by hand size and working temperature, tongs and clamps hung from copper rails overhead. Apprentices arrive with a master's list and are watched to see whether they buy what is on it. The stalls repair as well as sell, and a bench with a queue of repairs waiting on it is read as a recommendation rather than as a backlog. The good sellers let a buyer take a tool away for a shift and bring it back, on the theory that a tool that comes back was never going to sell anyway.

The Thermal Device Stalls.description: Traders in thermal devices — regulators, personal cooling units, heat-reading instruments and small engineered gear for living in Ignivex conditions. Buyers test units at the stall before purchase. The gear is engineered rather than crafted, regulators, personal cooling units and heat-reading instruments laid out with their casings open so buyers can see the work inside. Outsiders buy personal cooling here far more often than residents do, and the traders neither mock them for it nor discount it. A unit that reads wrong twice at the counter is pulled off the table there and then. Most stallholders can repair what they sell, and being unable to is treated as proof the device was not theirs to begin with.

Ceremonial Goods Row.description: The row supplying Volen ceremonial items and regalia: banners, ceremonial fittings, ritual dress and the equipment civic rites call for. Families buy here ahead of a First Flame or an oath. The row is quieter and better lit than the rest of the market, its goods laid on cloth rather than on boards: banners, formal clasps, ritual dress, shoulder pieces and the fittings a civic rite calls for. The Volen triple flame in its broken heat ring appears on much of it, because civic emblems default to Volen outside a family district. Families arrive with an older piece to be matched or repaired as often as they arrive to buy new. Trade is quieter and more careful in this row, and haggling over a ceremonial piece is considered poor form rather than shrewd.

The Food Rows.description: The market's eating and provisioning quarter, where prepared food, produce and cooked portions are sold from close-packed counters. Market workers eat standing up between shifts. Counters run close on both sides with geothermal cooking lines built straight into them, and the air is thick with steam, spice and the smell of things held at working heat since before the market opened. Heat waivers and spice rankings are posted where they can be read before ordering rather than after. Portions are handed over fast and eaten standing, and the argument about which counter is best is conducted at volume by people who decided years ago. The cooking heat here stacks on top of the city's own, and the rows are still the busiest part of Ashglass at every hour it is open.

The Corsair Trade Post.description: The established Corsair trade presence keeps a fixed post at the market's edge, dealing in imported and unusual goods. Business is conducted courteously and without much explanation. The post is a fixed frontage at the market's edge, shuttered when it is not trading, plainly built and noticeably tidier than its neighbours. Goods appear on the counter in small quantities, unusual materials, imported oddities, things nobody else in the rows can source, and they are priced without haggling. The staff are unfailingly pleasant and answer almost nothing. Nobody at the post confirms which crew it answers to or how the cargo reaches Ignivex, and asking twice tends to end the conversation politely.

The Rumor Tables.description: A cluster of communal tables where traders, buyers and idlers sit to hear what is moving — prices, arrivals, festival plans, who is arguing with whom. Information is the actual commodity here. The tables are communal, scarred and shaded, with a drinks counter nearby and no obligation on anyone to buy in order to sit. Traders come between customers, porters between loads, and people with nothing to trade come simply to listen, which everyone understands and nobody objects to. Accuracy varies wildly and is corrected in public, at volume, by whoever believes they know better. A story that starts at these tables will reach the Hearth Rows before the person it concerns hears it.

The Dispute Bench.description: A plain bench where market disagreements are put in front of other merchants and argued out on the spot. Most trade quarrels end here. The bench is plain stone under an awning, set where the rows can see it, with room for both parties and for the merchants who will hear them out. There is no appointed arbiter; whoever is trading nearby stops, listens, and the weight of the row's opinion does the work. Settlements are verbal and remembered, and a trader who ignores one finds the next argument going against them before it has started. The ones that do not become the kind of grievance that reaches the Smoke Court, and both parties usually know which category theirs is before they sit down.

The Second Helping.description: A family-run restaurant in the Food Rows built around a geothermal cooking line, with a shared dining floor, smaller family tables and a takeaway counter. The unnamed household that runs it cooks for market workers, buyers and artisans finishing commissions. The floor runs noisy and close, and the geothermal line is open behind the counter so that guests can watch what is being done to their food and the takeaway queue can watch it too. Heat waivers hang on the wall as they do everywhere else, but this household treats them as paperwork rather than as a dare. Regulars have their usual order started before they have finished sitting down. Staff ask how hot a guest actually wants the food instead of treating the answer as a loyalty test.

The Cooling Steps.name: The Cooling Steps
The Cooling Steps.basicInfo: The Cooling Steps is Ignivex's recovery and medical district: a terraced quarter of engineered cooling canals, mist chambers, shaded courtyards and recovery baths. Workers, trainees, visitors and injured citizens come here when the city's heat becomes too much to carry. The district is terraced and its engineering is the point: cooling canals step down through it carrying treated water, mist chambers hold fine regulated vapour, shaded courts sit screened overhead, and sunken baths are held at graded temperatures for bringing a body back in stages. The sound throughout is moving water, which makes this the least loud ground in a loud city. An ordinary day is medical and unglamorous: heat injury, burns, collapse, the wear of industrial work, trainees off the Crucible Yard's floors, visitors the city has simply overwhelmed, and citizens serving a Cooling Oath doing the recovery work the Oath requires alongside the regular staff. Clinical work stays with qualified practitioners. The friction is cultural, since Ignivex patients understate everything and treat needing this district at all as something to be got through quietly. It is one of the quieter parts of Ignivex, and conversations happen here that would never be said aloud in the Emberward.
The Cooling Steps.hiddenInfo: Pride has a cost, and this district is where the city pays it. Medics see the same injuries the Crucible Yard produces and the same exhaustion the forges and the Wallworks produce, and they see who refuses treatment until it is nearly too late. House Meravil connects here — the house that counts casualties has business where the casualties are — so Meravil record keepers and continuity officers move through these terraces gathering the numbers that feed the surrender argument. That makes the district politically loaded in a way its calm surface hides: a conversation on the Quiet Terrace can be a genuine kindness or an intelligence visit, and sometimes both. Citizens serving a Cooling Oath perform their recovery work here under public obligation, which puts people who owe the city something in daily contact with people the city has already failed. Outsiders overwhelmed by Ignivex end up in the Outsider Ward, where their first honest impressions of the city get spoken to a stranger.

The Cooling Canals.description: Engineered canals step down through the district, carrying treated water that drops in temperature at each terrace. The sound of moving water is everywhere. The channels are cut in pale stone with low edges built for sitting on, and the water runs clear and fast enough to hear from anywhere on a terrace. Grates and stepped weirs handle the drop between runs. Workers coming off a shift arrive with their forearms still ash-marked and put them straight in, and the etiquette along the lower runs is that nobody remarks on anybody's condition. People sit along the edges with their feet in the lower runs, and the district's whole layout is legible from how cold a given step's water is.

The Mist Chambers.description: Chambers filled with fine regulated mist, used to bring core temperature down without shocking a body that has been working in heat all day. Occupants sit in near-silence. The chambers are enclosed and dim, softly lit, with benching around the walls and the mist fed from regulated nozzles that hiss at a rhythm occupants stop hearing within minutes. Attendants set the duration and look in without speaking. Everything inside beads with water almost immediately, which is why nothing is carried in that cannot be left damp. Visibility inside is short enough that two people can share a chamber for an hour without ever seeing each other clearly.

The Shaded Courtyards.description: Broad shaded courts between the terraces, screened overhead and kept several degrees below the street. Recovering patients, families and visitors gather in them through the day. The courts are broad and paved, screened overhead against the district's own light, with low seating, running water at the edges and room enough for a family to spread out for an afternoon. Food is brought in rather than cooked here. Children play in them while somebody recovers a few doors away, and the two facts are held together on purpose. They are the district's social ground, and the fact that ordinary life goes on here is deliberate rather than accidental.

The Medical Stations.description: Working medical stations equipped for heat injury, burns, collapse and the ordinary damage of an industrial city. Medics triage arrivals as they come in off the transit lines. The stations are plain, well-lit working rooms with treatment bays, cooled surfaces and supplies laid out in the same order in every one of them, so that a medic moving between stations never has to look for anything. Triage happens at the door. Practitioners here are qualified and jealous about it, and relatives who want to help are given water to carry rather than anything clinical to do. Staff here are direct to the point of bluntness, having long since learned that Ignivex patients will understate everything they are asked about.

The Recovery Baths.description: Sunken baths held at graded temperatures, used to bring people back from overheating in controlled stages. Attendants move between them with timers. Each one in the series is held at its own temperature, with handrails at every rim and steps down into the water rather than a drop. People enter at the stage that suits their state and are moved down through the series rather than straight to the coldest. An attendant will refuse a regular who wants to skip a stage, and the refusal is not a negotiation, because cooling too fast does more damage than the heat did. Regulars know which bath suits which kind of shift, and arguing about that ranking is one of the district's standing pastimes.

The Outsider Ward.description: A ward held at conditions tolerable to visitors whose bodies are not adapted to Ignivex, for people the city has simply overwhelmed. Staff are used to embarrassment as a symptom. The ward is held at conditions an unadapted body can manage, screened, quiet and deliberately unremarkable, its beds spaced for privacy rather than for volume. Most admissions are simple: somebody walked too far in the open, worked a shift they were not built for, or ate at a food counter and took the spice ranking as a dare. Staff take the history without comment and hand over water first. More candid opinions about Ignivex are spoken in this ward than anywhere else in the city, usually to a medic who has heard them all before.

The Quiet Terrace.description: A high terrace kept deliberately still, with low seating and sightlines out over the district. Conversations happen here that would not happen in the Emberward. The terrace sits apart, with low stone seating, screening at the edges and sightlines that let a person see who is approaching well before they arrive. No attendant is posted and no register is kept. Water is left out and nothing else is provided, and the district's staff have a settled habit of not walking through unless somebody calls. Nobody is asked their business on this terrace, which is exactly why some of the people using it are not there to recover.

The Post-Training Rooms.description: Rooms set aside for trainees coming off the Crucible Yard's floors — cooling, treatment and somewhere to sit until the shaking stops. Attendance is routine, not disgraceful. The rooms are small and functional, cooled benching, water, treatment kit, a basin and somewhere to put a head down, with an attendant checking through at intervals rather than standing over anyone. Trainees arrive shaking, sit, and are not spoken to until they speak first. Crucible Yard instructors send students here as routine and are told plainly when one has been sent back onto the floor too soon. Some students still arrive by the least visible route they can find, and the staff have stopped commenting on it.

The Cooling Oath Service Rooms.description: Service rooms where citizens under a Cooling Oath perform the recovery work the Oath requires, alongside the district's regular staff. The work is real and unglamorous. The rooms are working spaces rather than penitential ones: laundry, supply preparation, bath attendance, fetching and cleaning, done alongside regular staff who direct the work and make no speeches about it. Oath-servers are here because they caused harm through reckless fire or reckless violence, and the service is a condition of being publicly trusted again. Nobody in the district treats that as a secret. Oath-servers and the people they tend often arrive as strangers and leave the rooms knowing more about each other than either intended.

The Held Cup.description: A café concession in the Shaded Courtyards, run by an unnamed civilian operator and a counter cook: a Cyrra counter, shaded tables, a soft-voice seating corner and a clean preparation recess kept apart from treatment work. Regulars are residents who prefer mild food and friends waiting for one another. The concession takes a corner of a shaded court with a low counter, a handful of tables and the soft-voice corner screened off from the rest. The menu runs mild by Ignivex standards and says so plainly, which is the entire point of the place. The preparation recess is kept clean and apart from treatment work, and the counter cook holds that boundary more strictly than anyone has ever asked. Nobody here is required to be sad.

Cinderline Transit.name: Cinderline Transit
Cinderline Transit.basicInfo: The Cinderline is Ignivex's internal movement system, treated as a single citywide location: heat-resistant lanes, thermal lift platforms and controlled vent routes threaded through a city built around its own heat. It connects the districts and provides protected access to the Lunar Gate. The Cinderline is infrastructure before it is a service: lanes surfaced against sustained heat and settling ash, thermal lift platforms driven off the city's own supply, and controlled vent routes gated and signed where people pass alongside moving hot gas. It hums, it runs warm, and it carries a dry mineral smell residents associate with getting somewhere. There are no per-district stations, and the network's topology and route geometry are not published; the crews hold the real knowledge of it in their heads. A working day is commuters, freight, response crews drilling the reserved paths, gate traffic moving under watch, and controllers reading lane conditions, lift states and vent pressures off live boards. The standing worry is deliberate damage rather than wear, because Dravon pressure targets systems more often than walls. Commuters, response crews and travellers heading for the gate all share it.
Cinderline Transit.hiddenInfo: The Cinderline is also one of Ignivex's most serious exposures. Standing Dravon pressure targets systems rather than open walls, and a movement network is the obvious system to target — which is why a lane fault, a stuck lift or a vent anomaly is never treated as merely mechanical here, and why transit crews get questioned in a way that occasionally curdles into suspicion of their own colleagues. The emergency response paths serve Rava Caldris's response teams, so the network's condition is directly a civilian-survival matter: if the paths are down when a breach happens, people who could have been evacuated are not. The Line Control Room carries that weight constantly. What the city has deliberately never written down is the Cinderline's actual topology — there are no per-district stations, and the route geometry and line count are undefined even to most of the people who ride it daily. The vent paths are among the routes the Cinder Run passes through, though the Run has no fixed course.

The Heat-Resistant Lanes.description: The network's main running lanes, surfaced in materials that shrug off sustained heat and the ash that settles on everything in this city. Traffic moves through them constantly. The running surfaces are laid in dark material that sheds ash and takes heat without softening, edged in ember-line marking so the boundary reads even in poor light. Traffic is mixed, people on foot, handcarts, loaded crews, and it sorts itself by pace without much instruction. Ash is swept off on a standing rotation, and a lane that has not been swept is the first thing riders complain about and the last thing anyone gets to. The lanes hum at a pitch riders stop noticing, and a change in that pitch will empty a crowded lane faster than any announcement.

The Thermal Lift Platforms.description: Powered lift platforms that move people and cargo between the city's levels, driven off the thermal supply. Crews load and clear them in quick cycles. The platforms are open decks with waist rails and marked loading zones, their machinery housed below and audible through the floor as a rising note. Crews call the load, clear the line and go. Cargo and people share a deck as a matter of course, which means a rider's ankles are the responsibility of whoever stacked the crates. The platforms rise smoothly and stop hard, and newcomers are easy to spot because they are the ones who forget to brace at the top.

The Controlled Vent Routes.description: Passages routed alongside the city's vent system, regulated so people can pass where hot gas also moves. Signage and gates govern access tightly. The passages are narrow, gated at both ends and marked at intervals with the route's condition and current state. Hot gas moves alongside the walkway behind grating and shielding, and the sound of it is a steady rush rather than a roar. Crews check the gates on rotation and find them propped often enough that the propping has become a recurring argument of its own. The routes run warmer than the lanes and carry a dry, mineral smell, and locals use them as a shortcut more often than the control room would like.

The Emergency Response Paths.description: Reserved paths kept clear for Rava Caldris's emergency response teams to cross the city fast during a breach, fire or evacuation. They are drilled regularly and never used casually. The paths are marked along their whole length and kept clear, with clearance points and equipment stations inventoried whether or not anything has been used. Drills run them at speed and without announcement while ordinary traffic is held back. Rava Caldris's crews have no patience for pride on these routes and less for obstruction, and whoever caused a blockage hears about it publicly. Finding one blocked is treated as a serious incident, because the difference it makes is measured in civilian lives.

Protected Gate Access.description: The secured run that carries traffic between the city and the Ignivex Lunar Gate, monitored along its whole length. Arrivals move inward through it under watch. The run is enclosed and monitored, with checkpoints at intervals, heat-armored fittings and lighting that leaves nowhere unobserved. Traffic moves under the direction of the crews working it rather than at its own pace. Arrivals come inward with their business already noted at the gate and departing travellers are counted again on the way out, because Ignivex is connected but not widely open and the difference is enforced here rather than argued about. It is the one stretch of the Cinderline where being asked who a traveller is and where they are going is entirely routine.

The Line Control Room.description: The network's control room, walled with live readouts of lane conditions, lift states, vent pressures and response-path status. Rotations on the desk are kept short by policy. The room is walled with live boards and kept dim enough to read them by, controller positions facing the displays and a standing space behind for whoever has come to ask about a fault. Rotations are short because attention is the job. Controllers speak in a clipped shorthand that visitors find rude and crews find efficient, and the shift handover is the longest conversation any of them have all day. Every fault that appears on these boards gets logged twice — once as a mechanical event, once as a question about whether it was one.

The Transit Crew Rooms.description: Crew rooms where transit workers change, eat and hand over shifts, with equipment lockers and a standing kettle nobody admits to owning. Crews talk shop constantly. The rooms are cramped and comfortable in the way working rooms become, with lockers, a long bench, a heat plate and gear hung to dry above it. Crews eat here, sleep here between doubled shifts, and argue about lanes, lifts and management in roughly that order. New crew are taught the network by being walked through it, because no document matches what the people who run it actually know. They know the network's real quirks far better than any official description of it, and they trade that knowledge as a kind of currency.

The Hearth Rows.name: The Hearth Rows
The Hearth Rows.basicInfo: The Hearth Rows are Ignivex's residential districts: housing built around communal heat cores, with shared courtyards, neighborhood fire markers and emergency shelters close at hand. This is everyday life under standing pressure — family kitchens, shared heat, children underfoot, and civic defense traditions carried at neighborhood level. The rows are built close and stepped, housing gathered around communal heat cores that are regulated and maintained as common property, with shared courtyards between the blocks, marked heat-safe routes threading through them and reinforced shelters never far from any door. The walls are dark stone, doors stand open for the air, and each block carries a fire marker at its corner with a small maintained flame identifying the row and its muster point. Ordinary life is loud and communal: kitchens opening toward the courts, cooking heat drawn off the shared core, children underfoot on the paving. Alerts interrupt all of it and drills rehearse the interruption, and then the rows go back to what they were doing, because the meals, the repairs and the festival work are what the defending is for. Hospitality arrives faster than a visitor expects, and privacy does not exist at all. Lysa Caldris coordinates the civilian-defense side of it.
The Hearth Rows.hiddenInfo: Ordinary domestic life here runs on the assumption that the city will be attacked again. Lysa Caldris's work — neighborhood defense shelters, emergency supply caches, heat-safe routes and civilian alert drills — is woven into the calendar alongside meals and school, and families who treat the drills casually get spoken to by their neighbours rather than by any official. That produces its own friction: households argue over stored supplies, over which children are trusted with shelter keys, and over whether readiness has tipped into fear. The Rows also sit downstream of every other district's tensions. A forge rivalry, a market grudge or a Crucible Yard humiliation comes home at the end of the shift and is aired on the Row Step, and a dispute that outgrows the Step becomes the kind that reaches the Smoke Court. Caldris Wallworks connects here, so the district that builds the shelters is the same one the residents already know by name.

The Communal Heat Cores.description: Shared heat cores sit at the centre of each housing cluster, regulated and maintained as common property. Households draw cooking and living heat from them. Each core stands enclosed at the centre of its cluster, plated and vented, with access panels only the maintenance rotation opens and a hum that carries through the walls of every house drawing from it. Feeds run out from there to kitchens and living spaces. Households take their turn on the checking roster, and a family that skips theirs hears about it at the Row Step rather than from anyone official. Core maintenance days are neighborhood events by default, because everyone's evening meal depends on the same assembly working properly.

The Family Kitchens.description: Household kitchens built directly off the shared heat supply, opening toward the courts rather than away from them. Cooking is social and loud. Kitchens run along the courtyard side of each house, open-fronted, the heat feed built into the counter and cookware hung where it can be reached without looking. Doors stay open through the evening. Meals are cooked in quantity on the assumption that somebody else's children will be eating, and the geothermal cooking methods that alarm outsiders are simply how a household gets a meal onto the table. Ignivex families argue over seasoning as seriously as over politics, and the smell of a neighbour's meal is a standing invitation nobody bothers to formalise.

The Shared Courtyards.description: Enclosed courts between the housing blocks, shaded and paved, where children play, neighbours sit and household life spills outdoors. Everything communal happens here. The courts are paved and screened overhead, furnished with whatever the households have put there: benches, drying lines, a worn patch of play surface, stored crates that are supposed to be moved and never are. The light is warm and controlled. The same court holds a musician's evening session, a drill muster and a long argument about the crates, sometimes in the same week. They are also where a household's business stops being private, which residents accept as the price of the arrangement.

The Emergency Shelters.description: Reinforced neighborhood shelters stocked and maintained under Lysa Caldris's civilian-defense coordination, with heat-sealed doors and marked capacities. Families know their assigned shelter by heart. The shelters are built into the blocks themselves, heat-sealed, stocked and signed with ember-line guidance running to the doors from every direction a resident might come from. Wardens check stock and seals on rotation under Lysa Caldris's coordination. Places are assigned by household rather than taken by whoever arrives first, and a family that turns up at the wrong door during a drill is corrected on the spot and does not forget it. Children are taught the route before they are taught to read the signs on it.

The Fire Markers.description: Neighborhood fire markers stand at the corners of each row, carrying small maintained flames that identify a block and its muster point. They are both practical and traditional. Each marker is a worked stand of dark metal at a row's corner, carrying a small regulated flame and the marks that identify the block, and the nearest households keep the housing clean and the feed clear. Children are shown their own marker before they can reliably find their way home without it. Neighbouring rows notice one another's markers, compare them silently, and say nothing until one goes dark. A marker allowed to go dark is a genuine embarrassment to the households responsible for it.

The Drill Yard.description: An open yard used for civilian alert drills — muster, headcount, route practice and shelter timing. Drills run on a schedule and unannounced. The yard is open and plainly surfaced, muster lines marked into the paving and a warden's position at one end, sited so that every row it serves can reach it without crossing a blocked route. Headcounts are called by household. The timing is recorded and read back afterwards, which is the part residents grumble about and the part that has occasionally saved a row. Residents grumble about them constantly and still turn out, because enough of them remember a raid where the drill was the reason a row emptied in time.

The Supply Caches.description: Secured emergency caches of water, food, treatment kit and heat-safe gear, distributed through the rows and checked on rotation. Stock is logged openly. The lockers themselves are hardened and sealed, set where a household can reach one without crossing open ground, and marked so that anyone can tell at a glance which is which. The checking rotation is public and the list hangs where it can be read. Holding a cache key is a household honour and a household burden at once, which is exactly why it gets argued over. Who gets to hold a cache key is a small but persistent source of neighborhood politics, argued out at the Row Step like everything else.

The Heat-Safe Routes.description: Marked routes through the rows that stay passable when heat conditions spike, kept clear of obstruction by neighborhood agreement. They link housing to shelters and out to the wider city. The routes are marked into the paving and along the walls with ember-line guidance, kept wide enough for a crowd moving quickly and for a stretcher coming the other way. Neighbourhood agreement rather than any posted authority is what keeps them clear. Residents shift stored goods off them without being asked when conditions spike, and the ones who do not are shifted for, by neighbours who do not ask either. Blocking one with stored goods is the fastest way to make enemies of an entire block.

The Row Step.description: The communal step at the head of each row where neighbours settle disagreements in front of whoever is sitting out that evening. Most local grievances end here. It is broad stone, shaded and worn smooth, with room for a dozen people and no formality at all about who may sit on it. Whoever is present says what they think, and being right in front of witnesses counts for more than being right later on. Food usually appears partway through, which residents insist is coincidence and which reliably shortens the argument. The ones that do not become the kind of dispute that reaches the Smoke Court, and the Step usually knows which is which first.

The Low Flame.description: An evening social venue held in the Shared Courtyards on an agreed neighborhood tenancy: a small music floor, courtyard seating, a drink-and-snack counter and a quieter side room. An unnamed civilian host books local musicians for advertised sessions. The venue takes over a court by agreement on advertised evenings, its raised floor set against a wall and the tables arranged so that the through-routes stay clear. Sessions are announced ahead and end at an agreed hour, because the people living around the court have shifts in the morning. Families come early and leave before the later sets. Light is warm and controlled, and the heat-safe routes stay open throughout.

The Smoke Court.name: The Smoke Court
The Smoke Court.basicInfo: The Smoke Court is Ignivex's dispute-settlement chamber — a civic institution rather than a royal court, where people are expected to speak plainly and accept the heat of the truth. Citizens bring personal conflicts, family grievances, public insults, broken agreements and honor disputes here. The Court is a chamber rather than a palace: a level speaking floor with benches ringing it, side rooms for family matters, an antechamber hazed with warm smoke from low vents, and a record desk where what is said on the floor is written down. The stone is dark, the light is muted red, and the acoustics are built to carry a raised voice cleanly to the back rather than to soften it. Ordinary days bring merchants whose dispute outgrew a market bench, neighbours whose argument outgrew a row step, families with grievances they cannot hold at home, and citizens facing public accountability in front of people who know them. What the chamber asks for is plain speech and what it refuses is evasion: a party found at fault is expected to stand and say what they did rather than have it said for them. Proceedings generate records that go on to the city's archive vaults. Selyra Volen serves and speaks in the chamber, and she lets people shout.
The Smoke Court.hiddenInfo: Selyra's method is deliberate: anger reveals the truth faster than politeness, so she permits the shouting and waits. Once the truth surfaces she expects accountability immediately, and excuses do not survive long in her chamber — which is why some parties arrive having rehearsed and leave having admitted something they never meant to say. Ignivex culture backs this up; public argument is not shameful here, and it is normal for two people to shout at each other across the Speaking Floor and eat together afterwards if the truth was reached. The Court is also where the city's other frictions converge. Market disputes that outgrew the Dispute Bench, neighborhood grievances that outgrew the Row Step, and forge accusations of sabotage all arrive as private conflicts with political shadows attached. Proceedings generate records, and the city's archive vaults sit in Meravil Ash Hall, which connects here — meaning the house that counts casualties also holds what was said.

The Speaking Floor.description: The chamber's central floor, open and unraised, where both parties stand at the same level and say their piece. Nobody sits above anyone else. The floor is dark stone, unraised and unfurnished, with benches stepping up around it on every side so that the crowd always sits higher than the people speaking. There is no rail and nothing to stand behind. Parties are placed within arm's reach of each other deliberately, and the chamber treats a case where nobody raises their voice as either already settled or not yet honest. The acoustics carry a raised voice to every bench without distortion, which is the point — the Court is built to be heard, not to be dignified.

Selyra’s Chamber.description: Selyra Volen's own working room off the main floor, where she reads submissions, takes parties aside and decides what a case actually is. It is plain and warm. The room is small and warm, plainly furnished: a working table, submissions stacked in order, water, and seating that puts everybody at the same height. Selyra reads before she speaks and asks short questions. She lets people shout on the floor because anger reveals the truth faster than politeness does, and in here she expects the accountability that is supposed to follow it. People who expected her to be impressed by their standing usually revise that opinion within a few minutes of sitting down in it.

The Grievance Benches.description: Benches where citizens waiting to be heard sit with the people they are about to argue with. Cases are called in order. The benches are long, worn and deliberately undivided, set where the chamber's noise carries out to them. An attendant calls the order and nobody is told how long the wait will be. Water is brought round to everyone at once, which means both parties to a grievance are handed a cup by the same person at the same moment. A surprising number of grievances are settled on these benches before they reach the floor, purely because sitting next to someone for an hour is harder than shouting at them.

The Family Rooms.description: Side rooms used when a dispute is a family matter and a public floor would make it worse. Doors close, but the expectation of plain speech does not change. The rooms are small and screened, with a door that closes, low seating and no bench for spectators, used when airing a matter publicly would do more damage than settling it. A clerk sits in and records; nothing else about the procedure changes. Families who have refused to discuss surrender at their own tables discuss it here, because plain speech is easier to manage in a room that belongs to none of them. These rooms see the Court's hardest conversations, including the ones about surrender that families cannot have at home.

The Accountability Step.description: A single raised step where a party who has been found at fault stands to answer for it in front of the chamber. There is no ceremony to it. The step is a single block of dark stone set at the floor's edge, unmarked and unornamented, low enough that standing on it is visibility rather than elevation. No formula is recited and nobody prompts the words. The chamber simply waits, which is worse than being questioned, and the waiting is the whole of the procedure. Standing on the step and saying plainly what one did is treated as settling the matter; refusing to is remembered far longer than the original offence.

The Waiting Smoke.description: The antechamber, hazed with fine warm smoke from low vents, where parties wait and cool their tempers before being called. The haze softens every face in the room. The antechamber is warm and low-lit, its haze fed from vents at floor level, thick enough to blur a face across the room without ever making it hard to breathe. Benches line the walls and there is nowhere to pace. Parties, relatives and advocates share the space without separation, and the Court's position is that a temper which cannot survive a wait in here was never going to survive the floor. Advocates and relatives use the time to talk people down, with mixed and frequently audible results.

The Record Desk.description: The desk where proceedings are recorded, submissions logged and rulings written up before being sent on to the city's archive vaults. Attendants work steadily through the noise. The desk stands at the chamber's edge in dark wood with bronze fittings, submissions stacked by case, rulings written out in a plain hand before they leave the building. Attendants work through the shouting without looking up. A party may ask what has been written and will have it read back, which has settled more arguments about the record than any seal ever has. What ends up in these records is often the only account of an argument that anyone can later point to.

The Verbal Duel Ring.description: A marked ring where a dispute is settled by formal verbal duel — two parties, strict turns, and the chamber judging who held the truth. It is bruising and entirely legitimate. The ring is marked into the floor in ember line, wide enough for two people to stand apart and not wide enough for either to walk away mid-turn. Turns are strict, an interruption ends a turn, and the chamber judges on the weight of what was said rather than its volume. Duellists shake hands afterwards as a matter of form, sometimes while still furious. Ignivex treats a well-landed word here with the same respect it gives a clean strike in the Crucible Yard.

The Festival Kiln.name: The Festival Kiln
The Festival Kiln.basicInfo: The Festival Kiln is Ignivex's public celebration space: a massive civic ground built to handle controlled flame at scale. Festivals, flame dances, cooking competitions, firework displays, oath ceremonies and endurance games all happen here, drawing citizens from across the city. The Kiln is a single civic ground engineered to take controlled flame at scale: a vast central floor ringed by access ramps, stepped spectator terraces with heat shielding built into the seating, worked channels feeding the flame dance ring, elevated stands for the firework crews, and a sunken hollow at the edge where memorial burns are held apart from everything else. The construction is heavy and plain, dark stone and copper-bronze, and the ground stays warm long after an event has ended. Between events it is swept, checked and largely empty. When it fills, it fills from every district at once: families claiming terrace positions early, cooks setting up working lines, oath-takers waiting with their witnesses, mourners gathering at the hollow. The friction is the crowd and the calendar. The same ground also holds the memorial burns for Ignivex's dead.
The Festival Kiln.hiddenInfo: That double use is the Kiln's character rather than a contradiction — the city celebrates and grieves in one place, sometimes within the same week, and the transition between the two is handled by people who do it often. Emberwake is a citywide remembrance event, not a Kiln monopoly: controlled flames are lit across Ignivex for the dead, lost family, old battles, failed apprentices and past disasters, and the Emberwake Lighting Ground is only this district's part in it. The Cinder Run is likewise not owned here. It is an uncoursed route through heat-heavy districts, vent paths, forge roads, firebreak routes and public stairs, with no fixed start, finish, order or district sequence — the Endurance Ground serves the Kiln's endurance events generally and is not the Run's starting line, whatever competitors claim. Under standing Dravon pressure, a full Kiln is both a morale instrument and a very large gathering of civilians in one place, and both facts are understood.

The Kiln Floor.description: The vast central floor, engineered to take controlled flame at civic scale without damage, ringed by access ramps. Everything large happens on it. The floor is laid in heat-rated stone bedded deep, channel covers set flush into it and ramps rising to it from the terraces, and it is cleared and inspected before anything is lit. Crews mark out the evening's layout in the morning. Sound behaves oddly across a space this size, so callers work from set positions and the crowd learns where to stand in order to hear them. Empty, it feels disproportionate to the city; full, it makes complete sense, and citizens use that contrast to explain Ignivex to visitors.

The Flame Dance Ring.description: The ring where flame dances are performed, with worked channels feeding regulated fire that dancers move through and around. Performances draw dense crowds. Its boundary is raised just enough to read clearly from the terraces, and the cycle the fire runs on is fixed long before an event so that dancers can rehearse against it for weeks. Crews stand at the channel controls throughout with the authority to cut the feed, and they have used it, which the dancers accept without complaint. The dancers' timing is governed by the flame cycle rather than the music, which is why a mistimed step is instantly obvious to everyone watching.

The Great Heat Table Grounds.description: The grounds holding the Kiln's cooking competition, with long working lines and communal tables set beyond them. Cooks compete on heat handling as much as flavour. The grounds hold long working lines with geothermal cooking stations built into them and communal tables set out beyond, where everything produced is eaten by whoever is sitting at them. Competitors bring family recipes and firm opinions about heat rankings. Visiting merchants enter every year and are underestimated by nobody except themselves, because outsiders consistently misjudge what Ignivex means by hot. Spectators taste, judge loudly, and argue about the results for considerably longer than the competition itself lasts.

The Firework Stands.description: Elevated stands from which firework displays are prepared and launched over the Kiln, worked by crews who treat the schedule as sacred. Preparation takes far longer than the display. The stands are elevated platforms at the floor's edge, fenced, cleared and worked only by the crews who prepare them, with stock kept shielded and checked against a list before anything is loaded. Preparation runs for days and is visible from the terraces the whole time. Nobody but the crews is permitted on the stands during setup, a rule enforced politely and absolutely. Children sit along the terraces below during setup, which the crews pretend to find annoying.

The Oath Platform.description: A raised platform where oath ceremonies are spoken in front of witnesses, including the public commitments Ignivex civic life runs on. The wording is plain and the audience close. The platform is raised plain stone with room for the speaker, the witnesses and no one else, set close enough to the terraces that the front rows can read a face. Oaths are spoken in the taker's own words rather than from any set form. The Kiln's crews hold the platform clear beforehand, and a taker who arrives without witnesses is sent to find some rather than heard. An oath taken here is understood to be binding socially long before it is binding in any administrative sense.

The Endurance Ground.description: The Kiln's ground for endurance events generally, laid out for sustained heat trials and stamina competition. Competitors train for it year-round. The surface is marked into runs and stations, weighted equipment stored along the edges and medics posted where they can reach anyone who drops. Entrants are checked before they start and watched throughout. Heat adaptation makes these events possible without making them safe, and most years the medics withdraw competitors over the loud objections of the competitors themselves. It is not the start of the Cinder Run and never has been, though every year someone declares otherwise and is corrected by the crowd.

The Memorial Burn Hollow.description: A sunken hollow at the Kiln's edge where memorial burns are held for the city's dead, shielded from the main floor. Families stand close around the rim. The hollow is sunk below the Kiln's floor and screened from it, reached by a short flight of steps, with a worked basin at the centre and a rim where families stand close together. Nothing is amplified and nobody speaks from a platform. Attendance is by relationship rather than invitation, and people who did not know the dead stay up on the floor above. The hollow is quiet in a way the rest of the district never is, and the ground stays warm for a long time afterwards.

The Emberwake Lighting Ground.description: The Kiln's Emberwake ground, where controlled flames are lit for the dead, lost family, old battles, failed apprentices and past disasters. It is this district's part in a citywide remembrance, not the whole of it. The ground is a marked area kept clear for the lighting, with stands set out for the flames and space for the families who bring them. Preparation is communal and unhurried, and the crews do little more than keep the ground clear and the feeds safe. The Kiln's part of Emberwake is the largest single gathering of the night and not the important one, which is a thing citizens say to visitors and mean. Across Ignivex the same flames go up on the same night, in courtyards and doorways and forge floors.

The Spectator Terraces.description: Stepped terraces ringing the floor, built to hold a substantial share of the city at once, with heat shielding built into the seating. Crowds arrive early for the good positions. The terraces step up in heat-shielded stone with wide walkways behind each tier, water points along them and no assigned places, so position is a matter of arriving early and holding what has been claimed. Families spread along an entire tier. Food is carried in from outside, passed sideways down the row, and pressed on strangers who made the mistake of sitting beside somebody's grandmother. Terrace factions form around particular competitors and carry their loyalties from one festival to the next.

Genesis Compound.name: Genesis Compound
Genesis Compound.basicInfo:
The Genesis Compound is the seat of House Genesis, built partly into the cliff face above the Arena and visible from most of the city below. It is not a palace but a working facility: family residence, training center and administrative heart, finished in dark green, black and bronze-gold with storm-metal columns. Access belongs to House Genesis, its staff and invited guests. Corridors run back into the rock where the weather cannot reach them and out onto tribunal balconies where it does nothing else, and reinforced glass gives almost every room the same view of the combat floor below. Arrival is by rooftop landing pad through the restricted approach airspace, which visitors enter with permission or an escort and never at speed. The daily traffic is administrative before it is martial: staff carrying schedules, petitioners waiting on a ruling, suppliers delivering to the kitchens, crews costing out the next round of repairs to the training ground. Training spaces are built like working halls rather than showpieces, and the house treats visible strength as a civic obligation instead of a luxury. Genesis does not rule from a throne, and nothing here is arranged to suggest one. The compound sits where the ladder's standard is permanently in sight of everyone climbing toward it.

Work on offer here: House Genesis — Word for Word (ask Tacitus Genesis).
Genesis Compound.hiddenInfo: Korrvane is actually governed from a single office here. Tacitus handles minor-house disputes, Arena policy, infrastructure, Contair maintenance relationships, visitor problems and citywide emergencies from a desk that never clears, and the city works because he treats administration as seriously as combat. Ark's presence anchors the city's challenge culture but he does not manage daily rule, and the replacement scheduling for the training ground he keeps breaking is now a routine line item. The compound's deeper undercurrents are personal. Aela Castro cannot fight by meaningful Starian standards and is nonetheless central here, which is the clearest ongoing demonstration that Korrvane can recognize strength outside combat even when its instincts favor visible power. Her Castro ties run into a live rivalry that the house does not discuss casually. Old Dravon conflict resurfaces in the compound's records and in Sorvina's and Orvanus's memory, and challenger invitations issued from the Visitor Hall carry political weight that recipients rarely read correctly. Corvinus maintains the armory to a standard that assumes the next emergency is close.

Main Compound.description: The shared operational and residential center of House Genesis, where administration, family traffic and training schedules cross. Storm-metal columns frame corridors cut back into the cliff, and the drop to the Arena is visible through reinforced glass at every turn. Floors are heavy stone with bronze-black thresholds worn hollow at the busiest doorways, and the wind noise changes audibly whenever an outer door opens. Messengers arrive on the pads above, house staff move between the offices and the kitchens without ceremony, and a maintenance crew is almost always working somewhere in the building. Staff move through it constantly; it is a workplace before it is a symbol.

Ark’s Training Ground.description: A reinforced open training space engineered for Genesis-level force and rebuilt more often than anyone admits publicly. Ark breaks parts of it regularly, and replacement planning has become routine administration rather than a crisis. The floor is anchored stone plated with storm-metal where the loads concentrate, and the perimeter is set well back because the debris does not always stay inside it. Crews arrive with replacement sections on a standing schedule, quietly log what failed and how, and argue about which anchoring method will last longer this time. The surfacing carries layered repair seams like growth rings.

Tacitus’s Office.description: The room where Korrvane is genuinely governed. Minor-house disputes, Arena policy, infrastructure schedules, Contair maintenance relationships, visitor issues and citywide emergencies all land on this desk. It is plain, well used, and busier than anywhere else in the compound; petitioners wait in the corridor with their arguments rehearsed. The desk faces away from the view so the work gets done, and the wall behind it carries the current lane closures and repair schedules rather than anything commemorative. Contair complaints about impact damage arrive here, minor-house objections arrive here, and a house leader who wants something settled quietly discovers it will be settled in front of whoever is next in line.

Residential Quarters.description: Private family housing with enough space and structural reinforcement for Genesis residents who occasionally forget their own strength indoors. The rooms are lived in rather than ceremonial, full of personal clutter and repaired furniture. Doorframes are set into structural stone, the glass is the heavy kind used on the outer balconies, and more than one wall carries a patch that matches nothing around it. Meals get eaten at odd hours because the training and administrative schedules never agree, and the corridors carry arguments, laundry and the sound of someone else's early start. Nothing here is arranged to impress a visitor, because visitors do not come this far in.

The Armory.description: Functional Genesis equipment and combat gear maintained by Corvinus, organized for use rather than display. Everything on the racks is serviced, logged and expected to be taken out again. The room is cut back into the cliff, dry and cool, with storm-metal racking bolted through to the rock and a work counter where repairs are made rather than sent out. Corvinus checks returned gear himself, notes what failed and why, and has a standing opinion about the condition in which items come back to him. Nothing is arranged for effect, and the only ornament in the room is the wear on the tools. Corvinus keeps it to a standard that quietly assumes the next emergency is not far away.

Visitor Hall.description: A formal but comfortable meeting space overlooking the Arena and the city stacked below it. The view does the work a throne room would do elsewhere, stating Genesis position without anyone having to say it. Seating is arranged for conversation rather than audience, the glass runs floor to ceiling along the outer wall, and on bracket days the combat floor is close enough to follow without commentary. Guests arrive by escort through the restricted approach and are received without ceremony, which unsettles some of them more than ceremony would. Challenger invitations and political meetings both happen here, sometimes in the same afternoon.

Younger Member Training Court.description: A controlled court where younger Genesis members learn technique, restraint, public responsibility and what the ladder will expect of them. Instructors spend as much time on restraint as on force, because the family's mistakes are visible citywide. Lane discipline, challenge courtesy and the difference between a declared contest and a civic incident are taught here alongside stance and footwork, and a student who endangers someone loses the floor for the day. The court is enclosed on the cliff side and open to the drop on the other, which teaches its own lesson about where mistakes end up. Sessions end with a review of what would have looked bad from the Arena below.

Household Commons.description: The shared family space that carries meals, arguments, Aela's social presence, Orvanus's commentary and Zephyra's attempted improvements. It is also the site of the recurring mystery of Ark's missing food, which nobody has solved and several people have profited from. The room is warm, heavily furnished and repaired rather than replaced, with a long window onto the city and a kitchen loud enough to be heard from every seat. Conversation runs from bracket results to infrastructure complaints to whatever Orvanus has decided someone needs to hear, and Aela handles the house's gentle ribbing with a composure the rest of the family has learned to respect. The table seats more people than it was built for.

Genesis Embassy.name: Genesis Embassy
Genesis Embassy.basicInfo: The Genesis Embassy is House Genesis's compound on the Concourse, Korrvane's house presence in the capital, and a standing reminder that Castro dominance is stable but not unquestioned. It is physically imposing and unusually open, built around strength presented as service rather than luxury, with training courts for assigned representatives and defenders rather than public tournaments. It does not attempt to recreate the Korrvane Arena, and visitors expecting one are gently corrected. The compound occupies old ground and shows it: heavy Genesis-era footings and supports carry the current buildings, ancient star-metal stands exposed at the wall bases where later facing was deliberately stopped short, and old conduit channels run inside the modern lighting and muster systems. The palette is its own, dark structural stone and unpolished metal against the paler frontages nearby, and nothing about it has been softened to match the shared ground it faces. Corelight reaches the courts through the paving and the lane markings and moves with city routing, brightening as the work period opens and thinning through the maintenance window, which the drill schedule is written around. The public galleries and the court are free to enter, while the house pays for its own training staff, stores, residence and the standing readiness that makes its emergency role credible.
Genesis Embassy.hiddenInfo: Most of the embassy's real work is done by Tacitus while Ark's office stays maintained and largely empty, a protocol fiction the staff manage with practised diplomacy. The Emergency Muster Deck is genuinely operational: Genesis personnel assemble there during capitol emergencies, sometimes before the Republic has formally requested assistance, and that willingness to move first is admired by the public and watched carefully by the Protection Coordination Chamber. Inside the house there is an unresolved argument about whether a formal challenge is civic duty or personal pride, and young representatives arriving from Korrvane frequently treat Relstaris as if it operated by Korrvane rules, which the Formal Challenge Floor is partly designed to contain. Aela's Guest Residence connects Genesis and Castro family life in a way both houses value and neither wants examined politically, and the friendly Castro-Genesis rivalry produces more diplomatic anxiety in other compounds than open hostility would.

Genesis Embassy Court.description: The public entrance, framed by heavy structure and visible capability rather than ornament, with an open approach wide enough for a crowd. Visitors are met at the threshold, not screened at a distance. The court is meant to read as protection offered rather than force displayed. The paving is broad dark slab over much older footings, the base of the frontage original Genesis-era work left uncased where the newer facing stops.
